   `cupsd -c {{path/to/cupsd.conf}}`
5. Start `cupsd` using the specified `cups-files.conf` configuration file:
   `cupsd -s {{path/to/cups-files.conf}}`
6. [t]est the `cupsd.conf` [c]onfiguration file for errors:
   `cupsd -t -c {{path/to/cupsd.conf}}`
7. [t]est the `cups-files.conf` configuration file for errors:
   `cupsd -t -s {{path/to/cups-files.conf}}`
8. Display [h]elp:
   `cupsd -h`
cupsdisable:
**`cupsdisable`**: Stop printers and classes.

**Examples:**
1. Stop one or more destination(s):
   `cupsdisable {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
2. Cancel all jobs of the specified destination(s):
   `cupsdisable -c {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
cupsenable:
**`cupsenable`**: Start printers and classes.

**Examples:**
1. Start one or more destination(s):
   `cupsenable {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
2. Resume printing of pending jobs of a destination (use after `cupsdisable` with `--hold`):
   `cupsenable --release {{destination}}`
3. Cancel all jobs of the specified destination(s):
   `cupsenable -c {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
cupsreject:
**`cupsreject`**: Reject jobs sent to printers.

**Examples:**
1. Reject print jobs to the specified destinations:
   `cupsreject {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
2. Specify a different server:
   `cupsreject -h {{server}} {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
3. Specify a reason string ("Reason Unknown" by default):
   `cupsreject -r {{reason}} {{destination1 destination2 ...}}`
cupstestppd:
**`cupstestppd`**: Test conformance of PPD files to the version 4.3 of the specification.

**Examples:**
1. Test the conformance of one or more files in quiet mode:
   `cupstestppd -q {{path/to/file1.ppd path/to/file2.ppd ...}}`
2. Get the PPD file from `stdin`, showing detailed conformance testing results:
   `cupstestppd < {{path/to/file.ppd}} -v -`
3. Test all PPD files under the current directory, printing the names of each file that does not conform:
   `find . -name \*.ppd \! -execdir cupstestppd -q '{}' \; -print`
curl:
**`curl`**: Transfers data from or to a server.

**Examples:**
1. Make an HTTP GET request and dump the contents in `stdout`:
   `curl {{https://example.com}}`
2. Make an HTTP GET request, follow any `3xx` redirects, and dump the reply headers and contents to `stdout`:
   `curl {{[-L|--location]}} {{[-D|--dump-header]}} - {{https://example.com}}`
3. Download a file, saving the output under the filename indicated by the URL:
   `curl {{[-O|--remote-name]}} {{https://example.com/filename.zip}}`
4. Send form-encoded data (POST request of type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`). Use `--data @file_name` or `--data @'-'` to read from `stdin`:
   `curl {{[-X|--request]}} POST {{[-d|--data]}} '{{name=bob}}' {{http://example.com/form}}`
5. Send a request with an extra header, using a custom HTTP method and over a proxy (such as BurpSuite), ignoring insecure self-signed certificates:
   `curl {{[-k|--insecure]}} {{[-x|--proxy]}} {{http://127.0.0.1:8080}} {{[-H|--header]}} '{{Authorization: Bearer token}}' {{[-X|--request]}} {{GET|PUT|POST|DELETE|PATCH|...}} {{https://example.com}}`
6. Send data in JSON format, specifying the appropriate Content-Type header:

cut:
**`cut`**: Cut out fields from `stdin` or files.

**Examples:**

2. Print the fifth to tenth character of each line of the specified file:
   `cut {{[-c|--characters]}} 5-10 {{path/to/file}}`
3. Split each line in a file by a delimiter into fields and print fields two and six (default delimiter is `TAB`):
   `cut {{[-f|--fields]}} 2,6 {{path/to/file}}`
4. Split each line by the specified delimiter and print all from the second field onward:
   `{{command}} | cut {{[-d|--delimiter]}} "{{delimiter}}" {{[-f|--fields]}} 2-`
5. Use space as a delimiter and print only the first 3 fields:
   `{{command}} | cut {{[-d|--delimiter]}} " " {{[-f|--fields]}} -3`
6. Only print lines that contain the delimiter:
   `{{command}} | cut {{[-d|--delimiter]}} "{{:}}" {{[-f|--fields]}} {{1}} {{[-s|--only-delimited]}}`
7. Print specific fields of lines that use `NUL` to terminate lines instead of newlines:
   `{{find . -print0}} | cut {{[-z|--zero-terminated]}} {{[-d|--delimiter]}} "{{/}}" {{[-f|--fields]}} {{2}}`
cvs:

cwebp:
**`cwebp`**: Compress an image file to a WebP file.

   `cwebp {{path/to/image_file}} -o {{path/to/output.webp}}`

cython:

2. Start the Deluge daemon on a specific port:

3. Start the Deluge daemon using a specific configuration file:
   `deluged {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/configuration_file}}`
4. Start the Deluge daemon and output the log to a file:
   `deluged {{[-l|--logfile]}} {{path/to/log_file}}`
deno:
**`deno`**: A secure runtime for JavaScript, TypeScript, and WebAssembly.

**Examples:**
1. Start a REPL (interactive shell, also known as Read-Eval-Print Loop):
   `deno`
2. Start a new project named sample and test it:
   `deno init sample && cd sample && deno test`
3. Run a file securely. It will ask (if needed) to allow net, read, etc:
   `deno run {{path/to/file.ts}}`
4. Run a file with explicit permissions or allow all (only if you trust the source):
   `deno run {{[--allow-env|--allow-net|--allow-write|--allow-all]}} {{jsr:@deno/deployctl}}`
5. List and run tasks from `deno.json` or scripts from `package.json`:
   `deno task`
6. Install dependencies listed in `deno.json` or `package.json` (also lock files):
   `deno install`
7. Check types, format, and lint (fix if possible):
   `deno check && deno fmt && deno lint --fix`
8. Compile the script, imported dependencies, and runtime into a self contained executable:
   `deno compile {{path/to/file.ts}}`
dep:
**`dep`**: Deploy PHP applications.

**Examples:**
1. Interactively initialize deployer in the local path (use a framework template with `--template=template`):
   `dep init`
2. Deploy an application to a remote host:
   `dep deploy {{hostname}}`
3. Rollback to the previous working release:
   `dep rollback`
4. Connect to a remote host via SSH:
   `dep ssh {{hostname}}`
5. List commands:
   `dep list`
6. Run any arbitrary command on the remote hosts:
   `dep run "{{command}}"`
7. Display help for a command:
   `dep help {{command}}`
depotdownloader:
**`depotdownloader`**: Content/depot downloader for Steam.

**Examples:**
1. Download an app:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}}`
2. Download a specific depot into a custom output directory:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -depot {{108603}} -dir {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Download using a Steam account:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -depot {{108603}} -username "{{gabecube}}"`
4. Download a depot and remember the password for future downloads:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -depot {{108603}} -username "{{gabecube}}" -remember-password`
5. Download a specific depot manifest:
   `depotdownloader -app {{346110}} -depot {{346111}} -manifest {{6154025194991279746}}`
6. Download from a specific branch:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -depot {{108603}} -branch "{{unstable}}"`
7. Download only the internal manifest excluding content:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -depot {{108603}} -manifest-only`
8. Download workshop content using the pubfile/workshop id:
   `depotdownloader -app {{108600}} -pubfile {{2503622437}}`
detox:
**`detox`**: Renames files to make them easier to work with.

**Examples:**
1. Remove spaces and other undesirable characters from a file's name:
   `detox {{path/to/file}}`
2. Show how detox would rename all the files in a directory tree:
   `detox {{[-n|--dry-run]}} -r {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Remove spaces and other undesirable characters from all files in a directory tree:
   `detox -r {{path/to/directory}}`
devcontainer:
**`devcontainer`**: Use a Docker container as a development environment.

**Examples:**
1. Create and run a Dev Container:
   `devcontainer up`
2. Apply a Dev Container Template to a workspace:
   `devcontainer templates apply {{[-t|--template-id]}} {{template_id}} {{[-a|--template-args]}} {{template_args}} {{[-w|--workspace-folder]}} {{path/to/workspace}}`
3. Execute a command on a running Dev Container in the current workspace:
   `devcontainer exec {{command}}`
4. Build a Dev Container image from `devcontainer.json`:
   `devcontainer build {{path/to/workspace}}`
5. Read and print the configuration of a Dev Container from `devcontainer.json`:
   `devcontainer read-configuration`
devenv:
**`devenv`**: Fast, declarative, reproducible, and composable developer environments using Nix.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize the environment:
   `devenv init`
2. Enter the Development Environment with relaxed hermeticity (state of being airtight):
   `devenv shell --impure`
3. Get detailed information about the current environment:
   `devenv info --verbose`
4. Start processes with `devenv`:
   `devenv up --config {{path/to/file}}`
5. Clean the environment variables and re-enter the shell in offline mode:
   `devenv --clean --offline`
6. Delete the previous shell generations:
   `devenv gc`
devpod:
**`devpod`**: Launch reproducible development environments using Docker, Kubernetes, or SSH.

**Examples:**
1. Add a provider such as Docker or Kubernetes:
   `devpod provider add {{provider_name}}`
2. List all available providers:
   `devpod provider list-available`
3. Start a workspace from a GitHub repository with a specific IDE:
   `devpod up {{github.com/user/repo}} {{[-i|--ide]}} {{vscode}}`
4. Start a workspace from a local directory:
   `devpod up {{path/to/project}}`
5. Recreate an existing workspace:
   `devpod up {{workspace_name}} {{[-r|--recreate]}}`
6. Reset a workspace to a clean state:
   `devpod up {{workspace_name}} {{[-x|--reset]}}`
7. Add a custom provider from a GitHub repository:
   `devpod provider add {{org/provider-repo}}`
devspace:
**`devspace`**: Develop, deploy, and debug applications inside Kubernetes.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize a new DevSpace project in the current directory:
   `devspace init`
2. Start development mode with port forwarding, file synchronization, and terminal access:
   `devspace dev`
3. Start development mode in a specific namespace:
   `devspace dev {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}}`
4. Deploy the project to Kubernetes:
   `devspace deploy`
5. Deploy the project with a specific profile:
   `devspace deploy {{[-p|--profile]}} {{profile-name}}`
6. Build all defined images:
   `devspace build`
7. Follow logs from a pod:
   `devspace logs {{[-f|--follow]}}`
8. Open the DevSpace UI in the browser:
   `devspace ui`
dexdump:
**`dexdump`**: Display information about Android DEX files.

**Examples:**
1. Extract classes and methods from an APK file:
   `dexdump {{path/to/file}}.apk`
2. Display header information of DEX files contained in an APK file:
   `dexdump -f {{path/to/file}}.apk`
3. Display the dis-assembled output of executable sections:
   `dexdump -d {{path/to/file}}.apk`
4. Output results to a file:
   `dexdump -o {{path/to/file}} {{path/to/file}}.apk`
dexter:
**`dexter`**: Authenticate the `kubectl` users with OpenId Connect.

**Examples:**
1. Create and authenticate a user with Google OIDC:
   `dexter auth {{[-i|--client-id]}} {{client_id}} {{[-s|--client-secret]}} {{client_secret}}`
2. Override the default kube configuration file location:
   `dexter auth {{[-i|--client-id]}} {{client_id}} {{[-s|--client-secret]}} {{client_secret}} {{[-k|--kube-config]}} {{sample/config}}`
df:
**`df`**: Display an overview of the filesystem disk space usage.

**Examples:**
1. Display all filesystems and their disk usage:
   `df`
2. Display all filesystems in human-readable form:
   `df {{[-h|--human-readable]}}`
3. Display the filesystem containing the specified file or directory:
   `df {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
4. Include statistics on the number of free inodes:
   `df {{[-i|--inodes]}}`
5. Display filesystems but exclude the specified types:
   `df {{[-x|--exclude-type]}} {{squashfs}} {{[-x|--exclude-type]}} {{tmpfs}}`
6. Display filesystem types:
   `df {{[-T|--print-type]}}`
dfc:
**`dfc`**: Get an overview of the filesystem disk space usage with colors and graphs.

**Examples:**
1. Display filesystems and their disk usage in human-readable form with colors and graphs:
   `dfc`
2. Display all filesystems including pseudo, duplicate, and inaccessible filesystems:
   `dfc -a`
3. Display filesystems without color:
   `dfc -c never`
4. Display filesystems containing "ext" in the filesystem type:
   `dfc -t ext`
dhclient:
**`dhclient`**: DHCP client.

**Examples:**
1. Get an IP address for the `eth0` interface:
   `sudo dhclient {{eth0}}`
2. Release an IP address for the `eth0` interface:
   `sudo dhclient -r {{eth0}}`
dhcpig:
**`dhcpig`**: Initiates an advanced DHCP exhaustion attack and stress test.

**Examples:**
1. Exhaust all of the available DHCP addresses using the specified interface:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{eth0}}`
2. Exhaust IPv6 addresses using eth1 interface:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-6|--ipv6]}} {{eth1}}`
3. Send fuzzed/malformed data packets using the interface:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-f|--fuzz]}} {{eth1}}`
4. Enable color output:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-c|--color]}} {{eth1}}`
5. Enable minimal verbosity and color output:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-c|--color]}} {{[-v|--verbosity]}} 1 {{eth1}}`
6. Use a debug verbosity of 100 and scan network of neighboring devices using ARP packets:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-c|--color]}} {{[-v|--verbosity]}} 100 {{[-n|--neighbors-scan-arp]}} {{eth1}}`
7. Enable printing lease information, attempt to scan and release all neighbor IP addresses:
   `sudo {{path/to}}/pig.py {{[-n|--neighbors-scan-arp]}} {{[-r|--neighbors-attack-release]}} {{[-o|--show-options]}} {{eth1}}`
dhcpwn:
**`dhcpwn`**: Test DHCP IP exhaustion attacks and sniff local DHCP traffic.

**Examples:**
1. Flood the network with IP requests:
   `dhcpwn {{[-i|--interface]}} {{network_interface}} flood {{[-c|--count]}} {{number_of_requests}}`
2. Sniff local DHCP traffic:
   `dhcpwn {{[-i|--interface]}} {{network_interface}} sniff`
dict:
**`dict`**: Dictionary that uses the DICT protocol.

**Examples:**
1. List available databases:
   `dict {{[-D|--dbs]}}`
2. Get information about a database:
   `dict {{[-i|--info]}} {{database_name}}`
3. Look up a word in a specific database:
   `dict {{[-d|--database]}} {{database_name}} {{word}}`
4. Look up a word in all available databases:
   `dict {{word}}`
5. Show information about the DICT server:
   `dict {{[-I|--serverinfo]}}`
diff-pdf:
**`diff-pdf`**: Compare two PDFs.

**Examples:**
1. Compare PDFs, indicating changes using return codes (`0` = no difference, `1` = PDFs differ):
   `diff-pdf {{path/to/a.pdf}} {{path/to/b.pdf}}`
2. Compare PDFs, outputting a PDF with visually highlighted differences:
   `diff-pdf --output-diff={{path/to/diff.pdf}} {{path/to/a.pdf}} {{path/to/b.pdf}}`
3. Compare PDFs, viewing differences in a simple GUI:
   `diff-pdf --view {{path/to/a.pdf}} {{path/to/b.pdf}}`
diff-so-fancy:
**`diff-so-fancy`**: Colorize `diff` output in a more human readable way.

**Examples:**
1. Colorize `diff`:
   `diff {{[-u|--unified]}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}} | diff-so-fancy`
2. Set `diff-so-fancy` to colorize the output during Git's interactive staging:
   `git config --global interactive.diffFilter "diff-so-fancy --patch"`
diff:
**`diff`**: Compare files and directories.

**Examples:**
1. Compare files (lists changes to turn `old_file` into `new_file`):
   `diff {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}}`
2. Compare files, ignoring white spaces:
   `diff {{[-w|--ignore-all-space]}} {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}}`
3. Compare files, showing the differences side by side:
   `diff {{[-y|--side-by-side]}} {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}}`
4. Compare files, showing the differences in unified format (as used by `git diff`):
   `diff {{[-u|--unified]}} {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}}`
5. Compare directories recursively (shows names for differing files/directories as well as changes made to files):
   `diff {{[-r|--recursive]}} {{path/to/old_directory}} {{path/to/new_directory}}`
6. Compare directories, only showing the names of files that differ:
   `diff {{[-r|--recursive]}} {{[-q|--brief]}} {{path/to/old_directory}} {{path/to/new_directory}}`
7. Create a patch file for Git from the differences of two text files, treating nonexistent files as empty:
   `diff {{[-a|--text]}} {{[-u|--unified]}} {{[-N|--new-file]}} {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}} > {{path/to/diff.patch}}`
8. Compare files, showing output in color, trying hard to find the smallest set of changes:
   `diff {{[-d|--minimal]}} --color=always {{path/to/old_file}} {{path/to/new_file}}`
diffimg:
**`diffimg`**: Calculate intersection between two images.

**Examples:**
1. Calculate the intersection between images and output an image where each pixel is the difference between corresponding pixels in input images:
   `diffimg {{path/to/input_image1.ext}} {{path/to/input_image2.ext}} {{path/to/output_image.ext}}`
diffoscope:
**`diffoscope`**: Compare files, archives, and directories.

**Examples:**
1. Compare two files:
   `diffoscope {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
2. Compare two files without displaying a progress bar:
   `diffoscope --no-progress {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
3. Compare two files and write an HTML-report to a file (use `-` for `stdout`):
   `diffoscope --html {{path/to/outfile|-}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
4. Compare two directories excluding files with a name matching a specified pattern:
   `diffoscope --exclude {{pattern}} {{path/to/directory1}} {{path/to/directory2}}`
5. Compare two directories and control whether directory metadata is considered:
   `diffoscope --exclude-directory-metadata {{auto|yes|no|recursive}} {{path/to/directory1}} {{path/to/directory2}}`
diffstat:
**`diffstat`**: Create a histogram from the output of the `diff` command.

**Examples:**
1. Display changes in a histogram:
   `diff {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}} | diffstat`
2. Display inserted, deleted, and modified changes as a table:
   `diff {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}} | diffstat -t`
difft:
**`difft`**: Compare files or directories based on the syntax of the programming language.

**Examples:**
1. Compare two files or directories:
   `difft {{path/to/file_or_directory1}} {{path/to/file_or_directory2}}`
2. Only report the presence of differences between the files:
   `difft --check-only {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
3. Specify the display mode (default is `side-by-side`):
   `difft --display {{side-by-side|side-by-side-show-both|inline|json}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
4. Ignore comments when comparing:
   `difft --ignore-comments {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
5. Enable/Disable syntax highlighting of source code (default is `on`):
   `difft --syntax-highlight {{on|off}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
6. Do not output anything at all if there are no differences between files:
   `difft --skip-unchanged {{path/to/file_or_directory1}} {{path/to/file_or_directory2}}`
7. Print all programming languages supported by the tool, along with their extensions:
   `difft --list-languages`
dig:
**`dig`**: DNS lookup utility.

**Examples:**
1. Lookup the IP(s) associated with a hostname (A records):
   `dig +short {{example.com}}`
2. Get a detailed answer for a given domain (A records):
   `dig +noall +answer {{example.com}}`
3. Query a specific DNS record type associated with a given domain name:
   `dig +short {{example.com}} {{A|MX|TXT|CNAME|NS}}`
4. Specify an alternate DNS server to query and optionally use DNS over TLS (DoT):
   `dig {{+tls}} @{{1.1.1.1|8.8.8.8|9.9.9.9|...}} {{example.com}}`
5. Perform a reverse DNS lookup on an IP address (PTR record):
   `dig -x {{8.8.8.8}}`
6. Find authoritative name servers for the zone and display SOA records:
   `dig +nssearch {{example.com}}`
7. Perform iterative queries and display the entire trace path to resolve a domain name:
   `dig +trace {{example.com}}`
8. Query a DNS server over a non-standard [p]ort using the TCP protocol:
   `dig +tcp -p {{port}} @{{dns_server_ip}} {{example.com}}`
dijkstra:
**`dijkstra`**: Compute shortest-path distances from a single source node in a graph.

**Examples:**
1. Compute distances from a given source node in a graph file:
   `dijkstra {{source_node_file}}`
2. Treat the graph as [d]irected when computing distances:
   `dijkstra -d {{source_node_file}}`
3. Record the [p]revious closest node for each node on the shortest path:
   `dijkstra -p {{source_node_file}}`
4. [a]ssign large distance values to unreachable nodes:
   `dijkstra -a {{source_node_file}}`
dillo:
**`dillo`**: A lightweight web browser intended for slow computers.

**Examples:**
1. Launch Dillo:
   `dillo`
2. Launch Dillo with a specific window size and screen location:
   `dillo {{[-g|--geometry]}} {{width}}x{{height}}+{{x_position}}+{{y_position}}`
3. Launch Dillo and open a specific URL:
   `dillo {{duckduckgo.com}}`
4. Launch Dillo and open a file or directory:
   `dillo {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
5. Launch Dillo in full-screen mode:
   `dillo {{[-f|--fullwindow]}}`
6. Display help:
   `dillo {{[-h|--help]}}`
7. Display version:
   `dillo {{[-v|--version]}}`
dircolors:
**`dircolors`**: Output commands to set the `$LS_COLOR` environment variable and style `ls`, `dir`, etc.

**Examples:**
1. Output commands to set `$LS_COLOR` using default colors:
   `dircolors`
2. Display each filetype with the color they would appear in `ls`:
   `dircolors --print-ls-colors`
3. Output commands to set `$LS_COLOR` using colors from a file:
   `dircolors {{path/to/file}}`
4. Output commands for Bourne shell:
   `dircolors {{[-b|--bourne-shell]}}`
5. Output commands for C shell:
   `dircolors {{[-c|--c-shell]}}`
6. View the default colors for file types and extensions:
   `dircolors {{[-p|--print-database]}}`
direnv:
**`direnv`**: Shell extension to load and unload environment variables depending on the current directory.

**Examples:**
1. Grant direnv permission to load the `.envrc` present in the current directory:
   `direnv allow {{.}}`
2. Revoke the authorization to load the `.envrc` present in the current directory:
   `direnv deny {{.}}`
3. Edit the `.envrc` file in the default text editor and reload the environment on exit:
   `direnv edit {{.}}`
4. Trigger a reload of the environment:
   `direnv reload`
5. Print some debug status information:
   `direnv status`
dirname:
**`dirname`**: Remove trailing filename portion from a path.

**Examples:**
1. Calculate the parent directory of a given path:
   `dirname {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
2. Calculate the parent directory of multiple paths:
   `dirname {{path/to/file_or_directory1 path/to/file_or_directory2 ...}}`
3. Delimit output with a NUL character instead of a newline (useful when combining with `xargs`):
   `dirname {{[-z|--zero]}} {{path/to/file_or_directory1 path/to/file_or_directory2 ...}}`
dirs:
**`dirs`**: Display or manipulate the directory stack.

**Examples:**
1. Display the directory stack with a space between each entry:
   `dirs`
2. Display the directory stack with one entry per line:
   `dirs -p`
3. Display a numbered list of entries in the directory stack:
   `dirs -v`
4. Display the directory stack without the tilde-prefix (`~`):
   `dirs -l`
5. Display only the `n`th entry in the directory stack, starting at 0 (Bash only):
   `dirs +{{n}}`
6. Display only the `n`th entry in the directory stack from the last, starting at 0 (Bash only):
   `dirs -{{n}}`
7. Clear the directory stack:
   `dirs -c`
dirsearch:
**`dirsearch`**: Web path scanner.

**Examples:**
1. Scan a web server for common paths with common extensions:
   `dirsearch {{[-u|--url]}} {{url}} --extensions-list`
2. Scan a list of web servers for common paths with given file extensions:
   `dirsearch {{[-l|--url-list]}} {{path/to/url-list.txt}} {{[-e|--extensions]}} {{php,jsp,aspx,...}}`
3. Scan a web server for user-defined paths with common extensions:
   `dirsearch {{[-u|--url]}} {{url}} --extensions-list {{[-w|--wordlists]}} {{path/to/url-paths1.txt,path/to/url-paths2.txt,...}}`
4. Scan a web server using a cookie:
   `dirsearch {{[-u|--url]}} {{url}} {{[-e|--extensions]}} {{php}} --cookie {{cookie}}`
5. Scan a web server using the `HEAD` HTTP method:
   `dirsearch {{[-u|--url]}} {{url}} {{[-e|--extensions]}} {{php}} {{[-m|--http-method]}} {{HEAD}}`
6. Scan a web server, saving the results to a `.json` file:
   `dirsearch {{[-u|--url]}} {{url}} {{[-e|--extensions]}} {{php}} --json-report {{path/to/report.json}}`
disable:
**`disable`**: Disable built-in shell commands in Zsh.

**Examples:**
1. Disable command:
   `disable {{command1 command2 ...}}`
2. List all disabled commands:
   `disable`
diskonaut:
**`diskonaut`**: Terminal disk space navigator, written in Rust.

**Examples:**
1. Start `diskonaut` in the current directory:
   `diskonaut`
2. Start `diskonaut` in a specific directory:
   `diskonaut {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Show file sizes rather than their block usage on the disk:
   `diskonaut --apparent-size {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Disable deletion confirmation:
   `diskonaut --disable-delete-confirmation`
disown:
**`disown`**: Allow sub-processes to live beyond the shell that they are attached to.

**Examples:**
1. Disown the current job:
   `disown`
2. Disown a specific job (run `jobs` to find the job number):
   `disown %{{job_number}}`
3. Disown all jobs (Bash only):
   `disown -a`
4. Keep job (do not disown it), but mark it so that no future SIGHUP is received on shell exit (Bash only):
   `disown -h %{{job_number}}`
distcc:
**`distcc`**: Distributed C/C++/ObjC compilation client that works with `distccd`.

**Examples:**
1. Compile a source file using a compiler like `gcc`:
   `distcc {{gcc}} -c {{path/to/source.c}} -o {{path/to/output.o}}`
2. Set remote hosts to distribute compilation:
   `export DISTCC_HOSTS="localhost {{ip1 ip2 ...}}"`
3. Compile a project with `make` using `distcc`:
   `make {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{parallel_jobs}} CC="distcc {{gcc}}"`
4. Show the list of current `distcc` hosts:
   `distcc --show-hosts`
5. Display help:
   `distcc --help`
6. Display version:
   `distcc --version`
distccd:
**`distccd`**: Server daemon for the distcc distributed compiler.

**Examples:**
1. Start a daemon with the default settings:
   `distccd --daemon`
2. Start a daemon, accepting connections from IPv4 private network ranges:
   `distccd --daemon --allow-private`
3. Start a daemon, accepting connections from a specific network address or address range:
   `distccd --daemon {{[-a|--allow]}} {{ip_address|network_prefix}}`
4. Start a daemon with a lowered priority that can run a maximum of 4 tasks at a time:
   `distccd --daemon {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{4}} {{[-N|--nice]}} {{5}}`
5. Start a daemon and register it via mDNS/DNS-SD (Zeroconf):
   `distccd --daemon --zeroconf`
dive:
**`dive`**: Explore a Docker image, layer contents, and discover ways to shrink it.

**Examples:**
1. Analyze a Docker image:
   `dive {{your_image_tag}}`
2. Build an image and start analyzing it:
   `dive build -t {{some_tag}}`
django-admin:
**`django-admin`**: Django's utility for administrative tasks.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new Django project:
   `django-admin startproject {{project_name}}`
2. Create a new app for the current project:
   `django-admin startapp {{app_name}}`
3. Display help for a specific command:
   `django-admin help {{command}}`
4. Display version:
   `django-admin --version`
djxl:
**`djxl`**: Decompress JPEG XL images.

**Examples:**
1. Decompress a JPEG XL image to another format:
   `djxl {{path/to/image.jxl}} {{path/to/output.ext}}`
2. Display an extremely detailed help:
   `djxl {{[-h -v -v -v -v|--help --verbose --verbose --verbose --verbose]}}`
dlv:
**`dlv`**: Debugger for the Go programming language.

**Examples:**
1. Compile and begin debugging the main package in the current directory (by default, with no arguments):
   `dlv debug`
2. Compile and begin debugging a specific package:
   `dlv debug {{package}} {{arguments}}`
3. Compile a test binary and begin debugging the compiled program:
   `dlv test`
4. Connect to a headless debug server:
   `dlv connect {{ip_address}}`
5. Attach to a running process and begin debugging:
   `dlv attach {{pid}}`
6. Compile and begin tracing a program:
   `dlv trace {{package}} --regexp '{{regex}}'`
dmd:

dnswalk:
**`dnswalk`**: DNS debugger.

**Examples:**

dnsx:
**`dnsx`**: A fast and multi-purpose DNS toolkit to run multiple DNS queries.

**Examples:**
1. Query the A record of a (sub)domain and show [re]sponse received:
   `echo {{example.com}} | dnsx -a {{[-re|-resp]}}`
2. Query all the DNS records (A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, TXT, SRV, PTR, MX, SOA, AXFR, CAA):
   `dnsx <<< {{example.com}} -recon {{[-re|-resp]}}`
3. Query a specific type of DNS record:
   `echo {{example.com}} | dnsx {{[-re|-resp]}} -{{a|aaaa|cname|ns|txt|srv|ptr|mx|soa|any|axfr|caa}}`
4. Output response only (do not show the queried domain or subdomain):
   `echo {{example.com}} | dnsx {{[-ro|-resp-only]}}`
5. Display raw response of a query, specifying resolvers to use and retry attempts for failures:
   `echo {{example.com}} | dnsx -{{debug|raw}} {{[-r|-resolver]}} {{1.1.1.1,8.8.8.8,...}} -retry {{number}}`
6. Brute force DNS records using a placeholder:
   `dnsx {{[-d|-domain]}} {{FUZZ.example.com}} {{[-w|-wordlist]}} {{path/to/wordlist.txt}} {{[-re|-resp]}}`
7. Brute force DNS records from a list of domains and wordlists, appending output to a file with no color codes:
   `dnsx {{[-d|-domain]}} {{path/to/domain.txt}} {{[-w|-wordlist]}} {{path/to/wordlist.txt}} {{[-re|-resp]}} {{[-o|-output]}} {{path/to/output.txt}} {{[-nc|-no-color]}}`
8. Extract `CNAME` records for the given list of subdomains, with rate limiting DNS queries per second:
   `subfinder -silent {{[-d|-domain]}} {{example.com}} | dnsx -cname {{[-re|-resp]}} {{[-rl|-rate-limit]}} {{number}}`
do:

doas:

dockdiver:
**`dockdiver`**: A tool for interacting with Docker registries, including listing and dumping repositories.

docker-buildx-prune:

   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{command}} {{[-t|--access-token]}} {{access_token}}`
2. Retrieve details about a database user:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[g|get]}} {{database_id}} {{user_name}}`
3. Retrieve a list of database users for a given database:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[ls|list]}} {{database_id}}`
4. Reset the auth password for a given user:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[rs|reset]}} {{database id}} {{user_name}}`
5. Reset the MySQL auth plugn for a given user:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[rs|reset]}} {{database_id}} {{user_name}} {{caching_sha2_password|mysql_native_password}}`
6. Create a user in the given database with a given username:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[c|create]}} {{database_id}} {{user_name}}`
7. Delete a user from the given database with the given username:
   `doctl {{[d|databases]}} {{[u|user]}} {{[rm|delete]}} {{database_id}} {{user_name}}`
doctl-databases:

doctl-kubernetes-options:

doctl-serverless:

doctum:

dog:
**`dog`**: DNS lookup utility.

1. Lookup the IP(s) associated with a hostname (A records):
   `dog {{example.com}}`
2. Query the MX records type associated with a given domain name:

doggo:

   `doggo {{example.com}} {{[-J|--json]}} | jq '{{.responses[0].answers[].address}}'`

   `doggo {{[-x|--reverse]}} {{8.8.4.4}} --short`
dokku:

dolt-add:
**`dolt-add`**: Add the contents of a table to the list of Dolt staged tables.

**Examples:**
1. Add a table to the list of staged tables (stage a table):
   `dolt add {{table}}`
2. Stage all tables:
   `dolt add {{[-A|--all]}}`
dolt-blame:
**`dolt-blame`**: Display commit information for each row of a Dolt table.

**Examples:**
1. Display the latest commit for each row of a table:
   `dolt blame {{table}}`
2. Display the latest commits for each row of a table when the specified commit was made:
   `dolt blame {{commit}} {{table}}`
3. Display help:
   `dolt blame --help`
dolt-branch:
**`dolt-branch`**: Manage Dolt branches.

**Examples:**
1. List local branches (current branch is highlighted by `*`):
   `dolt branch`
2. List all local and remote branches:
   `dolt branch {{[-A|--all]}}`
3. Create a new branch based on the current branch:
   `dolt branch {{branch_name}}`
4. Create a new branch with the specified commit as the latest:
   `dolt branch {{branch_name}} {{commit}}`
5. Rename a branch:

6. Duplicate a branch:

7. Delete a branch:

8. Display the name of the current branch:

dolt-checkout:
**`dolt-checkout`**: Checkout the work tree or tables to a branch or commit.

**Examples:**
1. Switch to a branch:
   `dolt checkout {{branch_name}}`
2. Revert unstaged changes to a table:
   `dolt checkout {{table}}`
3. Create new branch and switch to it:
   `dolt checkout -b {{branch_name}}`
4. Create new branch based on a specified commit and switch to it:
   `dolt checkout -b {{branch_name}} {{commit}}`
dolt-clone:
**`dolt-clone`**: Clone a repository into a new directory.

**Examples:**
1. Clone an existing repository into a specific directory (defaults to the repository name):
   `dolt clone {{repository_url}} {{path/to/directory}}`
2. Clone an existing repository and add a specific remote (defaults to origin):

3. Clone an existing repository only fetching a specific branch (defaults to all branches):

5. Clone a repository, using an AWS credentials file:
   `dolt clone --aws-creds-file {{credentials_file}} {{repository_url}}`
6. Clone a repository, using an AWS credentials profile (uses the default profile if none is provided):
   `dolt clone --aws-creds-profile {{profile_name}} {{repository_url}}`
7. Clone a repository, using an AWS credentials type:
   `dolt clone --aws-creds-type {{credentials_type}} {{repository_url}}`
dolt-commit:
**`dolt-commit`**: Commit staged changes to tables.

**Examples:**
1. Commit all staged changes, opening the editor specified by `$EDITOR` to enter the commit message:
   `dolt commit`
2. Commit all staged changes with the specified message:
   `dolt commit {{[-m|--message]}} "{{commit_message}}"`
3. Stage all unstaged changes to tables before committing:
   `dolt commit {{[-a|--all]}}`
4. Use the specified ISO 8601 commit date (defaults to current date and time):
   `dolt commit --date "{{2021-12-31T00:00:00}}"`
5. Use the specified author for the commit:
   `dolt commit --author "{{author_name}} <{{author_email}}>"`
6. Allow creating an empty commit, with no changes:
   `dolt commit --allow-empty`
7. Ignore foreign key warnings:
   `dolt commit {{[-f|--force]}}`
dolt-config:
**`dolt-config`**: Read and write local (per repository) and global (per user) Dolt configuration variables.

**Examples:**
1. List all local and global configuration options and their values:
   `dolt config --list`
2. Display the value of a local or global configuration variable:
   `dolt config --get {{name}}`
3. Modify the value of a local configuration variable, creating it if it doesn't exist:
   `dolt config --add {{name}} {{value}}`
4. Modify the value of a global configuration variable, creating it if it doesn't exist:
   `dolt config --global --add {{name}} {{value}}`
5. Delete a local configuration variable:
   `dolt config --unset {{name}}`
6. Delete a global configuration variable:
   `dolt config --global --unset {{name}}`
dolt-fetch:
**`dolt-fetch`**: Download objects and refs from another repository.

**Examples:**
1. Fetch the latest changes from the default remote upstream repository (origin):
   `dolt fetch`
2. Fetch latest changes from a specific remote upstream repository:
   `dolt fetch {{remote_name}}`
3. Update branches with the current state of the remote, overwriting any conflicting history:
   `dolt fetch -f`
dolt-gc:
**`dolt-gc`**: Search the repository for data that are no longer referenced and no longer needed.

**Examples:**
1. Clean up unreferenced data from the repository:
   `dolt gc`
2. Initiate a faster but less thorough garbage collection process:
   `dolt gc {{[-s|--shallow]}}`
dolt-init:
**`dolt-init`**: Create an empty Dolt data repository.

dolt-merge:
**`dolt-merge`**: Join two or more development histories together.

   `dolt merge {{branch_name}}`

   `dolt merge --squash {{branch_name}}`
3. Merge a branch and create a merge commit even when the merge resolves as a fast-forward:
   `dolt merge --no-ff {{branch_name}}`

5. Abort the current conflict resolution process:
   `dolt merge --abort`
dolt-sql:

**Examples:**

dolt-status:

1. Display the status:

dolt-version:

dolt:

doom:

doppler-projects:

doppler-secrets:

dosbox:

dot:

dotenvx:

dotnet-add-package:
**`dotnet-add-package`**: Add or update a .NET package reference in a project file.

dotnet-add-reference:
**`dotnet-add-reference`**: Add .NET project-to-project references.

1. Add a reference to the project in the current directory:

   `dotnet add {{path/to/project.csproj}} reference {{path/to/reference1.csproj path/to/reference2.csproj ...}}`
dotnet-build:
**`dotnet-build`**: Builds a .NET application and its dependencies.

**Examples:**
1. Compile the project or solution in the current directory:
   `dotnet build`
2. Compile a .NET project or solution in debug mode:

7. Specify the output directory:

dotnet-ef:
**`dotnet-ef`**: Perform design-time development tasks for Entity Framework Core.

**Examples:**
1. Update the database to a specified migration:
   `dotnet ef database update {{migration}}`
2. Drop the database:
   `dotnet ef database drop`
3. List available `DbContext` types:
   `dotnet ef dbcontext list`
4. Generate code for a `DbContext` and entity types for a database:
   `dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold {{connection_string}} {{provider}}`
5. Add a new migration:
   `dotnet ef migrations add {{name}}`
6. Remove the last migration, rolling back the code changes that were done for the latest migration:
   `dotnet ef migrations remove`
7. List available migrations:
   `dotnet ef migrations list`
8. Generate an SQL script from migrations range:
   `dotnet ef migrations script {{from_migration}} {{to_migration}}`
dotnet-publish:
**`dotnet-publish`**: Publish a .NET application and its dependencies to a directory for deployment to a hosting system.

**Examples:**
1. Compile a .NET project in release mode:
   `dotnet publish {{[-c|--configuration]}} Release {{path/to/project_file}}`
2. Publish the .NET Core runtime with your application for the specified runtime:
   `dotnet publish {{[-sc|--self-contained]}} true {{[-r|--runtime]}} {{runtime_identifier}} {{path/to/project_file}}`
3. Package the application into a platform-specific single-file executable:
   `dotnet publish {{[-r|--runtime]}} {{runtime_identifier}} -p:PublishSingleFile=true {{path/to/project_file}}`
4. Trim unused libraries to reduce the deployment size of an application:
   `dotnet publish {{[-sc|--self-contained]}} true {{[-r|--runtime]}} {{runtime_identifier}} -p:PublishTrimmed=true {{path/to/project_file}}`
5. Compile a .NET project without restoring dependencies:
   `dotnet publish --no-restore {{path/to/project_file}}`
6. Specify the output directory:

dotnet-restore:
**`dotnet-restore`**: Restores the dependencies and tools of a .NET project.

**Examples:**
1. Restore dependencies for a .NET project or solution in the current directory:
   `dotnet restore`
2. Restore dependencies for a .NET project or solution in a specific location:
   `dotnet restore {{path/to/project_or_solution}}`
3. Restore dependencies without caching the HTTP requests:
   `dotnet restore --no-http-cache`
4. Force all dependencies to be resolved even if the last restore was successful:
   `dotnet restore --force`
5. Restore dependencies using package source failures as warnings:
   `dotnet restore --ignore-failed-sources`
6. Restore dependencies with a specific verbosity level:
   `dotnet restore {{[-v|--verbosity]}} {{quiet|minimal|normal|detailed|diagnostic}}`
dotnet-run:
**`dotnet-run`**: Run a .NET application without explicit compile or launch commands.

**Examples:**
1. Run the project in the current directory:
   `dotnet run`
2. Run a specific project:
   `dotnet run --project {{path/to/file.csproj}}`
3. Run the project with specific arguments:
   `dotnet run -- {{arg1=foo arg2=bar ...}}`
4. Run the project using a target framework moniker:
   `dotnet run {{[-f|--framework]}} {{net7.0}}`
5. Specify architecture and OS, available since .NET 6 (Don't use `--runtime` with these options):
   `dotnet run {{[-a|--arch]}} {{x86|x64|arm|arm64}} --os {{win|win7|osx|linux|ios|android}}`
dotnet-test:
**`dotnet-test`**: Execute tests for a .NET application.

**Examples:**
1. Execute tests for a .NET project/solution in the current directory:
   `dotnet test`
2. Execute tests for a .NET project/solution in a specific location:
   `dotnet test {{path/to/project_or_solution}}`
3. Execute tests matching the given filter expression:
   `dotnet test --filter {{Name~TestMethod1}}`
dotnet-tool:
**`dotnet-tool`**: Manage .NET tools and search published tools in NuGet.

**Examples:**
1. Install a global tool (don't use `--global` for local tools):
   `dotnet tool install {{[-g|--global]}} {{dotnetsay}}`
2. Install tools defined in the local tool manifest:
   `dotnet tool restore`
3. Update a specific global tool (don't use `--global` for local tools):
   `dotnet tool update {{[-g|--global]}} {{tool_name}}`
4. Uninstall a global tool (don't use `--global` for local tools):
   `dotnet tool uninstall {{[-g|--global]}} {{tool_name}}`
5. List installed global tools (don't use `--global` for local tools):
   `dotnet tool list {{[-g|--global]}}`

   `dotnet tool search {{search_term}}`
7. Display help:

dotnet:

dotty:

doxx:
**`doxx`**: View `.docx` files in the terminal.

doxygen:
**`doxygen`**: A documentation system for various programming languages.

**Examples:**

drill:
**`drill`**: Perform various DNS queries.

**Examples:**
1. Lookup the IP(s) associated with a hostname (A records):
   `drill {{example.com}}`
2. Lookup the mail server(s) associated with a given domain name (MX record):
   `drill mx {{example.com}}`
3. Get all types of records for a given domain name:
   `drill any {{example.com}}`
4. Specify an alternate DNS server to query:
   `drill {{example.com}} @{{8.8.8.8}}`
5. Perform a reverse DNS lookup on an IP address (PTR record):
   `drill -x {{8.8.8.8}}`
6. Perform DNSSEC trace from root servers down to a domain name:
   `drill -TD {{example.com}}`
7. Show DNSKEY record(s) for a domain name:
   `drill -s dnskey {{example.com}}`
dropdb:
**`dropdb`**: Remove a PostgreSQL database.

**Examples:**
1. Destroy a database:
   `dropdb {{database_name}}`
2. Request a verification prompt before any destructive actions:
   `dropdb {{[-i|--interactive]}} {{database_name}}`
3. Connect with a specific username and destroy a database:
   `dropdb {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} {{database_name}}`
4. Force a password prompt before connecting to the database:
   `dropdb {{[-W|--password]}} {{database_name}}`
5. Suppress a password prompt before connecting to the database:
   `dropdb {{[-w|--no-password]}} {{database_name}}`
6. Specify the server host name:
   `dropdb {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{database_name}}`
7. Specify the server port:
   `dropdb {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{database_name}}`
8. Attempt to terminate existing connections before destroying the database:
   `dropdb {{[-f|--force]}} {{database_name}}`
dropuser:
**`dropuser`**: Remove an existing PostgreSQL user (role).

**Examples:**
1. Prompt for confirmation and the username before user removal:
   `dropuser {{[-i|--interactive]}}`
2. Remove user instantly:
   `dropuser {{username}}`
3. No error if the user to be removed doesn't exist:
   `dropuser --if-exists {{username}}`
4. Remove a user on the server with address 127.0.0.1 on port 4321:
   `dropuser {{[-h|--host]}} 127.0.0.1 {{[-p|--port]}} 4321 {{username}}`
5. Remove a user on the server with address 127.0.0.1 on port 4321 as user "admin":
   `dropuser {{[-U|--username]}} admin {{[-h|--host]}} 127.0.0.1 {{[-p|--port]}} 4321 {{username}}`
drupal-check:
**`drupal-check`**: Check Drupal PHP code for deprecations.

**Examples:**
1. Check the code in a specific directory for deprecations:
   `drupal-check {{path/to/directory}}`
2. Check the code excluding a comma-separated list of directories:
   `drupal-check {{[-e|--exclude-dir]}} {{path/to/excluded_directory}},{{path/to/excluded_files/*.php}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Don't show a progress bar:
   `drupal-check --no-progress {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Perform static analysis to detect bad coding practices:
   `drupal-check {{[-a|--analysis]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
drupal:
**`drupal`**: Generate boilerplate code, interact with and debug Drupal projects.

**Examples:**
1. Install a module:
   `drupal module:install {{module_name}}`
2. Uninstall a module:
   `drupal module:uninstall {{module_name}}`
3. Clear all caches:
   `drupal cache:rebuild`
4. View current Drupal installation status:
   `drupal site:status`
drush:
**`drush`**: Shell and scripting interface for Drupal.

**Examples:**
1. Enable module "foo":
   `drush en {{foo}}`
2. Uninstall module "foo":
   `drush pmu {{foo}}`
3. Clear all caches:
   `drush cr`
4. Clear CSS and JavaScript caches:
   `drush cc css-js`
dtc:
**`dtc`**: The Device Tree Compiler, a tool for recompiling device trees between formats.

**Examples:**
1. Compile a device tree source `.dts` file into a binary device tree blob `.dtb` file:
   `dtc -I dts -O dtb -o {{path/to/output_file.dtb}} {{path/to/input_file.dts}}`
2. Compile a device tree source `.dts` file into a binary device tree blob overlay `.dtbo` file:
   `dtc -@ -I dts -O dtb -o {{path/to/output_file.dtbo}} {{path/to/input_file.dts}}`
3. Decompile a device tree blob `.dtb` file into a readable device tree source `.dts` file:
   `dtc -I dtb -O dts -o {{path/to/output_file.dts}} {{path/to/input_file.dtb}}`

   `dtc -I fs -O dts /proc/device-tree`
dtrx:
**`dtrx`**: "Do The Right eXtraction" - extract any archive into new directory by guessing the tool from extension.

**Examples:**
1. Extract archive, guessing the extraction tool from extension:
   `dtrx {{path/to/file}}`
2. Extract archive, overwrite any existing target output:
   `dtrx --overwrite {{path/to/file}}`
3. Extract archive, put everything into current directory:
   `dtrx --flat {{path/to/file}}`
du:
**`du`**: Disk usage: estimate and summarize file and directory space usage.

**Examples:**
1. List the sizes of a directory and any subdirectories, in the given unit (B/KiB/MiB):
   `du -{{b|k|m}} {{path/to/directory}}`
2. List the sizes of a directory and any subdirectories, in human-readable form (i.e. auto-selecting the appropriate unit for each size):
   `du {{[-h|--human-readable]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Show the size of a single directory, in human-readable units:
   `du {{[-sh|--summarize --human-readable]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
4. List the human-readable sizes of a directory and of all the files and directories within it:
   `du {{[-ah|--all --human-readable]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
5. List the human-readable sizes of a directory and any subdirectories, up to `n` levels deep:
   `du {{[-h|--human-readable]}} {{[-d|--max-depth]}} {{n}} {{path/to/directory}}`
6. List the human-readable size of all `.jpg` files in current directory, and show a cumulative total at the end:
   `du {{[-ch|--total --human-readable]}} *.jpg`
7. List all files and directories (including hidden ones) above a certain threshold size (useful for investigating what is actually taking up the space):
   `du {{[-ah|--all --human-readable]}} {{[-t|--threshold]}} {{1G|1024M|1048576K}} .[^.]* *`
dua:
**`dua`**: Dua (Disk Usage Analyzer): get the disk space usage of a directory.

**Examples:**
1. Analyze specific directory:
   `dua {{path/to/directory}}`
2. Display apparent size instead of disk usage:
   `dua --apparent-size`
3. Count hard-linked files each time they are seen:
   `dua --count-hard-links`
4. Aggregate the consumed space of one or more directories or files:
   `dua aggregate`
5. Launch the terminal user interface:
   `dua interactive`
6. Format printing byte counts:
   `dua --format {{metric|binary|bytes|GB|GiB|MB|MiB}}`
7. Use a specific number of threads (defaults to the process number of threads):
   `dua --threads {{count}}`
dub:
**`dub`**: Package manager for D packages.

**Examples:**
1. Interactively create a new D project:
   `dub init {{project_name}}`
2. Non-interactively create a new D project:
   `dub init {{project_name}} {{[-n|--non-interactive]}}`
3. Build and run a D project:
   `dub`
4. Install dependencies specified in a D project's `dub.json` or `dub.sdl` file:
   `dub fetch`
5. Update the dependencies in a D project:
   `dub upgrade`
6. Display help:
   `dub {{[-h|--help]}}`
duc:
**`duc`**: A collection of tools for indexing, inspecting, and visualizing disk usage.

**Examples:**
1. Index the `/usr` directory, writing to the default database location `~/.duc.db`:
   `duc index {{/usr}}`

   `duc ls {{[-Fg|--classify --graph]}} {{/usr/local}}`
3. List all files and directories under `/usr/local` using treeview recursively:
   `duc ls {{[-Fg|--classify --graph]}} {{[-R|--recursive]}} {{/usr/local}}`

   `duc gui {{/usr}}`

   `duc info`
duckdb:
**`duckdb`**: Client for DuckDB, an in-process analytical SQL engine.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive shell with a transient in-memory database:
   `duckdb`
2. Start an interactive shell on a database file. If the file does not exist, a new database is created:
   `duckdb {{path/to/dbfile}}`

   `duckdb {{data_source.[csv|csv.gz|json|json.gz|parquet]}} -c "{{ SELECT * FROM file }}"`

   `duckdb -f {{path/to/script.sql}}`

   `duckdb {{path/to/dbfile}} -cmd "{{SELECT DISTINCT * FROM tbl}}"`

   `cat {{path/to/source.csv}} | duckdb -c "{{COPY (FROM read_csv('/dev/stdin')) TO '/dev/stdout' WITH (FORMAT CSV, HEADER)}}"`

duf:
**`duf`**: Disk Usage/Free Utility.

**Examples:**
1. List accessible devices:
   `duf`

   `duf --all`

   `duf {{path/to/directory1 path/to/directory2 ...}}`

7. Change the theme (if `duf` fails to use the right theme):

dumpcap:

dumpntlminfo.py:

dune:

dunst:
**`dunst`**: A lightweight and customizable notification daemon for X11 and Wayland.

duplicacy:
**`duplicacy`**: A lock-free deduplication cloud backup tool.

1. Use current directory as the repository, initialize a SFTP storage and encrypt the storage with a password:
   `duplicacy init {{[-e|-encrypt]}} {{snapshot_id}} {{sftp://user@192.168.2.100/path/to/storage}}/`

**`duplicity`**: Create incremental, compressed, encrypted, and versioned backups.

dust:

dvc-add:

dvc:

   `dwebp {{path/to/input.webp}} -bmp|-tiff|-pam|-ppm|-pgm|-yuv -o {{path/to/output}}`

   `dwebp {{path/to/input.webp}} -o {{path/to/output.png}} -mt`

   `dwebp {{input.webp}} -o {{output.png}} -crop {{x_pos}} {{y_pos}} {{width}} {{height}} -scale {{width}} {{height}}`
5. Convert a WebP file and flip the output:
   `dwebp {{path/to/input.webp}} -o {{path/to/output.png}} -flip`
6. Convert a WebP file and don't use in-loop filtering to speed up the decoding process:
   `dwebp {{path/to/input.webp}} -o {{path/to/output.png}} -nofilter`
dzdo:
**`dzdo`**: Execute privileged commands as root or another user via Active Directory roles.

**Examples:**
1. Run a command with elevated privileges:
   `dzdo {{command}}`

   `dzdo -u {{user}} {{command}}`

   `dzdo -e {{path/to/file}}`
4. Launch an interactive login shell with elevated privileges:
   `dzdo -i`
5. Launch the default shell with elevated privileges:
   `dzdo -s`
6. List allowed commands for the current user:
   `dzdo -l`
7. Validate and update authentication timestamp:
   `dzdo -v`
8. Display version:
   `dzdo -V`
ebook-convert:
**`ebook-convert`**: Can be used to convert e-books between common formats, e.g. PDF, EPUB, and MOBI.

**Examples:**
1. Convert an e-book into another format:
   `ebook-convert {{path/to/input_file}} {{output_file}}`
2. Convert Markdown or HTML to e-book with TOC, title, and author:
   `ebook-convert {{path/to/input_file}} {{output_file}} --level1-toc="//h:h1" --level2-toc="//h:h2" --level3-toc="//h:h3" --title={{title}} --authors={{author}}`
echo:
**`echo`**: Print given arguments.

**Examples:**
1. Print a text message. Note: Quotes are optional:
   `echo "{{Hello World}}"`
2. Print a message with environment variables:
   `echo "{{My path is $PATH}}"`
3. Print a message without the trailing newline:
   `echo -n "{{Hello World}}"`

   `echo "{{Hello World}}" >> {{file.txt}}`
5. Enable interpretation of backslash escapes (special characters):
   `echo -e "{{Column 1\tColumn 2}}"`
6. Print the exit status of the last executed command (Note: In Windows Command Prompt and PowerShell the equivalent commands are `echo %errorlevel%` and `$lastexitcode` respectively):
   `echo $?`
7. Pass text to another program through `stdin`:
   `echo "{{Hello World}}" | {{program}}`
ecpg:
**`ecpg`**: Embedded SQL preprocessor for C programs.

**Examples:**
1. Preprocess a specific file:
   `ecpg {{input.pgc}}`
2. Preprocess from `stdin` and output to `stdout`:
   `ecpg -o - -`
3. Preprocess from `stdin` and write to a file:
   `cat input.pgc | ecpg -o output.c -`

   `ecpg -o {{output.c}} {{input.pgc}}`
5. Preprocess a header file (`.pgh` extension):
   `ecpg {{input.pgh}}`
6. Preprocess in a specific compatibility mode:
   `ecpg -C {{INFORMIX|INFORMIX_SE|ORACLE}} {{input.pgc}}`
7. Preprocess with autocommit enabled:
   `ecpg -t {{input.pgc}}`
ect:
**`ect`**: Efficient Compression Tool.

**Examples:**
1. Compress a file:
   `ect {{path/to/file.png}}`
2. Compress a file with specified compression level and multithreading (1=Fastest (Worst), 9=Slowest (Best), default is 3):
   `ect -{{9}} --mt-deflate {{path/to/file.zip}}`
3. Compress all files in a directory recursively:
   `ect -recurse {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Compress a file, keeping the original modification time:
   `ect -keep {{path/to/file.png}}`
5. Compress a file, stripping metadata:
   `ect -strip {{path/to/file.png}}`
ed:
**`ed`**: The original Unix text editor.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive editor session with an empty document:
   `ed`
2. Start an interactive editor session with an empty document and a specific prompt:
   `ed {{[-p|--prompt]}} '{{> }}'`
3. Start an interactive editor session with user-friendly errors:
   `ed {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
4. Start an interactive editor session with an empty document and without diagnostics, byte counts and '!' prompt:
   `ed {{[-q|--quiet]}} {{[-s|--script]}}`
5. Start an interactive editor session without exit status change when command fails:
   `ed {{[-l|--loose-exit-status]}}`
6. Edit a specific file (this shows the byte count of the loaded file):
   `ed {{path/to/file}}`
7. [Interactive] Replace a string with a specific replacement for all lines:
   `,s/{{regex}}/{{replacement}}/g`
8. [Interactive] Exit `ed`:
   `q`
edgepaint:
**`edgepaint`**: Colorize edges of a graph layout to clarify crossing edges.

**Examples:**
1. Colorize edges of one or more graph layouts (that already have layout information) to clarify crossing edges:
   `edgepaint {{path/to/layout1.gv path/to/layout2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`

3. Lay out a graph and colorize its edges, then convert to a PNG image:
   `dot {{path/to/input.gv}} | edgepaint | dot -T {{png}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`

   `edgepaint -?`
edit:
**`edit`**: This command is an alias of `run-mailcap --action=edit`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr run-mailcap`
eget:
**`eget`**: Easily install prebuilt binaries from GitHub.

3. Specify the location to place the downloaded files:
   `eget {{zyedidia/micro}} --to {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Specify a Git tag instead of using the latest version:
   `eget {{zyedidia/micro}} {{[-t|--tag]}} {{v2.0.10}}`

egrep:
**`egrep`**: Find patterns in files using extended `regex`es.

**Examples:**
1. Search for one or more repeated characters:
   `egrep '{{a}}+' {{path/to/file}}`
2. Search for zero or one occurrences of a character (optional match):
   `egrep '{{a}}?' {{path/to/file}}`
3. Search for 10 repetitions of a character:
   `egrep '{{a}}{10}' {{path/to/file}}`
4. Search for 3 to 7 repetitions of a character:
   `egrep '{{a}}{3,7}' {{path/to/file}}`
5. Search for one of the listed options:
   `egrep '{{cat}}|{{dog}}|{{mouse}}' {{path/to/file}}`
6. Search for one of the listed options inside a larger pattern:
   `egrep 'c({{a}}|{{o}}|{{u}})p' {{path/to/file}}`
7. Search for a group of characters repeating one or more times:
   `egrep '({{aeiou}})+' {{path/to/file}}`
8. Search using standard character classes (more info: <https://www.regular-expressions.info/posixbrackets.html>):
   `egrep [[{{:alnum:|:alpha:|:space:|...}}]] {{path/to/file}}`
eim:
**`eim`**: Install and manage ESP-IDF.

   `eim install {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}}`
8. Install offline using a pre-downloaded archive file:
   `eim install --use-local-archive {{path/to/archive.zst}}`
eksctl:
**`eksctl`**: The official CLI for Amazon EKS.

elasticsearch-certutil:
**`elasticsearch-certutil`**: Generate and manage SSL certificates for Elasticsearch security.

**Examples:**

   `elasticsearch-certutil http`

   `elasticsearch-certutil transport {{[-s|--silent]}}`

   `elasticsearch-certutil csr`
7. Generate encrypted keystore passwords:
   `elasticsearch-certutil password`

elasticsearch-create-enrollment-token:
**`elasticsearch-create-enrollment-token`**: Create enrollment tokens for Elasticsearch nodes and Kibana instances.

elasticsearch-croneval:
**`elasticsearch-croneval`**: Validate and evaluate a `cron` expression. This command helps verify that `cron` expressions are valid for use with Elasticsearch and produce the expected results.

   `elasticsearch-croneval "{{cron_expression}}" {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
elasticsearch-keystore:
**`elasticsearch-keystore`**: Manage secure settings (e.g., passwords, tokens, and credentials) used by Elasticsearch.

**Examples:**

   `elasticsearch-keystore create`

   `elasticsearch-keystore passwd`

elasticsearch-node:

elasticsearch-reset-password:
**`elasticsearch-reset-password`**: Reset the passwords of users in the native realm and built-in users.

elasticsearch-saml-metadata:

elasticsearch-syskeygen:

electrum:
