   `glab alias list`
2. Create a `glab` subcommand alias:
   `glab alias set {{mrv}} '{{mr view}}'`
3. Set a shell command as a `glab` subcommand:
   `glab alias set {{[-s|--shell]}} {{alias_name}} {{command}}`
4. Delete a command shortcut:
   `glab alias delete {{alias_name}}`
5. Display the subcommand help:
   `glab alias`
glab-auth:
**`glab-auth`**: Authenticate with a GitLab host.

**Examples:**
1. Log in with interactive prompt:
   `glab auth login`
2. Log in with a token:
   `glab auth login {{[-t|--token]}} {{token}}`
3. Check authentication status:
   `glab auth status`
4. Log in to a specific GitLab instance:
   `glab auth login {{[-h|--hostname]}} {{gitlab.example.com}}`
glab-issue:
**`glab-issue`**: Manage GitLab issues.

**Examples:**
1. Display a specific issue:
   `glab issue view {{issue_number}}`
2. Display a specific issue in the default web browser:
   `glab issue view {{issue_number}} {{[-w|--web]}}`
3. Create a new issue in the default web browser:
   `glab issue create --web`
4. List the last 10 issues with the `bug` label:
   `glab issue list {{[-P|--per-page]}} {{10}} {{[-l|--label]}} "{{bug}}"`
5. List closed issues made by a specific user:
   `glab issue list {{[-c|--closed]}} --author {{username}}`
6. Reopen a specific issue:
   `glab issue reopen {{issue_number}}`
glab-mr-create:
**`glab-mr-create`**: Manage GitLab merge requests.

**Examples:**
1. Interactively create a merge request:
   `glab mr create`
2. Create a merge request, determining the title and description from the commit messages of the current branch:
   `glab mr create {{[-f|--fill]}}`
3. Create a draft merge request:
   `glab mr create --draft`
4. Create a merge request specifying the target branch, title, and description:
   `glab mr create {{[-b|--target-branch]}} {{target_branch}} {{[-t|--title]}} "{{title}}" {{[-d|--description]}} "{{description}}"`
5. Start opening a merge request in the default web browser:
   `glab mr create {{[-w|--web]}}`
glab-mr-merge:
**`glab-mr-merge`**: Merge GitLab merge requests.

**Examples:**
1. Merge the merge request associated with the current branch interactively:
   `glab mr merge`
2. Merge the specified merge request, interactively:
   `glab mr merge {{mr_number}}`
3. Merge the merge request, removing the branch on both the local and the remote:
   `glab mr merge {{[-d|--remove-source-branch]}}`
4. Squash the current merge request into one commit with the message body and merge:
   `glab mr merge {{[-s|--squash]}} {{[-m|--message]}} "{{commit_message_body}}"`
5. Display help:
   `glab mr merge --help`
glab-mr:
**`glab-mr`**: Manage GitLab merge requests.

**Examples:**
1. Create a merge request:
   `glab mr create`
2. Check out a specific merge request locally:
   `glab {{[co|mr checkout]}} {{mr_number}}`
3. Check out a merge request of a specific repo:
   `glab {{[co|mr checkout]}} {{mr_number}} {{[-R|--repo]}} {{repo-owner}}/{{repository}}`
4. View the changes made in the merge request:
   `glab mr diff`
5. Approve the merge request for the current branch:
   `glab mr approve`
6. Merge the merge request associated with the current branch interactively:
   `glab mr merge`
7. Edit a merge request interactively:
   `glab mr update`
8. Edit the target branch of a merge request:
   `glab mr update --target-branch {{branch_name}}`
glab-pipeline:
**`glab-pipeline`**: List, view, and run GitLab CI/CD pipelines.

**Examples:**
1. View a running pipeline on the current branch:
   `glab pipeline status`
2. View a running pipeline on a specific branch:
   `glab pipeline status --branch {{branch_name}}`
3. Get the list of pipelines:
   `glab pipeline list`
4. Run a manual pipeline on the current branch:
   `glab pipeline run`
5. Run a manual pipeline on a specific branch:
   `glab pipeline run --branch {{branch_name}}`
glab-release:
**`glab-release`**: Manage GitLab releases.

**Examples:**
1. List releases in a Gitlab repository, limited to 30 items:
   `glab release list`
2. Display information about a specific release:
   `glab release view {{tag}}`
3. Create a new release:
   `glab release create {{tag}}`
4. Delete a specific release:
   `glab release delete {{tag}}`
5. Download assets from a specific release:
   `glab release download {{tag}}`
6. Upload assets to a specific release:
   `glab release upload {{tag}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
glab-repo:
**`glab-repo`**: Work with GitLab repositories.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new repository (if the repository name is not set, the default name will be the name of the current directory):
   `glab repo create {{name}}`
2. Clone a repository:
   `glab repo clone {{owner}}/{{repository}}`
3. Fork and clone a repository:
   `glab repo fork {{owner}}/{{repository}} {{[-c|--clone]}}`
4. View a repository in the default web browser:
   `glab repo view {{owner}}/{{repository}} {{[-w|--web]}}`
5. Search some repositories in the GitLab instance:
   `glab repo search {{[-s|--search]}} {{search_string}}`
glab:
**`glab`**: Work seamlessly with GitLab.

**Examples:**
1. Clone a GitLab repository locally:
   `glab repo clone {{owner}}/{{repository}}`
2. Create a new issue:
   `glab issue create`
3. View and filter the open issues of the current repository:
   `glab issue list`
4. View an issue in the default browser:
   `glab issue view {{[-w|--web]}} {{issue_number}}`
5. Create a merge request:
   `glab mr create`
6. View a pull request in the default web browser:
   `glab mr view {{[-w|--web]}} {{pr_number}}`
7. Check out a specific pull request locally:
   `glab {{[co|mr checkout]}} {{pr_number}}`
gladtex:
**`gladtex`**: A LaTeX formula preprocessor for HTML files.

**Examples:**
1. Convert to HTML:
   `gladtex {{path/to/input.htex}}`
2. Save the converted file to a specific [o]utput file:

glances:
**`glances`**: A cross-platform system monitoring tool.

1. Run in terminal:
   `glances`

   `glances {{[-w|--webserver]}}`

7. Display help:
   `glances {{[-h|--help]}}`
gleam:
**`gleam`**: The compiler, build tool, package manager, and code formatter for Gleam, "a friendly language for building type-safe systems that scale!".

**Examples:**
1. Create a new gleam project:
   `gleam new {{project_name}}`

   `gleam test`

glib-compile-resources:
**`glib-compile-resources`**: Compiles resource files (e.g. images) into a binary resource bundle.

glow:
**`glow`**: Render Markdown in the terminal.

**Examples:**
1. Run glow and select a file to view:
   `glow`
2. Render a Markdown file to the terminal:
   `glow {{path/to/file}}`
3. View a Markdown file using a paginator:
   `glow {{[-p|--pager]}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. View a file from a URL:
   `glow {{https://example.com/file.md}}`
5. View a GitHub/GitLab README:

glxgears:
**`glxgears`**: Test OpenGL rendering.

**Examples:**
1. Run an OpenGL test window:
   `glxgears`
2. Display OpenGL renderer information:
   `glxgears -info`
3. Display help:
   `glxgears -h`
gml2gv:
**`gml2gv`**: Convert a graph from `gml` to `gv` format.

1. Convert a graph from `gml` to `gv` format:
   `gml2gv -o {{output.gv}} {{input.gml}}`
2. Convert a graph using `stdin` and `stdout`:
   `cat {{input.gml}} | gml2gv > {{output.gv}}`
3. Display help:

gmssl:
**`gmssl`**: Crypto toolkit supporting SM1, SM2, SM3, SM4, SM9, and ZUC/ZUC256.

1. Generate an SM3 hash for a file:
   `gmssl sm3 {{path/to/file}}`

   `gmssl sm2 -pubout -in {{path/to/file.pem}} -out {{path/to/file.pem.pub}}`

   `gmssl zuc -e -in {{path/to/file}} -out {{path/to/file.zuc}}`
7. Decrypt a file using the ZUC cipher:
   `gmssl zuc -d -in {{path/to/file.zuc}}`
8. Display version:
   `gmssl version`
gnatmake:
**`gnatmake`**: A low-level build tool for Ada programs (part of the GNAT toolchain).

**Examples:**
1. Compile an executable:
   `gnatmake {{source_file1.adb source_file2.adb ...}}`
2. Set a custom [o]utput executable name:

gnatprep:

gnmic-get:
**`gnmic-get`**: Get a snapshot of a gnmi network device operation data.

gnmic-set:

gnmic-sub:
**`gnmic-sub`**: This command is an alias of `gnmic subscribe`.

**Examples:**

   `tldr gnmic subscribe`
gnmic-subscribe:
**`gnmic-subscribe`**: Subscribe to a gnmic network device state updates.

**Examples:**
1. Subscribe to target state updates under the subtree of a specific path:
   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}}`

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}} --sample-interval 30s`

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}} --stream-mode on-change --heartbeat-interval {{1m}}`

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}} --mode once`

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}} {{[-e|--encoding]}} json_ietf`
gnmic:
**`gnmic`**: A gNMI client.

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} capabilities`

   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} get --path {{path}}`
4. Update device state at a specific path:
   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} set --update-path {{path}} --update-value {{value}}`
5. Subscribe to target state updates under the subtree at a specific path:
   `gnmic {{[-a|--address]}} {{ip:port}} {{[sub|subscribe]}} --path {{path}}`
gnomon:
**`gnomon`**: Utility to annotate console logging statements with timestamps and find slow processes.

   `{{npm test}} | gnomon`
2. Show number of seconds since the start of the process:

   `{{npm test}} | gnomon {{[-t|--type]}} absolute`

   `{{npm test}} | gnomon {{[-h|--high]}} 0.5`

gnucash-cli:

gnuplot:

   `gst-launch-1.0 audiotestsrc ! {{autoaudiosink}}`
2. Define what type of wave to generate:
   `gst-launch-1.0 audiotestsrc wave={{sine|square|saw|white-noise|pink-noise|ticks|...}} ! {{autoaudiosink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-capsfilter:
**`gst-launch-1.0-capsfilter`**: Filter pipeline capabilities.

**Examples:**
1. Filter to only allow greyscale format:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{videotestsrc}} ! capsfilter caps=video/x-raw,format=GRAY8 ! {{videoconvert ! autovideosink}}`
2. Do the same but in shortform:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{videotestsrc}} ! video/x-raw,format=GRAY8 ! {{videoconvert ! autovideosink}}`
3. Limit video capabilities to specific dimensions:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{videotestsrc}} ! video/x-raw,width={{640}},height={{480}} ! {{videoconvert ! autovideosink}}`
4. Specify a specific framerate:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{videotestsrc}} ! video/x-raw,framerate={{30}}/1 ! {{videoconvert ! autovideosink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-decodebin:
**`gst-launch-1.0-decodebin`**: Automatically decode data.

**Examples:**
1. Decode data to raw format:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{source}} ! decodebin ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-fakesink:
**`gst-launch-1.0-fakesink`**: Dummy sink that swallows everything.

**Examples:**
1. Consume data from a pipeline without outputting it:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{pipeline}} ! fakesink`
2. Print information on the received data:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{pipeline}} ! fakesink silent=false`
gst-launch-1.0-filesrc:
**`gst-launch-1.0-filesrc`**: Read data from a file.

**Examples:**
1. Read data from a file:
   `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location={{path/to/file}} ! {{pipeline}}`
gst-launch-1.0-identity:
**`gst-launch-1.0-identity`**: Diagnose data passed through the element.

**Examples:**
1. Print information on the passed through data:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{source}} ! identity silent=false ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-libcamerasrc:
**`gst-launch-1.0-libcamerasrc`**: Read frames from a libcamera device.

**Examples:**
1. View video in a window:
   `gst-launch-1.0 libcamerasrc ! videoconvert ! autovideosink`
2. Specify the device to read from:
   `gst-launch-1.0 libcamerasrc camera-name={{camera_name}} ! {{videoconvert ! autovideosink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-playbin:
**`gst-launch-1.0-playbin`**: Standalone media player.

**Examples:**
1. Play a local file:
   `gst-launch-1.0 playbin uri=file:///{{path/to/file}}`
2. Play a file from the internet:
   `gst-launch-1.0 playbin uri={{https://example.com/path/to/file}}`
3. Play track 4 of a CD:
   `gst-launch-1.0 playbin uri=cdda://4`
4. Play a DVD in a disc drive:
   `gst-launch-1.0 playbin uri=dvd://`
gst-launch-1.0-pulsesrc:
**`gst-launch-1.0-pulsesrc`**: Read audio data from a Pulseaudio source.

**Examples:**
1. Listen to the default microphone:
   `gst-launch-1.0 pulsesrc ! autoaudiosink`
2. Specify the source by name (can match a substring):
   `gst-launch-1.0 pulsesrc device="{{device_name}}" ! autoaudiosink`
3. Record the monitor of the default sink:
   `gst-launch-1.0 pulsesrc device=@DEFAULT_MONITOR@ ! {{opusenc}} ! {{oggmux}} ! filesink location={{path/to/file.ogg}}`
gst-launch-1.0-queue:
**`gst-launch-1.0-queue`**: Multithread the pipeline and buffer data.

**Examples:**
1. Separate a pipeline into multiple threads so that one blocking element doesn't block the rest:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{source}} ! queue ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-uridecodebin:
**`gst-launch-1.0-uridecodebin`**: Load data from an URI and automatically decode it.

**Examples:**
1. Load and decode data from the internet:
   `gst-launch-1.0 uridecodebin uri={{https://example.com/path/to/file}} ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-videoconvert:
**`gst-launch-1.0-videoconvert`**: Convert between raw video pixel formats.

**Examples:**
1. Convert the pixel format to be compatible with the output:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{source}} ! videoconvert ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-videorate:
**`gst-launch-1.0-videorate`**: Normalize input framerate.

**Examples:**
1. Normalize framerate and apply new timestamps:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{source}} ! videorate ! {{sink}}`
gst-launch-1.0-videoscale:
**`gst-launch-1.0-videoscale`**: Resize video frames.

**Examples:**
1. Scale video to fit the capabilities of both input and output:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{input}} ! videoscale ! {{output}}`
2. Scale video to an arbitrary resolution:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{input}} ! videoscale ! video/x-raw,width={{width}},height={{height}} ! {{output}}`
gst-launch-1.0-videotestsrc:
**`gst-launch-1.0-videotestsrc`**: Produce test video data.

**Examples:**
1. Produce a video with SMPTE color bars:
   `gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! {{autovideosink}}`
2. Define what type of test video to produce:
   `gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc pattern={{smpte|snow|green|ball|circular|...}} ! {{autovideosink}}`
gst-launch-1.0:
**`gst-launch-1.0`**: Build and run a GStreamer pipeline.

**Examples:**
1. Play test video in a window:
   `gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! autovideosink`
2. Play test audio and enable verbose output:
   `gst-launch-1.0 audiotestsrc {{[-v|--verbose]}} ! autoaudiosink`
3. Play a media file in a window:
   `gst-launch-1.0 playbin uri={{protocol}}://{{host}}/{{path/to/file}}`
4. Re-encode a media file:
   `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location={{path/to/file}} ! {{file_type}}demux ! {{codec_type}}dec ! {{codec_type}}enc ! {{file_type}}mux ! filesink location={{path/to/file}}`
5. Stream a file to an RTSP server:
   `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location={{path/to/file}} ! rtspclientsink location=rtsp://{{host_ip}}/{{path/to/file}}`
6. Force an End Of Stream event if the pipeline is shut down with `<Ctrl c>` for containers that require finalization such as `mp4`:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{[-e|--eos-on-shutdown]}} videotestsrc ! x264enc ! mp4mux ! filesink location={{path/to/file.mp4}}`
7. Multiplex together test video and test audio into a file:
   `gst-launch-1.0 {{[-e|--eos-on-shutdown]}} videotestsrc ! {{x264enc}} ! {{element_name}}. audiotestsrc ! {{opusenc}} ! {{element_name}}. {{matroskamux}} name={{element_name}} ! filesink location={{path/to/file.mkv}}`
8. Enable debug output and dump a pipeline into a `.dot` file which can then be rendered with tools like `dot`:
   `GST_DEBUG={{1..5}} GST_DEBUG_DUMP_DOT_DIR={{path/to/directory}} gst-launch-1.0 {{pipeline}}`
gst-play-1.0:
**`gst-play-1.0`**: Play media files using the playbin Gstreamer element.

**Examples:**
1. Play a media file:
   `gst-play-1.0 {{file1|directory1|uri1 file2|directory2|uri2 ...}}`
gst-transcoder-1.0:
**`gst-transcoder-1.0`**: Convert media between two filetypes.

**Examples:**
1. List available transcoding targets:
   `gst-transcoder-1.0 {{[-l|--list-targets]}}`
2. Convert from one media type to another:
   `gst-transcoder-1.0 {{path/to/input_file.webm}} {{path/to/output_file.mp4}}`
gst-typefind-1.0:
**`gst-typefind-1.0`**: Find the mime type of a file.

**Examples:**
1. Print the mime type of a file:
   `gst-typefind-1.0 {{path/to/file}}`
gsutil:
**`gsutil`**: Access Google Cloud Storage.

**Examples:**
1. List all buckets in a project you are logged into:
   `gsutil ls`
2. List the objects in a bucket:
   `gsutil ls -r 'gs://{{bucket_name}}/{{prefix}}**'`
3. Download an object from a bucket:
   `gsutil cp gs://{{bucket_name}}/{{object_name}} {{path/to/save_location}}`
4. Upload an object to a bucket:
   `gsutil cp {{object_location}} gs://{{destination_bucket_name}}/`
5. Rename or move objects in a bucket:
   `gsutil mv gs://{{bucket_name}}/{{old_object_name}} gs://{{bucket_name}}/{{new_object_name}}`
6. Create a new bucket in the project you are logged into:
   `gsutil mb gs://{{bucket_name}}`
7. Delete a bucket and remove all the objects in it:
   `gsutil rm -r gs://{{bucket_name}}`
gt:
**`gt`**: Create and manage sequences of dependent code changes (stacks) for Git and GitHub.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize `gt` for the repository in the current directory:
   `gt init`
2. Create a new branch stacked on top of the current branch and commit staged changes:
   `gt create {{branch_name}}`
3. Create a new commit and fix upstack branches:
   `gt modify -cam {{commit_message}}`
4. Force push all branches in the current stack to GitHub and create or update PRs:
   `gt stack submit`
5. Checkout different branch (prompts interactive mode when branch name is omitted):
   `gt co {{branch_name}}`
6. Sync stack with remote version (also deletes merged branches):
   `gt sync`
7. Log all tracked stacks:
   `gt log short`
8. Display help for a specified subcommand:
   `gt {{subcommand}} --help`
gtop:
**`gtop`**: System monitoring dashboard for the terminal.

**Examples:**
1. Show the system stats dashboard:
   `gtop`
2. Sort by CPU usage:
   `<c>`
3. Sort by memory usage:
   `<m>`
guacd:
**`guacd`**: Apache Guacamole proxy daemon.

2. Start in debug mode, keeping the process in the foreground:
   `guacd -f -L {{debug}}`
3. Start with TLS support:
   `guacd -C {{my-cert.crt}} -K {{my-key.pem}}`
4. Write the PID to a file:
   `guacd -p {{path/to/file.pid}}`
guetzli:
**`guetzli`**: JPEG image compression utility.

1. Compress a JPEG image:

   `guetzli {{input.png}} {{output.jpg}}`

   `guetzli --quality {{quality_value}} {{input.jpg}} {{output.jpg}}`
guile:
**`guile`**: Guile Scheme interpreter.

**Examples:**
1. Start a REPL (interactive shell):
   `guile`
2. Execute the script in a given Scheme file:
   `guile {{script.scm}}`
3. Execute a Scheme expression:
   `guile -c "{{expression}}"`
4. Listen on a port or a Unix domain socket (the default is port 37146) for remote REPL connections:
   `guile --listen={{port_or_socket}}`
gulp:
**`gulp`**: JavaScript task runner and streaming build system.

**Examples:**
1. Run the default task:
   `gulp`
2. Run individual tasks:
   `gulp {{task}} {{othertask}}`
3. Print the task dependency tree for the loaded gulpfile:

gum:
**`gum`**: Make glamorous shell scripts.

**Examples:**
1. Interactively pick a specific option to print to `stdout`:
   `gum choose {{"option1" "option2" "..."}}`
2. Open an interactive prompt for the user to input a string with a specific placeholder:
   `gum input --placeholder "{{value}}"`
3. Open an interactive confirmation prompt and exit with either `<0>` or `<1>`:
   `gum confirm "{{Continue?}}" --default=false --affirmative "{{Yes}}" --negative "{{No}}" {{&& echo "Yes selected" || echo "No selected"}}`
4. Show a spinner while a command is taking place with text alongside:
   `gum spin {{[-s|--spinner]}} {{dot|line|minidot|jump|pulse|points|globe|moon|monkey|meter|hamburger}} --title "{{loading...}}" {{command}}`

   `gum format {{[-t|--type]}} {{emoji}} "{{:smile: :heart: hello}}"`
6. Interactively prompt for multi-line text and write the input to a file:
   `gum write > {{path/to/file}}`
gunicorn:
**`gunicorn`**: Python WSGI HTTP Server.

1. Run Python web app:

   `gunicorn --certfile {{cert.pem}} --keyfile {{key.pem}} {{import.path:app_object}}`
gunzip:
**`gunzip`**: This command is an alias of `gzip --decompress`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:

gup:
**`gup`**: Update binaries installed by `go install` in parallel.

**Examples:**
1. Update all installed binaries:
   `gup update`
2. List all installed binaries, their package paths, and versions:
   `gup list`
3. Check for available updates without installing them:
   `gup check`
4. Export the list of installed binaries to a file:
   `gup export {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/gup.json}}`

   `gup update --latest {{binary1,binary2,...}}`
gv2gml:
**`gv2gml`**: Convert a graph from `gv` to `gml` format.

gv2gxl:
**`gv2gxl`**: Convert a graph from `gv` to `gxl` format.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a graph from `gv` to `gxl` format:
   `gv2gxl -o {{output.gxl}} {{input.gv}}`
2. Convert a graph using `stdin` and `stdout`:
   `cat {{input.gv}} | gv2gxl > {{output.gxl}}`
3. Display help:
   `gv2gxl -?`
gvcolor:
**`gvcolor`**: Colorize a ranked digraph with a range of colors.

**Examples:**
1. Colorize one or more ranked digraph (that were already processed by `dot`):
   `gvcolor {{path/to/layout1.gv path/to/layout2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`

   `dot {{path/to/input.gv}} | gvcolor | dot -T {{png}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`
3. Display help:
   `gvcolor -?`
gvedit:
**`gvedit`**: Simple Graphviz graph editor and viewer.

3. Enable [v]erbose mode:
   `gvedit -v {{path/to/graph.gv}}`
4. Display help:
   `gvedit -?`
gvgen:
**`gvgen`**: Generate simple, structured abstract graphs.

   `gvgen -c {{10}}`
2. Generate a 4×3 [g]rid:
   `gvgen -g {{4,3}}`
3. Generate a binary [t]ree of height 5:
   `gvgen -t {{5}}`
4. Generate a complete [b]ipartite graph with 3 and 4 vertices:
   `gvgen -b {{3,4}}`
5. Create a [r]andom graph and [o]utput it to a file:
   `gvgen -r {{10,5}} -o {{random.gv}}`
6. Generate a [d]irected graph with [v]erbose output:
   `gvgen -d -v -c {{6}}`
7. Display help:
   `gvgen -?`
gvim:
**`gvim`**: A Graphical User Interface version of Vim (Vi IMproved), a command-line text editor.

**Examples:**
1. Open `gvim`:

2. Open a specific file:
   `gvim {{path/to/file}}`
gvmap:
**`gvmap`**: Find clusters and creates a geographical map highlighting clusters.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a clustered map layout from a DOT format graph:
   `gvmap {{graph.gv}} -o {{output.xdot}}`
2. Generate a map using existing cluster subgraphs from the input:
   `gvmap -D {{graph.gv}}`

   `gvmap -e {{graph.gv}} -o {{output.xdot}}`
4. Specify a [c]olor scheme (1: pastel, 2: blue-yellow, 3: white-red, etc.):

   `gvmap -highlight={{2}} {{graph.gv}} -o {{output.xdot}}`
gvpack:
**`gvpack`**: Combine several graph layouts (that already have layout information).

1. Combine several graph layouts (that already have layout information):
   `gvpack {{path/to/layout1.gv path/to/layout2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`
2. Combine several graph layouts at the graph level, keeping graphs separate:

   `gvpack -n {{path/to/layout1.gv path/to/layout2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`

   `gvpack -u {{path/to/layout1.gv path/to/layout2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`
5. Display help:

gxl2gv:
**`gxl2gv`**: Convert a graph from `gxl` to `gv` format.

gyb:
**`gyb`**: Locally back up Gmail messages using Gmail's API over HTTPS.

gzip:
**`gzip`**: Compress/uncompress files with `gzip` compression (LZ77).

**Examples:**
1. Compress a file, replacing it with a `gzip` archive:
   `gzip {{path/to/file}}`
2. Decompress a file, replacing it with the original uncompressed version:
   `gzip {{[-d|--decompress]}} {{path/to/file.gz}}`
3. Display the name and reduction percentage for each file compressed:
   `gzip {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{path/to/file.gz}}`
4. Compress a file, keeping the original file:
   `gzip {{[-k|--keep]}} {{path/to/file}}`

hadolint:

hakyll-init:

hangups:

   `hledger add {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/2024.journal}} {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/2023.journal}}`
3. Provide answers for the first four prompts:
   `hledger add {{today}} '{{best buy}}' {{expenses:supplies}} '{{$20}}'`
4. Show `add`'s options and documentation with `$PAGER`:
   `hledger add {{[-h|--help]}}`
5. Show `add`'s documentation with `info` or `man` if available:
   `hledger help add`
hledger-aregister:
**`hledger-aregister`**: Show the transactions and running balances in one account, with each transaction on one line.

**Examples:**
1. Show transactions and running balance in the `assets:bank:checking` account:
   `hledger {{[areg|aregister]}} assets:bank:checking`
2. Show transactions and running balance in the first account whose name contains `savings`:
   `hledger {{[areg|aregister]}} savings`
3. Show the checking account's cleared transactions, with a specified width:
   `hledger {{[areg|aregister]}} checking {{[-C|--cleared]}} {{[-w|--width]}} {{120}}`
4. Show the checking register, including transactions from forecast rules:
   `hledger {{[areg|aregister]}} checking --forecast`
hledger-balance:
**`hledger-balance`**: A flexible, general purpose "summing" report that shows accounts with some kind of numeric data.

**Examples:**
1. Show the balance change in all accounts from all postings over all time:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}}`
2. Show the balance change in accounts whose name contains `expenses`, as a tree, summarising the top two levels only:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} {{expenses}} {{[-t|--tree]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}}`
3. Show expenses each month, and their totals and averages, sorted by total; and their monthly budget goals:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} {{expenses}} {{[-M|--monthly]}} {{[-T|--row-total]}} {{[-A|--average]}} {{[-S|--sort-amount]}} --budget`
4. Similar to the above, matching accounts by `Expense` type, as a two level tree without squashing boring accounts:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} type:{{X}} {{[-MTAS|--monthly --row-total --average --sort-amount]}} --budget {{[-t|--tree]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}} --no-elide`
5. Show end balances (including from postings before the start date), quarterly in 2024, in accounts whose name contains `assets` or `liabilities`:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} {{[-H|--historical]}} {{[-p|--period]}} '{{quarterly in 2024}}' {{assets}} {{liabilities}}`
6. Similar to the above, also show zero balances, sort by total and summarise to three levels:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} {{[-HQ|--historical --quarterly]}} date:{{2024}} type:{{AL}} {{[-ES|--empty --sort-amount]}} {{[-3|--depth 3]}}`
7. Show investment assets' market [V]alue in base currency at the end of each quarter:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} {{[-HVQ|--historical --market --quarterly]}} {{assets:investments}}`
8. Show unrealised capital gains/losses from market price changes in each quarter, for non-cryptocurrency investment assets:
   `hledger {{[bal|balance]}} --gain {{[-Q|--quarterly]}} {{assets:investments}} not:{{cryptocurrency}}`
hledger-balancesheet:
**`hledger-balancesheet`**: Show the end balances in asset and liability accounts.

**Examples:**
1. Show the current balances in `Asset` and `Liability` accounts, excluding zeros:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}}`
2. Show just the liquid assets (`Cash` account type):
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} type:C`
3. Include accounts with zero balances, and show the account hierarchy:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} {{[-E|--empty]}} {{[-t|--tree]}}`
4. Show the balances at the end of each month:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} {{[-M|--monthly]}}`
5. Show the balances' market value in home currency at the end of each month:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} {{[-M|--monthly]}} {{[-V|--market]}}`
6. Show quarterly balances, with just the top two levels of account hierarchy:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} {{[-Qt|--quarterly --tree]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}}`
7. Same as above, and generate HTML output in `bs.html`:
   `hledger {{[bs|balancesheet]}} {{[-Qt|--quarterly --tree]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}} {{[-o|--output-file]}} bs.html`
hledger-import:
**`hledger-import`**: Import new transactions from one or more data files to the main journal.

**Examples:**
1. Import new transactions from `bank.csv`, using `bank.csv.rules` to convert:
   `hledger import {{path/to/bank.csv}}`
2. Show what would be imported from these two files, without doing anything:
   `hledger import {{path/to/bank1.csv}} {{path/to/bank2.csv}} --dry-run`
3. Import new transactions from all CSV files, using the same rules for all:
   `hledger import --rules-file {{common.rules}} *.csv`

5. Mark `bank.csv`'s current data as seen, as if already imported:
   `hledger import --catchup {{path/to/bank.csv}}`
6. Mark `bank.csv` as all new, as if not yet imported:
   `rm {{[-f|--force]}} .latest.bank.csv`
hledger-incomestatement:
**`hledger-incomestatement`**: Show revenue inflows and expense outflows during the report period.

**Examples:**
1. Show revenues and expenses (changes in `Revenue` and `Expense` accounts):

2. Show revenues and expenses each month:
   `hledger {{[is|incomestatement]}} {{[-M|--monthly]}}`
3. Show monthly revenues/expenses/totals, largest first, summarised to 2 levels:
   `hledger {{[is|incomestatement]}} {{[-MTAS|--monthly --row-total --average --sort-amount]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}}`
4. Same as above, and generate HTML output in `is.html`:
   `hledger {{[is|incomestatement]}} {{[-MTAS|--monthly --row-total --average --sort-amount]}} {{[-2|--depth 2]}} {{[-o|--output-file]}} is.html`
hledger-print:
**`hledger-print`**: Show full journal entries, representing transactions.

**Examples:**
1. Show all transactions in the default journal file:
   `hledger print`
2. Show transactions, with any implied amounts or costs made explicit:
   `hledger print {{[-x|--explicit]}} --infer-costs`
3. Show transactions from two specified files, with amounts converted to cost:
   `hledger print {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/2023.journal}} {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/2024.journal}} {{[-B|--cost]}}`
4. Show `$` transactions this month in accounts whose name contains `food` but not `groceries`:

   `hledger print amt:'>50' desc:'whole foods'`
6. Show cleared transactions, with `EUR` amounts rounded and with decimal commas:
   `hledger print {{[-C|--cleared]}} --commodity '1000, EUR' --round hard`
7. Write transactions from `foo.journal` as a CSV file:
   `hledger print {{[-f|--file]}} {{path/to/foo.journal}} {{[-o|--output-file]}} {{path/to/output_file.csv}}`
hledger-ui:
**`hledger-ui`**: A terminal interface (TUI) for `hledger`, a robust, friendly plain text accounting app.

**Examples:**
1. Start in the main menu screen, reading from the default journal file:
   `hledger-ui`

   `hledger-ui --info`
7. Display help:
   `hledger-ui {{[-h|--help]}}`
hledger-web:
**`hledger-web`**: A web interface and API for `hledger`, a robust, friendly plain text accounting app.

**Examples:**
1. Start the web app, and a browser if possible, for local viewing and adding only:

   `hledger-web --value now --infer-market-prices`
6. Show the manual in Info format if possible:
   `hledger-web --info`
7. Display help:
   `hledger-web {{[-h|--help]}}`
hledger:
**`hledger`**: A robust, friendly plain text accounting app.

**Examples:**

hlsq:
**`hlsq`**: Display HLS manifests with color and basic filtering.

hn:
**`hn`**: Command-line interface for Hacker News.

1. View stories on Hacker News:

holehe:
**`holehe`**: Check if an email is attached to an account on sites like Twitter, Instagram, Imgur, and over 120 others.

home-manager:

host:

hostapd:

hostess:
**`hostess`**: Manage the `/etc/hosts` file.

hostid:
**`hostid`**: Print the numeric identifier for the current host (not necessarily the IP address).

   `hostid`
hostname:
**`hostname`**: Show or set the system's host name.

**Examples:**
1. Show current host name:

hping:
**`hping`**: This command is an alias of `hping3`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr hping3`
hping3:
**`hping3`**: Advanced ping utility which supports protocols such TCP, UDP, and raw IP.

**Examples:**
1. Ping a destination with 4 ICMP ping requests:
   `hping3 {{[-1|--icmp]}} {{[-c|--count]}} 4 {{ip_or_hostname}}`
2. Ping an IP address over UDP on port 80:
   `hping3 {{[-2|--udp]}} {{[-p|--destport]}} 80 {{[-S|--syn]}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
3. Scan TCP port 80, scanning from the specific local source port 5090:
   `hping3 {{[-V|--verbose]}} {{[-S|--syn]}} {{[-p|--destport]}} 80 {{[-s|--baseport]}} 5090 {{ip_or_hostname}}`
4. Traceroute using a TCP scan to a specific destination port:
   `hping3 {{[-T|--traceroute]}} {{[-V|--verbose]}} {{[-S|--syn]}} {{[-p|--destport]}} {{80}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
5. Scan a set of TCP ports on a specific IP address:
   `hping3 {{[-8|--scan]}} {{80,3000,9000}} {{[-S|--syn]}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
6. Perform a TCP ACK scan to check if a given host is alive:
   `hping3 {{[-c|--count]}} {{2}} {{[-V|--verbose]}} {{[-p|--destport]}} {{80}} {{[-A|--ack]}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
7. Perform a charge test on port 80:
   `hping3 --flood {{[-p|--destport]}} 80 {{[-S|--syn]}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
hr:

hsd-cli:
**`hsd-cli`**: The REST tool for the Handshake blockchain.

1. Retrieve information about the current server:
   `hsd-cli info`
2. Broadcast a local transaction:
   `hsd-cli broadcast {{transaction_hex}}`
3. Retrieve a mempool snapshot:
   `hsd-cli mempool`
4. View a transaction by address or hash:
   `hsd-cli tx {{address_or_hash}}`
5. View a coin by its hash index or address:
   `hsd-cli coin {{hash_index_or_address}}`
6. View a block by height or hash:
   `hsd-cli block {{height_or_hash}}`
7. Reset the chain to the specified block:
   `hsd-cli reset {{height_or_hash}}`
8. Execute an RPC command:
   `hsd-cli rpc {{command}} {{args}}`
hsw-cli:
**`hsw-cli`**: The REST tool for the Handshake wallet.

**Examples:**
1. Unlock the current wallet (timeout in seconds):
   `hsw-cli unlock {{passphrase}} {{timeout}}`
2. Lock the current wallet:
   `hsw-cli lock`
3. View the current wallet's details:
   `hsw-cli get`

html5validator:
**`html5validator`**: Validate HTML5.

1. Validate a specific file:

htmlq:
**`htmlq`**: Use CSS selectors to extract content from HTML files.

htop:

htpasswd:
**`htpasswd`**: Create and manage htpasswd files to protect web server directories using basic authentication.

1. Create/overwrite htpasswd file:
   `htpasswd -c {{path/to/file}} {{username}}`

http-server-upload:

http-server:

http:
**`http`**: HTTPie: an HTTP client designed for testing, debugging, and generally interacting with APIs and HTTP servers.

**Examples:**
1. Make a simple GET request (shows response headers and content):
   `http {{https://example.com}}`
2. Print specific parts of the content (`H`: request headers, `B`: request body, `h`: response headers, `b`: response body, `m`: response metadata):
   `http {{[-p|--print]}} {{H|B|h|b|m|Hh|Hhb|...}} {{https://example.com}}`
3. Specify the HTTP method when sending a request and use a proxy to intercept the request:
   `http {{GET|POST|HEAD|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|...}} --proxy {{http|https}}:{{http://localhost:8080|socks5://localhost:9050|...}} {{https://example.com}}`
4. Follow any `3xx` redirects and specify additional headers in a request:
   `http {{[-F|--follow]}} {{https://example.com}} {{'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0' 'Accept-Encoding: gzip'}}`
5. Authenticate to a server using different authentication methods:
   `http {{[-a|--auth]}} {{username:password|token}} {{[-A|--auth-type]}} {{basic|digest|bearer}} {{GET|POST|...}} {{https://example.com/auth}}`
6. Construct a request but do not send it (similar to a dry-run):
   `http --offline {{GET|DELETE|...}} {{https://example.com}}`
7. Use named sessions for persistent custom headers, auth credentials and cookies:
   `http --session {{session_name|path/to/session.json}} {{[-a|--auth]}} {{username}}:{{password}} {{https://example.com/auth}} {{API-KEY:xxx}}`
8. Upload a file to a form (the example below assumes that the form field is `<input type="file" name="cv" />`):
   `http {{[-f|--form]}} {{POST}} {{https://example.com/upload}} {{cv@path/to/file}}`
httpflow:

1. Capture traffic on all interfaces:

3. Use a `regex` to filter requests by URLs:
   `httpflow -u '{{regex}}'`
4. Read packets from PCAP format binary file:
   `httpflow -r {{out.cap}}`
5. Write the output to a directory:
   `httpflow -w {{path/to/directory}}`
httpie:
**`httpie`**: Management interface for HTTPie.

https:

httpx:

**Examples:**

   `indent {{[-linux|--linux-style]}} {{path/to/source1.c path/to/source2.c ...}}`
2. Format C/C++ source according to the GNU style, saving the indented version to a different file:
   `indent {{[-gnu|--gnu-style]}} {{path/to/source.c}} -o {{path/to/indented_source.c}}`
3. Format C/C++ source according to the style of Kernighan & Ritchie (K&R), no tabs, 3 spaces per indent, and wrap lines at 120 characters:
   `indent {{[-kr|--k-and-r-style]}} {{[-il|--indent-level]}}3 {{[-nut|--no-tabs]}} {{[-l|--line-length]}}120 {{path/to/source.c}} -o {{path/to/indented_source.c}}`
infection:
**`infection`**: A mutation testing framework for PHP.

**Examples:**
1. Analyze code using the configuration file (or create one if it does not exist):
   `infection`
2. Use a specific number of threads:
   `infection {{[-j|--threads]}} {{number_of_threads}}`
3. Specify a minimum Mutation Score Indicator (MSI):
   `infection --min-msi {{percentage}}`
4. Specify a minimum covered code MSI:
   `infection --min-covered-msi {{percentage}}`
5. Use a specific test framework (defaults to PHPUnit):
   `infection --test-framework {{phpunit|phpspec}}`
6. Only mutate lines of code that are covered by tests:
   `infection --only-covered`
7. Display the mutation code that has been applied:
   `infection {{[-s|--show-mutations]}}`
8. Specify the log verbosity:
   `infection --log-verbosity {{default|all|none}}`
influx:
**`influx`**: InfluxDB v1 client.

**Examples:**
1. Connect to an InfluxDB running on localhost with no credentials:
   `influx`
2. Connect with a specific username (will prompt for a password):
   `influx -username {{username}} -password ""`
3. Connect to a specific host:
   `influx -host {{hostname}}`
4. Use a specific database:
   `influx -database {{database_name}}`
5. Execute a given command:
   `influx -execute "{{influxql_command}}"`
6. Return output in a specific format:
   `influx -execute "{{influxql_command}}" -format {{json|csv|column}}`
info:
**`info`**: Read documentation stored in the info format.

**Examples:**
1. Start reading top-level directory menu:
   `info`
2. Start reading at given menu item node from top-level directory:
   `info {{menu_item}}`
3. Start reading at second menu item within first menu item manual:
   `info {{first_menu_item}} {{second_menu_item}}`
initdb:
**`initdb`**: Create a PostgreSQL database cluster on disk.

**Examples:**
1. Create a database cluster at `/usr/local/var/postgres`:
   `initdb {{[-D|--pgdata]}} /usr/local/var/postgres`
inkmake:
**`inkmake`**: GNU Makefile-style SVG exporting using Inkscape's backend.

**Examples:**
1. Export an SVG file executing the specified Inkfile:
   `inkmake {{path/to/Inkfile}}`
2. Execute an Inkfile and show detailed information:
   `inkmake {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{path/to/Inkfile}}`
3. Execute an Inkfile, specifying SVG input file(s) and an output file:
   `inkmake {{[-s|--svg]}} {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-o|--out]}} {{path/to/output_image}} {{path/to/Inkfile}}`
4. Use a custom Inkscape binary as the backend:
   `inkmake {{[-i|--inkscape]}} {{/Applications/Inkscape.app/Contents/Resources/bin/inkscape}} {{path/to/Inkfile}}`
5. Display help:
   `inkmake {{[-h|--help]}}`
inkscape:
**`inkscape`**: An SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) editing program.

**Examples:**
1. Open an SVG file in the Inkscape GUI:
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}}`
2. Export an SVG file into a bitmap with the default format (PNG) and the default resolution (96 DPI):
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-o|--export-filename]}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
3. Export an SVG file into a bitmap of 600x400 pixels (aspect ratio distortion may occur):
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-o|--export-filename]}} {{path/to/file.png}} {{[-w|--export-width]}} 600 {{[-h|--export-height]}} 400`
4. Export the drawing (bounding box of all objects) of an SVG file into a bitmap:
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-o|--export-filename]}} {{path/to/file.png}} {{[-D|--export-area-drawing]}}`
5. Export a single object, given its ID, into a bitmap:
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-i|--export-id]}} {{id}} {{[-o|--export-filename]}} {{object.png}}`
6. Export an SVG document to PDF, converting all texts to paths:
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} {{[-o|--export-filename]}} {{path/to/file.pdf}} {{[-T|--export-text-to-path]}}`
7. Duplicate the object with id="path123", rotate the duplicate 90 degrees, save the file, and quit Inkscape:
   `inkscape {{path/to/file.svg}} --select=path123 --verb="{{EditDuplicate;ObjectRotate90;FileSave;FileQuit}}"`
inkview:
**`inkview`**: Inkscape graphical SVG previewer.

**Examples:**
1. Preview an SVG:
   `inkview {{path/to/file.svg}}`
2. Preview multiple SVGs (use `<ArrowKeys>` to navigate):
   `inkview {{path/to/file1.svg path/to/file2.svg ...}}`
install-nodeversion:
**`install-nodeversion`**: Install Node.js runtime versions for `ps-nvm`.

**Examples:**
1. Install a specific Node.js version:
   `Install-NodeVersion {{node_version}}`
2. Install multiple Node.js versions:
   `Install-NodeVersion {{node_version1 , node_version2 , ...}}`
3. Install latest available version of Node.js 20:
   `Install-NodeVersion ^20`
4. Install the x86 (x86 32-bit) / x64 (x86 64-bit) / arm64 (ARM 64-bit) version of Node.js:
   `Install-NodeVersion {{node_version}} -Architecture {{x86|x64|arm64}}`
5. Use a HTTP proxy to download Node.js:
   `Install-NodeVersion {{node-version}} -Proxy {{http://example.com}}`
install-tl:
**`install-tl`**: TeX Live cross-platform installer.

**Examples:**
1. Start the text-based installer (default on Unix systems):
   `install-tl -no-gui`
2. Start the GUI installer (default on macOS and Windows, requires Tcl/Tk):
   `install-tl -gui`
3. Install TeX Live as defined in a specific profile file:
   `install-tl -profile {{path/to/texlive.profile}}`
4. Start the installer with the settings from a specific profile file:
   `install-tl -init-from-file {{path/to/texlive.profile}}`
5. Start the installer for installation on a portable device, like a USB stick:
   `install-tl -portable`
6. Display help:
   `install-tl -help`
install:
**`install`**: Copy files and set attributes.

**Examples:**
1. Copy files to the destination:
   `install {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
2. Copy files to the destination, setting their ownership:
   `install {{[-o|--owner]}} {{user}} {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
3. Copy files to the destination, setting their group ownership:
   `install {{[-g|--group]}} {{user}} {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
4. Copy files to the destination, setting their `mode`:
   `install {{[-m|--mode]}} {{+x}} {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
5. Copy files and apply access/modification times of source to the destination:
   `install {{[-p|--preserve-timestamps]}} {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
6. Copy files and create the directories at the destination if they don't exist:
   `install -D {{path/to/source_file1 path/to/source_file2 ...}} {{path/to/destination}}`
interdiff:
**`interdiff`**: Show differences between two diff files.

**Examples:**
1. Compare diff files:
   `interdiff {{old_file}} {{new_file}}`
2. Compare diff files, ignoring whitespace:
   `interdiff {{[-w|--ignore-all-space]}} {{old_file}} {{new_file}}`
ionic:
**`ionic`**: A framework to build hybrid mobile apps.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new project:
   `ionic start`
2. Start a local dev server for app dev/testing:
   `ionic serve`
3. Generate new app component, directive, page, pipe, provider, or tabs:
   `ionic g {{page}}`
4. Run app on an Android/iOS device:
   `ionic cordova run {{android|ios}} --device`
5. Check the health of an Ionic app:
   `ionic doctor {{check}}`
6. Display versions of Ionic, Cordova, environment, etc.:
   `ionic info`
ioping:
**`ioping`**: Monitor I/O latency in real time.

**Examples:**
1. Show disk I/O latency using the default values and the current directory:
   `ioping .`
2. Measure latency on `/tmp` using 10 requests of 1 megabyte each:
   `ioping {{[-c|-count]}} 10 {{[-s|-size]}} 1M /tmp`
3. Measure disk seek rate on `/dev/sdX`:
   `ioping {{[-R|-rapid]}} {{/dev/sdX}}`
4. Measure disk sequential speed on `/dev/sdX`:
   `ioping {{[-RL|-rapid -linear]}} {{/dev/sdX}}`
iotop:
**`iotop`**: Display a table of current I/O usage by processes or threads.

**Examples:**
1. Start top-like I/O monitor:
   `sudo iotop`
2. Show only processes or threads actually doing I/O:
   `sudo iotop {{[-o|--only]}}`
3. Show I/O usage in non-interactive mode:
   `sudo iotop {{[-b|--batch]}}`
4. Show only I/O usage of processes (default is to show all threads):
   `sudo iotop {{[-P|--processes]}}`
5. Show I/O usage of given PID(s):
   `sudo iotop {{[-p|--pid]}} {{pid}}`
6. Show I/O usage of a given user:
   `sudo iotop {{[-u|--user]}} {{user}}`
7. Show accumulated I/O instead of bandwidth:
   `sudo iotop {{[-a|--accumulated]}}`
ipaggcreate:
**`ipaggcreate`**: Produce aggregate statistics of TCP/IP dumps.

**Examples:**
1. Count the number of packets sent from each source address appearing in a PCAP file:
   `ipaggcreate --src {{path/to/file.pcap}}`
2. Group and count packets read from a network interface by IP packet length:
   `ipaggcreate --interface {{eth0}} --length`
3. Count the number of bytes sent between each address pair appearing in a PCAP file:
   `ipaggcreate --address-pairs --bytes {{path/to/file.pcap}}`
ipaggmanip:
**`ipaggmanip`**: Manipulate aggregate statistics produced by `ipaggcreate`.

**Examples:**
1. Combine labels equal in their high-order bits:
   `ipaggmanip {{[-p|--prefix]}} {{16}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Remove labels with a count smaller than a given number of bytes and output a random sample of such labels:
   `ipaggmanip --cut-smaller {{100}} --cull-labels {{5}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Replace each label's count with 1 if it is non-zero:
   `ipaggmanip {{[-P|--posterize]}} {{path/to/file}}`
ipcalc:
**`ipcalc`**: Calculate IP information (subnet, broadcast, host range) from an IP address and netmask.

**Examples:**
1. Display network info for an IP address:
   `ipcalc {{192.168.0.1}}`
2. Display network info using CIDR notation:
   `ipcalc {{192.168.0.1}}/{{24}}`
3. Display network info using a dotted decimal netmask:
   `ipcalc {{192.168.0.1}} {{255.255.255.0}}`
4. Suppress bitwise output:
   `ipcalc {{[-b|--nobinary]}} {{192.168.0.1}}`
5. Split a network into specified sized blocks:
   `ipcalc {{[-s|--split]}} {{size1 size2 size3 ...}} {{192.168.0.1}}`
6. Display version:
   `ipcalc {{[-v|--version]}}`
ipcs:
**`ipcs`**: Show information about the usage of System V IPC facilities: shared memory segments, message queues, and semaphore arrays.

**Examples:**
1. Show information about all active IPC facilities:
   `ipcs`
2. Show information about active shared [m]emory segments, message [q]ueues or [s]emaphore sets:
   `ipcs {{--shmems|--queues|--semaphores}}`
3. Show full details on the resource with a specific ID:
   `ipcs {{--shmems|--queues|--semaphores}} {{[-i|--id]}} {{resource_id}}`
4. Show limits in [b]ytes or in a human-readable format:
   `ipcs {{[-l|--limits]}} {{--bytes|--human}}`
5. Show summary about current usage:
   `ipcs {{[-u|--summary]}}`
6. Show creator's and owner's UIDs and PIDs for all IPC facilities:
   `ipcs {{[-c|--creator]}}`
7. Show the PID of the last operators for all IPC facilities:
   `ipcs {{[-p|--pid]}}`
8. Show last access times for all IPC facilities:
   `ipcs {{[-t|--time]}}`
iperf:
**`iperf`**: Measure network bandwidth between computers.

**Examples:**
1. Run on server:
   `iperf {{[-s|--server]}}`
2. Run on server using UDP mode and set server port to listen on 5001:
   `iperf {{[-u|--udp]}} {{[-s|--server]}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{5001}}`
3. Run on client:
   `iperf {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_address}}`
4. Run on client every 2 seconds:
   `iperf {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_address}} {{[-i|--interval]}} {{2}}`
5. Run on client with 5 parallel threads:
   `iperf {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_address}} {{[-P|--parallel]}} {{5}}`
6. Run on client using UDP mode:
   `iperf {{[-u|--udp]}} {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_address}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{5001}}`
iperf3:
**`iperf3`**: Traffic generator for testing network bandwidth.

**Examples:**
1. Run iperf3 as a server:
   `iperf3 {{[-s|--server]}}`
2. Run an iperf3 server on a specific port:
   `iperf3 {{[-s|--server]}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}}`
3. Start bandwidth test:
   `iperf3 {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_ip}}`
4. Run iperf3 in multiple parallel streams:
   `iperf3 {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_ip}} {{[-P|--parallel]}} {{streams}}`
5. Run the test in reverse direction (server sends data to client):
   `iperf3 {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_ip}} {{[-R|--reverse]}}`
6. Set the duration of the test:
   `iperf3 {{[-c|--client]}} {{server_ip}} {{[-t|--time]}} {{seconds}}`
ipfs:
**`ipfs`**: Inter Planetary File System.

**Examples:**
1. Add a file from local to the filesystem, pin it, and print the relative hash:
   `ipfs add {{path/to/file}}`
2. Add a directory and its files recursively from local to the filesystem and print the relative hash:
   `ipfs add {{[-r|--recursive]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Save a remote file and give it a name but not pin it:
   `ipfs get {{hash}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. Pin a remote file locally:
   `ipfs pin add {{hash}}`
5. Display pinned files:
   `ipfs pin ls`
6. Unpin a file from the local storage:
   `ipfs pin rm {{hash}}`
7. Remove unpinned files from local storage:
   `ipfs repo gc`
ipinfo:
**`ipinfo`**: Official CLI for the IPinfo.io IP geolocation and network intelligence API.

**Examples:**
1. Display details for your current IP address:
   `ipinfo myip`
2. Display details for a specific IP address:
   `ipinfo {{ip_address}}`
3. Display details for multiple IP addresses in bulk from a file:
   `ipinfo bulk {{path/to/ips.txt}}`
4. Display details for a CIDR or IP range:
   `ipinfo bulk {{cidr_range}}`
5. Display only specific fields from IP lookup results:
   `ipinfo {{ip_address}} {{[-f|--field]}} {{hostname,country,org}}`
6. Summarize details for a group of IP addresses:
   `ipinfo summarize {{path/to/ips.txt}}`
7. Extract IP addresses from text and highlight them:
   `ipinfo grepip {{path/to/file.txt}}`
8. Display help:
   `ipinfo {{[-h|--help]}}`
ipmitool:
**`ipmitool`**: Interface with the Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI).

**Examples:**
1. Start the IPMI driver for local connections:
   `systemctl start ipmidrv`
2. Open IPMI shell on the local hardware:
   `sudo ipmitool shell`
3. Open IPMI shell on a remote host:
   `ipmitool -H {{ip_address}} -U {{user_name}} shell`
ippeveprinter:
**`ippeveprinter`**: A simple IPP Everywhere printer server.

**Examples:**
1. Run the server with a specific service name:
   `ippeveprinter "{{service_name}}"`
2. Load printer attributes from a PPD file:
   `ippeveprinter -P {{path/to/file.ppd}} "{{service_name}}"`
3. Run the `file` command whenever a job is sent to the server:
   `ippeveprinter -c {{/usr/bin/file}} "{{service_name}}"`
4. Specify the directory that will hold the print files (by default, a directory under the user's temporary directory):
   `ippeveprinter -d {{spool_directory}} "{{service_name}}"`
5. Keep the print documents in the spool directory rather than deleting them:
   `ippeveprinter -k "{{service_name}}"`
6. Specify the printer speed in pages/minute unit (10 by default):
   `ippeveprinter -s {{speed}} "{{service_name}}"`
ippfind:
**`ippfind`**: Find services registered with a DNS server or available through local devices.

**Examples:**
1. List IPP printers registered on the network with their status:
   `ippfind {{[-l|--ls]}}`
2. Send a specific PostScript document to every PostScript printer on the network:
   `ippfind --txt-pdl application/postscript {{[-x|--exec]}} ipptool -f {{path/to/document.ps}} '{}' print-job.test \;`

   `ippfind --txt-pdl application/postscript {{[-x|--exec]}} ipptool -f onepage-letter.ps '{}' print-job.test \;`
4. Send a PostScript test document to every PostScript printer on the network, whose name matches a `regex`:
   `ippfind --txt-pdl application/postscript {{[-h|--host]}} {{regex}} {{[-x|--exec]}} ipptool -f onepage-letter.ps '{}' print-job.test \;`
ipptool:
**`ipptool`**: Issue IPP requests and receive printer's/server's responses.

**Examples:**
1. Get all attributes and their values supported by a printer:
   `ipptool ipp://{{printer_uri}} get-completed-jobs.test`
2. Get the list of completed jobs of a printer:
   `ipptool ipp://{{printer_uri}} get-completed-jobs.test`
3. Send an email notification when a printer changes:
   `ipptool -d recipient=mailto:{{email}} ipp://{{printer_uri}} create-printer-subscription.test`
iproxy:
**`iproxy`**: A proxy that binds local TCP ports to be forwarded to the specified ports on a usbmux device.

**Examples:**
1. Bind a local TCP port and forward it to a port on the connected USB device:
   `iproxy {{local_port}}:{{device_port}}`
2. Bind multiple local TCP ports and forward them to the respective ports on the connected USB device:
   `iproxy {{local_port1}}:{{device_port1}} {{local_port2}}:{{device_port2}}`
3. Bind a local port and forward it to a specific device by UDID:
   `iproxy --udid {{device_udid}} {{local_port}}:{{device_port}}`
4. Bind a local port and forward it to a network-connected device with Wi-Fi sync enabled:
   `iproxy --network {{local_port}}:{{device_port}}`
ipscan:
**`ipscan`**: A fast network scanner designed to be simple to use.

**Examples:**
1. Scan a specific IP address:
   `ipscan {{192.168.0.1}}`
2. Scan a range of IP addresses:
   `ipscan {{192.168.0.1-254}}`
3. Scan a range of IP addresses and save the results to a file:
   `ipscan {{192.168.0.1-254}} -o {{path/to/output.txt}}`
4. Scan IPs with a specific set of ports:
   `ipscan {{192.168.0.1-254}} -p {{80,443,22}}`
5. Scan with a delay between requests to avoid network congestion:
   `ipscan {{192.168.0.1-254}} -d {{200}}`
6. Display help:
   `ipscan --help`
ipsumdump:
**`ipsumdump`**: Summarise TCP/IP dumps into a human and machine readable ASCII format.

1. Print the source and destination IP addresses of all packets in a PCAP file:
   `ipsumdump --src --dst {{path/to/file.pcap}}`

   `ipsumdump --src --dst --length --anonymize {{path/to/file.pcap}}`
ipython:
**`ipython`**: A Python shell with automatic history, dynamic object introspection, easier configuration, command completion, access to the system shell and more.

1. Start a REPL (interactive shell):
   `ipython`

   `ipython history clear`
irb:
**`irb`**: Interactive Ruby shell.

**Examples:**
1. Start the interactive shell:
   `irb`
irssi:
**`irssi`**: Text based IRC client.

**Examples:**
1. Open Irssi and connect to a server with a nickname:
   `irssi {{[-n|--nick]}} {{nickname}} {{[-c|--connect]}} {{irc.example.com}}`
2. Open Irssi and connect with a specific server on a given port:
   `irssi {{[-c|--connect]}} {{irc.example.com}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}}`
3. [Interactive] Join a channel:
   `/join {{#channelname}}`
4. [Interactive] Change active window (starts at 1):
   `/win {{window_number}}`
5. [Interactive] Exit the application cleanly and quitting any server(s):
   `/quit`
6. Display help:
   `irssi {{[-?|--help]}}`
is-up:
**`is-up`**: Check whether a website is up or down.

**Examples:**
1. Check the status of the specified website:
   `is-up {{example.com}}`
isisdl:
**`isisdl`**: A downloading utility for ISIS of TU-Berlin. Download all your files and videos from ISIS.

**Examples:**
1. Start the synchronization process:
   `isisdl`
2. Limit the download rate to 20 MiB/s and download with 5 threads:
   `isisdl --download-rate {{20}} --max-num-threads {{5}}`
3. Run the initialization configuration wizard:
   `isisdl --init`
4. Run the additional configuration wizard:
   `isisdl --config`

   `isisdl --compress`
ispell:
**`ispell`**: Interactive spell checking.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive session:
   `ispell`
2. Check for typos in the specified file and interactively apply suggestions:
   `ispell {{path/to/file}}`
3. Display version:
   `ispell -v`
isutf8:
**`isutf8`**: Check whether text files contain valid UTF-8.

**Examples:**
1. Check whether the specified files contain valid UTF-8:
   `isutf8 {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
2. Print errors using multiple lines:
   `isutf8 {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
3. Do not print anything to `stdout`, indicate the result merely with the exit code:
   `isutf8 {{[-q|--quiet]}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
4. Only print the names of the files containing invalid UTF-8:
   `isutf8 {{[-l|--list]}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`

   `isutf8 {{[-i|--invert]}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
iverilog:
**`iverilog`**: Preprocesses and compiles Verilog HDL (IEEE-1364) code into executable programs for simulation.
