   `nix registry pin {{entry}} {{github:owner/repo/branch_or_revision}}`
3. Add a new entry that always points to the latest version of a GitHub repository, updating automatically:
   `nix registry add {{entry}} {{github:owner/repo}}`
4. Remove a registry entry:
   `nix registry remove {{entry}}`
5. See documentation about what Nix flake registries are:
   `nix registry --help`
nix-repl:
**`nix-repl`**: Start an interactive environment for evaluating Nix expressions.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive environment for evaluating Nix expressions:
   `nix repl`
2. Load all packages from a flake (e.g. `nixpkgs`) into scope:
   `:lf {{nixpkgs}}`
3. Build a package from an expression:
   `:b {{expression}}`
4. Start a shell with package from the expression available:
   `:u {{expression}}`
5. Start a shell with dependencies of the package from the expression available:
   `:s {{expression}}`
nix-run:
**`nix-run`**: Run an application from a Nix flake.

**Examples:**
1. Run the default application in the flake in the current directory:
   `nix run`
2. Run a command whose name matches the package name from nixpkgs (if you want a different command from that package, see `tldr nix shell`):
   `nix run nixpkgs#{{pkg}}`
3. Run a command with provided arguments:
   `nix run nixpkgs#{{vim}} -- {{path/to/file}}`
4. Run from a remote repository:
   `nix run {{remote_name}}:{{owner}}/{{repository}}`
5. Run from a remote repository using a specific tag, revision, or branch:
   `nix run {{remote_name}}:{{owner}}/{{repository}}/{{reference}}`
6. Run from a remote repository specifying a subdirectory and a program:
   `nix run "{{remote_name}}:{{owner}}/{{repository}}?dir={{dir_name}}#{{app}}"`
7. Run the flake of a GitHub pull request:
   `nix run github:{{owner}}/{{repository}}/pull/{{number}}/head`
nix-search:
**`nix-search`**: Search for packages in a Nix flake.

**Examples:**
1. Search `nixpkgs` for a package based on its name or description:
   `nix search {{nixpkgs}} {{search_term}}`
2. Show description of a package from nixpkgs:
   `nix search {{nixpkgs#pkg}}`
3. Show all packages available from a flake on github:
   `nix search {{github:owner/repo}}`
nix-shell.2:
**`nix-shell.2`**: Start an interactive shell based on a Nix expression.

**Examples:**
1. Start with nix expression in `shell.nix` or `default.nix` in the current directory:
   `nix-shell`
2. Run shell command in non-interactive shell and exit:
   `nix-shell --run "{{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}"`
3. Start with expression in `default.nix` in the current directory:
   `nix-shell {{default.nix}}`
4. Start with packages loaded from nixpkgs:
   `nix-shell {{[-p|--packages]}} {{package1 package2 ...}}`
5. Start with packages loaded from specific nixpkgs revision:
   `nix-shell {{[-p|--packages]}} {{package1 package2 ...}} {{[-I|--include]}} nixpkgs={{https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/archive/nixpkgs_revision.tar.gz}}`
6. Evaluate rest of file in specific interpreter, for use in `#!-scripts` (see <https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/#use-as-a-interpreter>):
   `nix-shell -i {{interpreter}} {{[-p|--packages]}} {{package1 package2 ...}}`
nix-shell.3:
**`nix-shell.3`**: Start a shell in which the specified packages are available.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive shell with some packages from `nixpkgs`:
   `nix shell {{nixpkgs#pkg1 nixpkgs#packageSet.pkg2 ...}}`
2. Start a shell providing a package from an older version of `nixpkgs` (21.05):
   `nix shell {{nixpkgs/nixos-21.05#pkg}}`
3. Start a shell with the "default package" from a flake in the current directory, printing build logs if any builds happen:
   `nix shell -L`
4. Start a shell with a package from a flake on GitHub:
   `nix shell {{github:owner/repo#pkg}}`
5. Run a command in a shell with a package:
   `nix shell {{nixpkgs#pkg}} -c {{some-cmd --someflag 'Some other arguments'}}`
nix-shell:
**`nix-shell`**: `nix-shell` can refer to multiple commands with the same name.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the traditional shell before version 2.4 of Nix:
   `tldr nix-shell.2`
2. View documentation for nix3 shell:
   `tldr nix shell.3`
nix-store.2:
**`nix-store.2`**: Manipulate or query the Nix store.

**Examples:**
1. Collect garbage, such as removing unused paths:
   `nix-store --gc`
2. Hard-link identical files together to reduce space usage:
   `nix-store --optimise`
3. Delete a specific store path (must be unused):
   `nix-store --delete /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
4. Show all dependencies of a store path (package), in a tree format:
   `nix-store {{[-q|--query]}} --tree /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
5. Calculate the total size of a certain store path with all the dependencies:
   `du {{[-cLsh|--total --dereference --summarize --human-readable]}} $(nix-store {{[-q|--query]}} --references /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}})`
6. Show all dependents of a particular store path:
   `nix-store {{[-q|--query]}} --referrers /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
nix-store.3:
**`nix-store.3`**: Manipulate the Nix store.

**Examples:**
1. Collect garbage, i.e. remove unused paths to reduce space usage:
   `nix store gc`
2. Hard-link identical files together to reduce space usage:
   `nix store optimise`
3. Delete a specific store path (must be unused):
   `nix store delete /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
4. List a contents of the store path, on a remote store:
   `nix store --store {{https://cache.nixos.org}} ls /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
5. Show the differences in versions between two store paths, with their respective dependencies:
   `nix store diff-closures /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}} /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
nix-store:
**`nix-store`**: `nix-store` can refer to multiple commands with the same name.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the traditional store before version 2.4 of Nix:
   `tldr nix-store.2`
2. View documentation for nix3 store:
   `tldr nix store.3`
nix-why-depends:
**`nix-why-depends`**: Show why a package depends on another package.

**Examples:**
1. Show why the currently running NixOS system requires a certain store path:
   `nix why-depends {{/run/current-system}} /nix/store/{{checksum-package-version.ext}}`
2. Show why a package from nixpkgs requires another package as a build-time dependency:
   `nix why-depends --derivation {{nixpkgs#dependent}} {{nixpkgs#dependency}}`
nix:
**`nix`**: A powerful package manager that makes package management reliable, reproducible, and declarative.

**Examples:**
1. Enable the `nix` command:
   `mkdir {{[-p|--parents]}} ~/.config/nix; echo 'experimental-features = nix-command flakes' > ~/.config/nix/nix.conf`
2. Search for a package in nixpkgs via its name or description:
   `nix search nixpkgs {{search_term}}`
3. Start a shell with the specified packages from nixpkgs available:
   `nix shell {{nixpkgs#pkg1 nixpkgs#pkg2 nixpkgs#pkg3 ...}}`
4. Install some packages from nixpkgs permanently:
   `nix profile install {{nixpkgs#pkg1 nixpkgs#pkg2 nixpkgs#pkg3 ...}}`
5. Remove unused paths from Nix store to free up space:
   `nix store gc`
6. Start an interactive environment for evaluating Nix expressions:
   `nix repl`
7. Display help for a specific subcommand:
   `nix help {{subcommand}}`
nixpkgs-review:
**`nixpkgs-review`**: Review pull requests in the NixOS packages repository (nixpkgs).

**Examples:**
1. Build changed packages in the specified pull request:
   `nixpkgs-review pr {{pr_number|pr_url}}`
2. Build changed packages and post a comment with a report (requires setting up a token in `hub`, `gh`, or the `$GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable):
   `nixpkgs-review pr --post-result {{pr_number|pr_url}}`
3. Build changed packages and print a report:
   `nixpkgs-review pr --print-result {{pr_number|pr_url}}`
4. Build changed packages in a local commit:
   `nixpkgs-review rev {{HEAD}}`
5. Build changed packages that haven't been committed yet:
   `nixpkgs-review wip`
6. Build changed packages that have been staged:
   `nixpkgs-review wip --staged`
nkf:
**`nkf`**: Network kanji filter: convert kanji code from one encoding to another.

**Examples:**
1. Convert to UTF-8 encoding:
   `nkf -w {{path/to/file.txt}}`
2. Convert to SHIFT_JIS encoding:
   `nkf -s {{path/to/file.txt}}`
3. Convert to UTF-8 encoding and overwrite the file:
   `nkf -w --overwrite {{path/to/file.txt}}`
4. Use LF as the new line code and overwrite (UNIX type):
   `nkf -d --overwrite {{path/to/file.txt}}`
5. Use CRLF as the new line code and overwrite (windows type):
   `nkf -c --overwrite {{path/to/file.txt}}`
6. Decrypt mime file and overwrite:
   `nkf -m --overwrite {{path/to/file.txt}}`
nl:
**`nl`**: Number lines from a file or from `stdin`.

**Examples:**
1. Number non-blank lines in a file:
   `nl {{path/to/file}}`
2. Read from `stdin`:
   `{{command}} | nl`
3. Number [a]ll body lines including blank lines or do [n]ot number body lines:
   `nl {{[-b|--body-numbering]}} {{a|n}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. Number only the body lines that match a basic `regex` (BRE) [p]attern:
   `nl {{[-b|--body-numbering]}} p'FooBar[0-9]' {{path/to/file}}`
5. Use a specific increment for line numbering:
   `nl {{[-i|--line-increment]}} {{increment}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Specify the line numbering format to [r]ight or [l]eft justified, keeping leading [z]eros or [n]ot:
   `nl {{[-n|--number-format]}} {{rz|ln|rn}}`
7. Specify the line numbering's width (6 by default):
   `nl {{[-w|--number-width]}} {{col_width}} {{path/to/file}}`
8. Use a specific string to separate the line numbers from the lines (`TAB` by default):
   `nl {{[-s|--number-separator]}} {{separator}} {{path/to/file}}`
nload:
**`nload`**: Visualize network usage in the terminal.

**Examples:**
1. View all network traffic (use the `<ArrowKeys>` to switch interfaces):
   `nload`
2. View network traffic on specific interfaces (use the `<ArrowKeys>` to switch interfaces):
   `nload devices {{interface1 interface2 ...}}`
nm-classic:
**`nm-classic`**: This command is an alias of `nm`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr nm`
nm:
**`nm`**: List symbol names in object files.

**Examples:**
1. List global (extern) functions in a file (prefixed with T):
   `nm {{[-g|--extern-only]}} {{path/to/file.o}}`
2. List only undefined symbols in a file:
   `nm {{[-u|--undefined-only]}} {{path/to/file.o}}`
3. List all symbols, even debugging symbols:
   `nm {{[-a|--debug-syms]}} {{path/to/file.o}}`
4. Demangle C++ symbols (make them readable):
   `nm {{[-C|--demangle]}} {{path/to/file.o}}`
nmap:
**`nmap`**: Network exploration tool and security/port scanner.

**Examples:**
1. Scan the top 1000 ports of a remote host with various [v]erbosity levels:
   `nmap -v{{1|2|3}} {{ip_or_hostname}}`
2. Run a ping sweep over an entire [s]ub[n]et or individual hosts very aggressively:
   `nmap -T5 -sn {{192.168.0.0/24|ip_or_hostname1,ip_or_hostname2,...}}`
3. Enable OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute of hosts from a file:
   `sudo nmap -A -iL {{path/to/file.txt}}`
4. Scan a specific list of [p]orts (use `-p-` for all ports from 1 to 65535):
   `nmap -p {{port1,port2,...}} {{ip_or_host1,ip_or_host2,...}}`
5. Perform service and version detection of the top 1000 ports using default NSE scripts, writing results (`-oA`) to output files:
   `nmap -sC -sV -oA {{top-1000-ports}} {{ip_or_host1,ip_or_host2,...}}`
6. Scan target(s) carefully using `default and safe` NSE scripts:
   `nmap --script "default and safe" {{ip_or_host1,ip_or_host2,...}}`
7. Scan for web servers running on standard [p]orts 80 and 443 using all available `http-*` NSE scripts:
   `nmap --script "http-*" {{ip_or_host1,ip_or_host2,...}} -p 80,443`
8. Attempt evading IDS/IPS detection by using an extremely slow scan (`-T0`), [D]ecoy source addresses, [f]ragmented packets, random data and other methods:
   `sudo nmap -T0 -D {{decoy_ip1,decoy_ip2,...}} --source-port {{53}} -f --data-length {{16}} -Pn {{ip_or_host}}`
nmblookup:
**`nmblookup`**: Discover SMB shares.

**Examples:**
1. Find hosts in the local network with SMB shares:
   `nmblookup {{[-S|--status]}} '*'`
2. Find hosts in the local network with SMB shares run by SAMBA:
   `nmblookup {{[-S|--status]}} __SAMBA__`
nms:
**`nms`**: Tool that recreates the famous data decryption effect seen in the 1992 movie Sneakers from `stdin`.

**Examples:**
1. Decrypt text after a keystroke:
   `echo "{{Hello, World!}}" | nms`
2. Decrypt output immediately, without waiting for a keystroke:
   `{{ls -la}} | nms -a`
3. Decrypt the content of a file, with a custom output color:
   `cat {{path/to/file}} | nms -a -f {{blue|white|yellow|black|magenta|green|red}}`
4. Clear the screen before decrypting:
   `{{command}} | nms -a -c`
nnn:
**`nnn`**: Interactive terminal file manager and disk usage analyzer.

**Examples:**
1. Open the current directory (or specify one as the first argument):
   `nnn`
2. Start in [d]etailed mode:
   `nnn -d`
3. Show [H]idden files:
   `nnn -H`
4. Open an existing [b]ookmark (defined in the `$NNN_BMS` environment variable):
   `nnn -b {{bookmark_name}}`
5. Sort files on [a]pparent disk usage / [d]isk usage / [e]xtension / [r]everse / [s]ize / [t]ime / [v]ersion:
   `nnn -T {{a|d|e|r|s|t|v}}`
6. Open a file you have selected. Select the file then press `<o>`, and type a program to open the file in:
   `nnn -o`
node:
**`node`**: Server-side JavaScript platform (Node.js).

**Examples:**
1. Run a JavaScript file:
   `node {{path/to/file}}`
2. Start a REPL (interactive shell):
   `node`
3. Execute the specified file restarting the process when an imported file is changed (requires Node.js version 18.11+):
   `node --watch {{path/to/file}}`
4. Evaluate JavaScript code by passing it as an argument:
   `node {{[-e|--eval]}} "{{code}}"`
5. Evaluate and print the result, useful to print node's dependencies versions:
   `node {{[-p|--print]}} "process.versions"`
6. Activate inspector, pausing execution until a debugger is connected once source code is fully parsed:
   `node --no-lazy --inspect-brk {{path/to/file}}`
nodemon:
**`nodemon`**: Watch files and automatically restart a node application when changes are detected.

**Examples:**
1. Execute the specified file and watch a specific file for changes:
   `nodemon {{path/to/file.js}}`
2. Manually restart nodemon (note nodemon must already be active for this to work):
   `rs`
3. Ignore specific files:
   `nodemon {{[-i|--ignore]}} {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
4. Pass arguments to the node application:
   `nodemon {{path/to/file.js}} {{arguments}}`
5. Pass arguments to node itself if they're not nodemon arguments already (e.g. `--inspect`):
   `nodemon {{arguments}} {{path/to/file.js}}`
6. Run an arbitrary non-node script:
   `nodemon {{[-x|--exec]}} "{{command_to_run_script}} {{options}}" {{path/to/script}}`
7. Run a Python script:
   `nodemon {{[-x|--exec]}} "python {{options}}" {{path/to/file.py}}`
nodenv:
**`nodenv`**: Manage Node.js versions.

**Examples:**
1. Install a specific version of Node.js:
   `nodenv install {{version}}`
2. Display a list of available versions:
   `nodenv install --list`
3. Use a specific version of Node.js across the whole system:
   `nodenv global {{version}}`
4. Use a specific version of Node.js with a directory:
   `nodenv local {{version}}`
5. Display the Node.js version for the current directory:
   `nodenv version`
6. Display the location of a Node.js installed command (e.g. `npm`):
   `nodenv which {{command}}`
noglob:
**`noglob`**: Execute a command in Zsh without globbing (expanding wildcard patterns).

**Examples:**
1. Fetch an unquoted and unescaped URL:
   `noglob curl {{https://example.com?a=1}}`
2. Open a file named with a literal asterisk:
   `noglob less {{*.txt}}`
nohup:
**`nohup`**: Allows for a process to live when the terminal gets killed.

**Examples:**
1. Run a process that can live beyond the terminal:
   `nohup {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}`
2. Launch `nohup` in background mode:
   `nohup {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}} &`
3. Run a shell script that can live beyond the terminal:
   `nohup {{path/to/script.sh}} &`
4. Run a process and write the output to a specific file:
   `nohup {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}} > {{path/to/output_file}} &`
nokogiri:
**`nokogiri`**: An HTML, XML, SAX, and Reader parser.

**Examples:**
1. Parse the contents of a URL or file:
   `nokogiri {{url|path/to/file}}`
2. Parse as a specific type:
   `nokogiri {{url|path/to/file}} --type {{xml|html}}`
3. Load a specific initialization file before parsing:
   `nokogiri {{url|path/to/file}} -C {{path/to/config_file}}`
4. Parse using a specific encoding:
   `nokogiri {{url|path/to/file}} {{[-E|--encoding]}} {{encoding}}`
5. Validate using a RELAX NG file:
   `nokogiri {{url|path/to/file}} --rng {{url|path/to/file}}`
nomad:
**`nomad`**: Distributed, highly available, datacenter-aware scheduler.

**Examples:**
1. Show the status of nodes in the cluster:
   `nomad node status`
2. Validate a job file:
   `nomad job validate {{path/to/file.nomad}}`
3. Plan a job for execution on the cluster:
   `nomad job plan {{path/to/file.nomad}}`
4. Run a job on the cluster:
   `nomad job run {{path/to/file.nomad}}`
5. Show the status of jobs currently running on the cluster:
   `nomad job status`
6. Show the detailed status information about a specific job:
   `nomad job status {{job_name}}`
7. Follow the logs of a specific allocation:
   `nomad alloc logs {{alloc_id}}`
8. Show the status of storage volumes:
   `nomad volume status`
nop:
**`nop`**: Check validity and pretty-print graphs in canonical format.

**Examples:**
1. Pretty-print one or more graphs in canonical format:
   `nop {{path/to/input1.gv path/to/input2.gv ...}} > {{path/to/output.gv}}`
2. Check one or more graphs for validity, producing no output graph:
   `nop -p {{path/to/input1.gv path/to/input2.gv ...}}`
3. Display help:
   `nop -?`
noseyparker:
**`noseyparker`**: Scan text and Git history for secrets and sensitive information.

**Examples:**
1. Scan a local file or directory for secrets:
   `noseyparker scan {{path/to/file_or_directory}} {{[-d|--datastore]}} {{path/to/datastore.np}}`
2. Show a report from a previous scan:
   `noseyparker report {{[-d|--datastore]}} {{path/to/datastore.np}}`
3. Show a report in different format (default is `human`):
   `noseyparker report {{[-d|--datastore]}} {{path/to/datastore.np}} {{[-f|--format]}} {{human|json|jsonl|sarif}}`
4. Scan a remote Git repo (and Git history) for secrets:
   `noseyparker scan --git-url {{url}} {{[-d|--datastore]}} {{path/to/datastore.np}}`
5. Scan all GitHub repositories of a user or organization for secrets:
   `noseyparker scan {{--github-user|--github-organization}} {{username_or_org_name}} {{[-d|--datastore]}} {{path/to/datastore.np}}`
6. List all scan rules:
   `noseyparker rules list`
7. List all GitHub repositories of a user or organization:
   `noseyparker github repos list {{--user|--organization}} {{username_or_org_name}}`
noti:
**`noti`**: Monitor a process and trigger a banner notification.

**Examples:**
1. Display a notification when `tar` finishes compressing files:
   `noti {{tar -cjf example.tar.bz2 example/}}`
2. Display a notification even when you put it after the command to watch:
   `{{command_to_watch}}; noti`
3. Monitor a process by PID and trigger a notification when the PID disappears:
   `noti {{[-w|--pwatch]}} {{process_id}}`
notify-send:
**`notify-send`**: Use the current desktop environment's notification system to create a notification.

**Examples:**
1. Show a notification with the title "Test" and the content "This is a test":
   `notify-send "Test" "This is a test"`
2. Show a notification with a custom icon:
   `notify-send {{[-i|--icon]}} {{icon.png}} "{{Test}}" "{{This is a test}}"`
3. Show a notification for 5 seconds:
   `notify-send {{[-t|--expire-time]}} 5000 "{{Test}}" "{{This is a test}}"`
4. Show a notification with the specified urgency level (default: normal):
   `notify-send {{[-u|--urgency]}} {{low|normal|critical}} "{{Test}}" "{{This is a test}}"`
5. Show a notification with an app's icon and name:
   `notify-send "{{Test}}" {{[-i|--icon]}} {{google-chrome}} {{[-a|--app-name]}} "{{Google Chrome}}"`
notmuch:
**`notmuch`**: Index, search, read, and tag large collections of email messages.

**Examples:**
1. Configure for first use:
   `notmuch setup`
2. Add a tag for all messages matching a search term:
   `notmuch tag +{{custom_tag}} "{{search_term}}"`
3. Remove a tag for all messages matching a search term:
   `notmuch tag -{{custom_tag}} "{{search_term}}"`
4. Count messages matching the given search term:
   `notmuch count --output={{messages|threads}} "{{search_term}}"`
5. Search for messages matching the given search term:
   `notmuch search --format={{json|text}} --output={{summary|threads|messages|files|tags}} "{{search_term}}"`
6. Limit the number of search results to X:
   `notmuch search --format={{json|text}} --output={{summary|threads|messages|files|tags}} --limit={{X}} "{{search_term}}"`
7. Create a reply template for a set of messages:
   `notmuch reply --format={{default|headers-only}} --reply-to={{sender|all}} "{{search_term}}"`
now:
**`now`**: Cloud platform for serverless deployment.

**Examples:**
1. Deploy the current directory:
   `now`
2. Display a list of deployments:
   `now list`
3. Display information related to a deployment:
   `now inspect {{deployment_url}}`
4. Remove a deployment:
   `now remove {{deployment_id}}`
5. Log in into an account or create a new one:
   `now login`
6. Initialize an example project (a new directory will be created):
   `now init`
nping:
**`nping`**: Network packet generation tool/ping utility.

**Examples:**
1. Ping a specified host using ICMP if the user is allowed to, otherwise using TCP:
   `nping {{example.com}}`
2. Ping a specified host using ICMP assuming that the user is allowed to do so:
   `nping --icmp --privileged {{example.com}}`
3. Ping a specified host using UDP:
   `nping --udp {{example.com}}`
4. Ping a specified host on a given port using TCP:
   `nping --tcp --dest-port {{443}} {{example.com}}`
5. Ping a certain number of times:
   `nping --count {{10}} {{example.com}}`
6. Wait a certain amount of time between each ping:
   `nping --delay {{5s}} {{example.com}}`
7. Send the request over a specified interface:
   `nping --interface {{eth0}} {{example.com}}`
8. Ping an IP range:
   `nping {{10.0.0.1-10}}`
npm-access:
**`npm-access`**: Set access level on published packages.

**Examples:**
1. List packages for a user or scope:
   `npm access list packages {{user|scope|scope:team}} {{package_name}}`
2. List collaborators on a package:
   `npm access list collaborators {{package_name}} {{username}}`
3. Get status of a package:
   `npm access get status {{package_name}}`
4. Set package status (public or private):
   `npm access set status={{public|private}} {{package_name}}`
5. Grant access to a package:
   `npm access grant {{read-only|read-write}} {{scope:team}} {{package_name}}`
6. Revoke access to a package:
   `npm access revoke {{scope:team}} {{package_name}}`
7. Configure two-factor authentication requirement:
   `npm access set mfa={{none|publish|automation}} {{package_name}}`
npm-adduser:
**`npm-adduser`**: Add a registry user account.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new user in the specified registry and save credentials to `.npmrc`:
   `npm adduser --registry {{registry_url}}`
2. Log in to a private registry with a specific scope:
   `npm login --scope {{@organization}} --registry {{https://registry.example.com}}`
3. Log out from a specific scope and remove the auth token:
   `npm logout --scope {{@organization}}`
4. Create a scoped package during initialization:
   `npm init --scope {{@organization}} {{[-y|--yes]}}`
npm-audit:
**`npm-audit`**: Scan project dependencies for known security vulnerabilities.

**Examples:**
1. Scan the project's dependencies for known vulnerabilities:
   `npm audit`
2. Automatically fix vulnerabilities in the project's dependencies:
   `npm audit fix`
3. Force an automatic fix to dependencies with vulnerabilities:
   `npm audit fix {{[-f|--force]}}`
4. Update the lock file without modifying the `node_modules` directory:
   `npm audit fix --package-lock-only`
5. Simulate the fix process without making any changes:
   `npm audit fix --dry-run`
6. Output audit results in JSON format:
   `npm audit --json`
7. Configure the audit to only fail on vulnerabilities above a specified severity:
   `npm audit --audit-level {{info|low|moderate|high|critical}}`
npm-author:
**`npm-author`**: This command is an alias of `npm owner`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm owner`
npm-bugs:
**`npm-bugs`**: Report bugs for a package in a web browser.

**Examples:**
1. Report bugs for a specific package by opening the bug tracker for the specified package:
   `npm bugs {{package_name}}`
2. Open the bug tracker for the current package by searching for a `package.json` file and using its name:
   `npm bugs`
3. Configure the browser used to open URLs by setting your preferred browser for `npm` commands:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} set browser {{browser_name}}`
4. Control URL opening: set `browser` to `true` for the system URL opener, or `false` to print URLs in the terminal:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} set browser {{true|false}}`
npm-cache:
**`npm-cache`**: Manage the npm package cache.

**Examples:**
1. Add a specific package to the cache:
   `npm cache add {{package_name}}`
2. Clear a specific cached item by key:
   `npm cache clean {{key}}`
3. Clear the entire npm cache:
   `npm cache clean {{[-f|--force]}}`
4. List cached packages:
   `npm cache ls`
5. List cached packages matching a specific name and version:
   `npm cache ls {{name}}@{{version}}`
6. Verify the integrity of the npm cache:
   `npm cache verify`
7. List all entries in the npx cache:
   `npm cache npx ls`
npm-check:
**`npm-check`**: Check for outdated, incorrect, and unused npm package dependencies.

**Examples:**
1. Display a report of outdated, incorrect, and unused dependencies:
   `npm-check`
2. Interactively update out-of-date packages:
   `npm-check {{[-u|--update]}}`
3. Update everything without prompting:
   `npm-check {{[-y|--update-all]}}`
4. Don't check for unused packages:
   `npm-check {{[-s|--skip-unused]}}`
npm-ci:
**`npm-ci`**: Clean install of `npm` project dependencies for automated environments.

**Examples:**
1. Install project dependencies from `package-lock.json` or `npm-shrinkwrap.json`:
   `npm ci`
2. Install project dependencies but skip the specified dependency type:
   `npm ci --omit {{dev|optional|peer}}`
3. Install project dependencies without running any pre-/post-scripts defined in `package.json`:
   `npm ci --ignore-scripts`
npm-completion:
**`npm-completion`**: Enable or set up tab-completion for npm commands.

**Examples:**
1. Enable tab-completion for the current shell session:
   `npm completion`
2. Add completion to the shell profile (Bash):
   `npm completion >> ~/.bashrc`
3. Add completion to the shell profile (Zsh):
   `npm completion >> ~/.zshrc`
4. Write completions script to a specific file:
   `npm completion > {{path/to/file}}`
npm-config:
**`npm-config`**: Manage the `npm` configuration settings.

**Examples:**
1. Show all configuration settings:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} list`
2. List all configuration settings as `JSON`:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} list --json`
3. Get the value of a specific configuration key:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} get {{key}}`
4. Set a configuration key to a specific value:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} set {{key}} {{value}}`
5. Delete a configuration key:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} delete {{key}}`
6. Edit the npm configuration file in the default editor (use the `--global` flag to edit the global config):
   `npm {{[c|config]}} edit`
7. Attempt to repair invalid configuration items:
   `npm {{[c|config]}} fix`
npm-dedupe:
**`npm-dedupe`**: Reduce duplication in the `node_modules` directory.

**Examples:**
1. Deduplicate packages in `node_modules`:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}}`
2. Follow `package-lock.json` or `npm-shrinkwrap.json` during deduplication:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}} --lock`
3. Run deduplication in strict mode:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}} --strict`
4. Skip optional/peer dependencies during deduplication:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}} --omit {{optional|peer}}`
5. Enable detailed logging for troubleshooting:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}} --loglevel verbose`
6. Limit deduplication to a specific package:
   `npm {{[ddp|dedupe]}} {{package_name}}`
npm-deprecate:
**`npm-deprecate`**: Mark a version or range of versions of an `npm` package as deprecated.

**Examples:**
1. Deprecate a specific version of a package:
   `npm deprecate {{package_name}}@{{version}} "{{deprecation_message}}"`
2. Deprecate a range of versions of a package:
   `npm deprecate {{package_name}}@"<{{version_range}}" "{{deprecation_message}}"`
3. Un-deprecate a specific version of a package:
   `npm deprecate {{package_name}}@{{version}} ""`
npm-diff:
**`npm-diff`**: Compare package versions from the `npm` registry and show differences.

**Examples:**
1. Compare two specific package versions:
   `npm diff --diff {{package_name}}@{{version1}} --diff {{package_name}}@{{version2}}`
2. Compare current local packages with latest published version:
   `npm diff`
3. Compare current local package with a specific version:
   `npm diff --diff {{package_name}}@{{version}}`
4. Compare a package in the current directory with the registry version:
   `npm diff --diff {{package_name}}`
5. Show only filenames that differ:
   `npm diff --diff-name-only --diff {{package_name}}@{{version1}} --diff {{package_name}}@{{version2}}`
6. Compare specific files or directories only:
   `npm diff {{path/to/file_or_directory}} --diff {{package_name}}@{{version1}} --diff {{package_name}}@{{version2}}`
7. Ignore whitespace when comparing:
   `npm diff --diff-ignore-all-space --diff {{package_name}}@{{version1}} --diff {{package_name}}@{{version2}}`
npm-dist-tag:
**`npm-dist-tag`**: Manage distribution tags on packages.

**Examples:**
1. List all distribution tags for a package:
   `npm dist-tag ls {{package_name}}`
2. List all distribution tags for the current package:
   `npm dist-tag ls`
3. Add a distribution tag to a specific package version:
   `npm dist-tag add {{package_name}}@{{version}} {{tag}}`
4. Remove a distribution tag from a package:
   `npm dist-tag rm {{package_name}} {{tag}}`
5. Add a tag using the configured tag from npm config:
   `npm dist-tag add {{package_name}}@{{version}}`
6. Add a tag with two-factor authentication:
   `npm dist-tag add {{package_name}}@{{version}} {{tag}} --otp {{one_time_password}}`
npm-docs:
**`npm-docs`**: Open the documentation for one or more packages in the default web browser.

**Examples:**
1. Open a specific package's documentation page:
   `npm docs {{package}}`
2. Open documentation for multiple packages at once:
   `npm docs {{package1 package2 ...}}`
npm-doctor:
**`npm-doctor`**: Check the health of the npm environment.

**Examples:**
1. Run all default health checks for `npm`:
   `npm doctor`
2. Check the connection to the `npm` registry:
   `npm doctor connection`
3. Check the versions of Node.js and `npm` in use:
   `npm doctor versions`
4. Check for permissions issues with `npm` directories and cache:
   `npm doctor permissions`
5. Validate the cached package files and checksums:
   `npm doctor cache`
npm-edit:
**`npm-edit`**: Select a dependency in the current project and open the package folder in the default editor (`$EDITOR`).

**Examples:**
1. Edit a locally installed package in the default editor:
   `npm edit {{package_name}}`
npm-exec:
**`npm-exec`**: Execute binaries from `npm` packages.

**Examples:**
1. Execute the command from a local or remote `npm` package:
   `npm {{[x|exec]}} {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}`
2. Specify the package explicitly (useful if multiple commands with the same name exist):
   `npm {{[x|exec]}} --package {{package}} {{command}}`
3. Run a command if it exists in the current path or in `node_modules/.bin`:
   `npm {{[x|exec]}} --no-install {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}`
4. Execute a specific command, suppressing any output from `npm` itself:
   `npm {{[x|exec]}} --quiet {{command}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}`
5. Display help:
   `npm {{[x|exec]}} --help`
npm-explain:
**`npm-explain`**: Explain how a package is installed, detailing its dependencies and reasons for inclusion.

**Examples:**
1. Explain why a specific package is installed:
   `npm {{[why|explain]}} {{package_name}}`
2. Show explanation in JSON format:
   `npm {{[why|explain]}} {{package_name}} --json`
3. Include peer dependencies in the explanation:
   `npm {{[why|explain]}} {{package_name}} --include peer`
4. Limit explanation depth to 2 levels deep:
   `npm {{[why|explain]}} {{package_name}} --depth 2`
npm-explore:
**`npm-explore`**: Browse an installed npm package.

**Examples:**
1. Browse an installed package:
   `npm explore {{package_name}}`
2. Browse a package and run a command inside it:
   `npm explore {{package_name}} -- {{command}}`
npm-find-dupes:
**`npm-find-dupes`**: Identify duplicate dependencies in `node_modules`.

**Examples:**
1. List all duplicate packages within `node_modules`:
   `npm find-dupes`
2. Include `devDependencies` in duplicate detection:
   `npm find-dupes --include dev`
3. List all duplicate instances of a specific package in `node_modules`:
   `npm find-dupes {{package_name}}`
4. Exclude optional dependencies from duplicate detection:
   `npm find-dupes --omit optional`
5. Set the logging level for output:
   `npm find-dupes --loglevel {{silent|error|warn|info|verbose}}`
6. Output duplicate information in JSON format:
   `npm find-dupes --json`
7. Limit duplicate search to specific scopes:
   `npm find-dupes --scope {{@scope1,@scope2}}`
8. Exclude specific scopes from duplicate detection:
   `npm find-dupes --omit-scope {{@scope1,@scope2}}`
npm-fund:
**`npm-fund`**: Retrieve funding information from packages.

**Examples:**
1. List dependencies with funding URL for the project in the current directory:
   `npm fund`
2. Open the funding URL for a specific package in the default web browser:
   `npm fund {{package}}`
3. List dependencies with a funding URL for a specific workspace for the project in the current directory:
   `npm fund {{[-w|--workspace]}} {{workspace}}`
npm-help-search:
**`npm-help-search`**: Search npm help documentation using a keyword.

**Examples:**
1. Search for commands or topics related to a keyword:
   `npm help-search {{keyword}}`
2. Search with multiple words:
   `npm help-search {{keyword1 keyword2 ...}}`
npm-help:
**`npm-help`**: Display an overview of `npm` syntax, frequently used commands, and a short description of each command.

**Examples:**
1. Display the documentation for a specific command:
   `npm help {{command}}`
npm-home:
**`npm-home`**: Open the `npm` page, Yarn page, or GitHub repository of a package in the web browser.

**Examples:**
1. Open the `npm` page of a specific package in the web browser:
   `npm-home {{package}}`
2. Open the GitHub repository of a specific package in the web browser:
   `npm-home {{[-g|--github]}} {{package}}`
3. Open the Yarn page of a specific package in the web browser:
   `npm-home {{[-y|--yarn]}} {{package}}`
npm-hook:
**`npm-hook`**: Manage `npm` registry hooks for packages.

**Examples:**
1. List all active hooks:
   `npm hook ls`
2. Add a new hook for a package:
   `npm hook add {{package_name}} {{event}} {{target_url}}`
3. Remove a specific hook by its ID:
   `npm hook rm {{hook_id}}`
4. Update a hook with new information:
   `npm hook update {{hook_id}} {{target_url}}`
npm-init:
**`npm-init`**: Create a `package.json` file.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize a new package with prompts:
   `npm init`
2. Initialize a new package with default values:
   `npm init {{[-y|--yes]}}`
3. Initialize a new package using a specific initializer:
   `npm init {{create-react-app}} {{my-app}}`
npm-install-ci-test:
**`npm-install-ci-test`**: Install project dependencies and run tests in a single command, mainly used in continuous integration (CI) environments.

**Examples:**
1. Install dependencies and run tests:
   `npm {{[cit|install-ci-test]}}`
2. Display detailed logs during installation and testing:
   `npm {{[cit|install-ci-test]}} --verbose`
npm-install-test:
**`npm-install-test`**: Equivalent to running `npm install` followed by `npm test`.

**Examples:**
1. Install all dependencies and then run tests:
   `npm {{[it|install-test]}}`
2. Install a specific package and then run tests:
   `npm {{[it|install-test]}} {{package_name}}`
3. Install a package and save it as a dependency before running tests:
   `npm {{[it|install-test]}} {{package_name}} {{[-S|--save]}}`
4. Install dependencies globally and then run tests:
   `npm {{[it|install-test]}} {{[-g|--global]}}`
npm-install:
**`npm-install`**: Install Node packages.

**Examples:**
1. Install dependencies listed in `package.json`:
   `npm {{[i|install]}}`
2. Download a specific version of a package and add it to the list of dependencies in `package.json`:
   `npm {{[i|install]}} {{package_name}}@{{version}}`
3. Download the latest version of a package and add it to the list of dev dependencies in `package.json`:
   `npm {{[i|install]}} {{package_name}} {{[-D|--save-dev]}}`
4. Download the latest version of a package and install it globally (set install location with `npm config set prefix`):
   `npm {{[i|install]}} {{package_name}} {{[-g|--global]}}`
npm-it:
**`npm-it`**: This command is an alias of `npm install-test`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm install-test`
npm-link:
**`npm-link`**: Symlink a local package into the global `node_modules` or another project for development.

**Examples:**
1. Symlink the current package globally:
   `npm {{[ln|link]}}`
2. Link a globally linked package into another project's `node_modules`:
   `npm {{[ln|link]}} {{package_name}}`
3. Unlink a package from the current project:
   `npm {{[r|unlink]}} {{package_name}}`
npm-list:
**`npm-list`**: This command is an alias of `npm ls`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm ls`
npm-login:
**`npm-login`**: Log in to a registry user account.

**Examples:**
1. Log in to a registry user account and save the credentials to the `.npmrc` file:
   `npm login`
2. Log in using a custom registry:
   `npm login --registry {{registry_url}}`
3. Log in using a specific authentication strategy:
   `npm login --auth-type {{legacy|web}}`
npm-logout:
**`npm-logout`**: Log out of the registry user account.

**Examples:**
1. Log out of the registry user account:
   `npm logout`
2. Log out using a custom registry:
   `npm logout --registry {{registry_url}}`
npm-ls:
**`npm-ls`**: Print installed packages to `stdout`.

**Examples:**
1. Print all versions of direct dependencies in the current project to `stdout`:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}}`
2. Print all installed packages including peer dependencies:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}} {{[-a|--all]}}`
3. Print all globally installed packages:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}} {{[-g|--global]}}`
4. Print dependencies with extended information:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}} {{[-l|--long]}}`
5. Print dependencies in parseable format:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}} {{[-p|--parseable]}}`
6. Print dependencies in JSON format:
   `npm {{[ls|list]}} --json`
npm-name:
**`npm-name`**: Check whether a package or organization name is available on npm.

**Examples:**
1. Check if a specific package name is available in the `npm` registry:
   `npm-name {{package}}`
2. Find similar package names in the `npm` registry:
   `npm-name --similar {{package}}`
npm-org:
**`npm-org`**: Manage organizations.

**Examples:**
1. Add a new user to an organization:
   `npm org set {{organization_name}} {{username}}`
2. Change a user's role in an organization:
   `npm org set {{organization_name}} {{username}} {{developer|admin|owner}}`
3. Remove a user from an organization:
   `npm org rm {{organization_name}} {{username}}`
4. List all users in an organization:
   `npm org ls {{organization_name}}`
5. List all users in an organization, output in JSON format:
   `npm org ls {{organization_name}} --json`
6. Display a user's role in an organization:
   `npm org ls {{organization_name}} {{username}}`
npm-outdated:
**`npm-outdated`**: Check for outdated npm package dependencies.

**Examples:**
1. Find packages that are outdated in a project:
   `npm outdated`
2. Find packages that are outdated regardless of the current project:
   `npm outdated {{[-a|--all]}}`
npm-owner:
**`npm-owner`**: Manage ownership of published packages.

**Examples:**
1. Add a new user as a maintainer of a package:
   `npm owner add {{username}} {{package_name}}`
2. Remove a user from a package's owner list:
   `npm owner rm {{username}} {{package_name}}`
3. List all owners of a package:
   `npm owner ls {{package_name}}`
npm-pack:
**`npm-pack`**: Create a tarball from a package.

**Examples:**
1. Create a tarball from the current package in the current directory:
   `npm pack`
2. Create a tarball from a specific package folder:
   `npm pack {{path/to/package_directory}}`
3. Run a dry run to preview the tarball contents without creating it:
   `npm pack --dry-run`
4. Create a tarball without running lifecycle scripts:
   `npm pack --ignore-scripts`
5. Specify a custom registry to fetch package metadata from:
   `npm pack --registry {{https://registry.npmjs.org/}}`
npm-ping:
**`npm-ping`**: Ping `npm` registry.

**Examples:**
1. Ping the default `npm` registry:
   `npm ping`
2. Ping custom `npm` registry:
   `npm ping --registry {{custom_registry_url}}`
npm-pkg:
**`npm-pkg`**: Show or modify `package.json` properties.

**Examples:**
1. Get the value of a specific property:
   `npm pkg get {{name}}`
2. Get multiple properties at once:
   `npm pkg get {{name|version|...}}`
3. Get multiple values across all workspaces:
   `npm pkg get {{name}} {{version}} {{[--ws|--workspaces]}}`
4. Get a nested or array property value:
   `npm pkg get {{contributors[0].email}}`
5. Set a property to a specific value:
   `npm pkg set {{property}}={{value}}`
6. Set multiple properties at once:
   `npm pkg set {{property1}}={{value1}} {{property2}}={{value2}}`
7. Delete a property from `package.json`:
   `npm pkg delete {{scripts.build}}`
8. Auto-fix common errors in `package.json`:
   `npm pkg fix`
npm-prefix:
**`npm-prefix`**: Print the local or global prefix to `stdout`.

**Examples:**
1. Print the local prefix:
   `npm prefix`
2. Print the global prefix:
   `npm prefix {{[-g|--global]}}`
npm-profile:
**`npm-profile`**: Manage the npm profile and related settings.

**Examples:**
1. View the npm profile details:
   `npm profile get`
2. View a specific property of the profile:
   `npm profile get {{property}}`
3. Set or update a profile property:
   `npm profile set {{property}} {{value}}`
4. Set the public email address:
   `npm profile set email {{email}}`
5. Set the public name:
   `npm profile set fullname {{name}}`
6. Set a new password interactively:
   `npm profile set password`
7. Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) (defaults to `auth-and-writes`):
   `npm profile enable-2fa {{auth-only|auth-and-writes}}`
8. Disable two-factor authentication (2FA):
   `npm profile disable-2fa`
npm-prune:
**`npm-prune`**: Remove extraneous packages from `node_modules`.

**Examples:**
1. Remove all extraneous packages not listed in dependencies:
   `npm prune`
2. Remove extraneous packages and devDependencies (useful for production builds):
   `npm prune --production`
3. Show what would be removed without making any changes:
   `npm prune --dry-run`
4. Output the changes as JSON:
   `npm prune --json`
5. Remove specific packages by name:
   `npm prune {{package_name}}`
npm-publish:
**`npm-publish`**: Publish a package to the npm registry.

**Examples:**
1. Publish the current package to the default npm registry:
   `npm publish`
2. Publish a package from a specific directory:
   `npm publish {{path/to/package_directory}}`
3. Publish a scoped package with public access:
   `npm publish --access public`
4. Publish a scoped package with restricted (private) access:
   `npm publish --access restricted`
5. Publish a package to a custom registry:
   `npm publish --registry {{https://registry.npmjs.org/}}`
6. Run a dry run to see what would be published without uploading:
   `npm publish --dry-run`
7. Publish a package with a specific distribution tag (e.g., beta):
   `npm publish --tag {{beta}}`
8. Publish with a one-time password for 2FA-enabled accounts:
   `npm publish --otp {{one_time_password}}`
npm-query:
**`npm-query`**: Print an array of dependency objects using CSS-like selectors.

**Examples:**
1. Print direct dependencies:
   `npm query ':root > *'`
2. Print all direct production/development dependencies:
   `npm query ':root > .{{prod|dev}}'`
3. Print dependencies with a specific name:
   `npm query '#{{package}}'`
4. Print dependencies with a specific name and within a semantic versioning range:
   `npm query '#{{package}}@{{semantic_version}}'`
5. Print dependencies which have no dependencies:
   `npm query ':empty'`
6. Find all dependencies with postinstall scripts and uninstall them:
   `npm query ":attr(scripts, [postinstall])" | jq 'map(.name) | join("\n")' {{[-r|--raw-output]}} | xargs -I _ npm uninstall _`
7. Find all Git dependencies and print which application requires them:
   `npm query ":type(git)" | jq 'map(.name)' | xargs -I _ npm why _`
npm-rb:
**`npm-rb`**: This command is an alias of `npm-rebuild`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm-rebuild`
npm-rebuild:
**`npm-rebuild`**: Rebuild native Node.js packages after Node or dependency changes.

**Examples:**
1. Rebuild a specific package:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}} {{package}}`
2. Rebuild all installed packages:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}}`
3. Rebuild with verbose output:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}} --verbose`
4. Rebuild a package in a specific directory:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}} --prefix {{path/to/dir}} {{package}}`
5. Rebuild without using the npm cache:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}} --no-cache`
6. Rebuild in global mode:
   `npm {{[rb|rebuild]}} {{[-g|--global]}}`
npm-repo:
**`npm-repo`**: Open the repository page of a package in the browser.

**Examples:**
1. Open the repository page of the current project (based on `package.json`):
   `npm repo`
2. Open the repository page of a specific package from the registry:
   `npm repo {{package_name}}`
3. Open repository pages for multiple packages:
   `npm repo {{package_name1 package_name2 ...}}`
4. Print the repository URL instead of opening it in the browser:
   `npm repo --browser false`
5. Open the repository page for a package in a specific browser:
   `npm repo --browser {{browser_name}}`
6. Open the repository page of a package in a specific workspace:
   `npm repo --workspace {{workspace_name}}`
npm-restart:
**`npm-restart`**: This command is an alias of `npm run restart`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm run`
npm-root:
**`npm-root`**: Display path to `node_modules` directory.

**Examples:**
1. Display path to the local `node_modules` directory:
   `npm root`
2. Display path to the global `node_modules` directory:
   `npm root {{[-g|--global]}}`
npm-run-script:
**`npm-run-script`**: This command is an alias of `npm run`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr npm run`
npm-run:
**`npm-run`**: Run a script.

**Examples:**
1. List available scripts:
   `npm run`
2. Run a script:
   `npm run {{script_name}}`
3. Pass arguments to a script:
   `npm run {{script_name}} -- {{argument}} {{--option}}`
4. Run a script named `start`:
   `npm start`
5. Run a script named `stop`:
   `npm stop`
6. Run a script named `restart`:
   `npm restart`
7. Run a script named `test`:
   `npm {{[t|test]}}`
npm-sbom:
**`npm-sbom`**: Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for your Node.js project.

**Examples:**
1. Output a list of all dependencies in your project:
   `npm sbom`
2. Exclude both `dev` and `optional` dependencies:
   `npm sbom --omit dev --omit optional`
3. Generate an SBOM based only on the `package-lock.json`:
   `npm sbom --package-lock-only`
npm-search:
**`npm-search`**: Search for packages in the `npm` registry.

**Examples:**
1. Search for a package by name:
   `npm {{[s|search]}} {{package}}`
2. Search for packages by a specific keyword:
   `npm {{[s|search]}} {{keyword}}`
3. Search for packages, including detailed information (e.g., description, author, version):
   `npm {{[s|search]}} {{package}} --long`
4. Search for packages maintained by a specific author:
   `npm {{[s|search]}} --author {{author}}`
5. Search for packages with a specific organization:
   `npm {{[s|search]}} --scope {{organization}}`
6. Search for packages with a specific combination of terms:

2. Execute the specified SQL query on the target server:
   `nxc mssql {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} {{[-q|--query]}} '{{SELECT * FROM sys.databases;}}'`
3. Execute the specified shell command on the target server through MSSQL:
   `nxc mssql {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -x {{whoami}}`
4. Execute the specified PowerShell command on the target server through MSSQL without retrieving output:
   `nxc mssql {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -X {{whoami}} --no-output`
5. Download a remote file from the target server and store it in the specified location:
   `nxc mssql {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --get-file {{C:\path\to\remote_file}} {{path/to/local_file}}`
6. Upload a local file to the specified location on the target server:
   `nxc mssql {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --put-file {{path/to/local_file}} {{C:\path\to\remote_file}}`
nxc-nfs:
**`nxc-nfs`**: Pentest and exploit NFS servers. Currently supports anonymous mode only.

**Examples:**

   `nxc nfs {{192.168.178.0/24}}`
2. List the available NFS shares:
   `nxc nfs {{192.168.178.2}} --shares`
3. Enumerate the exposed shares recursively to the specified depth:
   `nxc nfs {{192.168.178.2}} --enum-shares {{5}}`
4. Download the specified remote file:
   `nxc nfs {{192.168.178.2}} --get-file {{path/to/remote_file}} {{path/to/local_file}}`
5. Upload the specified local file to the remote share:
   `nxc nfs {{192.168.178.2}} --put-file {{path/to/local_file}} {{path/to/remote_file}}`
nxc-rdp:
**`nxc-rdp`**: Pentest and exploit RDP servers.

**Examples:**
1. Search for valid credentials by trying out every combination in the specified lists of usernames and passwords:

2. Take a screenshot after waiting the for specified number of seconds:
   `nxc rdp {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --screenshot --screentime {{10}}`
3. Take a screenshot in the specified resolution:
   `nxc rdp {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --screenshot --res {{1024x768}}`
4. Take a screenshot of the RDP login prompt if Network Level Authentication is disabled:
   `nxc rdp {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --nla-screenshot`
nxc-smb:
**`nxc-smb`**: Pentest and exploit SMB servers.

**Examples:**
1. Search for valid domain credentials by trying out every combination in the specified lists of usernames and passwords:
   `nxc smb {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{path/to/usernames.txt}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{path/to/passwords.txt}}`
2. Search for valid credentials for local accounts instead of domain accounts:
   `nxc smb {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{path/to/usernames.txt}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{path/to/passwords.txt}} --local-auth`
3. Enumerate SMB shares and the specified users' access rights to them on the target hosts:
   `nxc smb {{192.168.178.0/24}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --shares`
4. Enumerate network interfaces on the target hosts, performing authentication via pass-the-hash:
   `nxc smb {{192.168.178.30-45}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-H|--hash]}} {{NTLM_hash}} --interfaces`
5. Scan the target hosts for common vulnerabilities:
   `nxc smb {{path/to/target_list.txt}} {{[-u|--username]}} '' {{[-p|--password]}} '' {{[-M|--module]}} zerologon {{[-M|--module]}} petitpotam`
6. Attempt to execute a command on the target hosts:
   `nxc smb {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -x {{command}}`
nxc-ssh:
**`nxc-ssh`**: Pentest and exploit SSH servers.

**Examples:**
1. Spray the specified password against a list of usernames on the specified target:
   `nxc ssh {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{path/to/usernames.txt}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}}`
2. Search for valid credentials by trying out every combination in the specified lists of usernames and passwords:
   `nxc ssh {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{path/to/usernames.txt}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{path/to/passwords.txt}}`
3. Use the specified private key for authentication, using the supplied password as the key's passphrase:
   `nxc ssh {{192.186.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{path/to/usernames.txt}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --key-file {{path/to/id_rsa}}`
4. Try a combination of username and password on a number of targets:
   `nxc ssh {{192.168.178.0/24}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}}`
5. Check for `sudo` privileges on a successful login:
   `nxc ssh {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{path/to/passwords.txt}} --sudo-check`
nxc-vnc:
**`nxc-vnc`**: Pentest and exploit VNC servers.

**Examples:**

2. Avoid rate limiting through VNC-sleep:

nxc-winrm:
**`nxc-winrm`**: Pentest and exploit Windows Remote Management (winrm).

   `nxc winrm {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -d {{domain_name}}`
3. Execute the specified command on the host:
   `nxc winrm {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -x {{whoami}}`
4. Execute the specified PowerShell command on the host as administrator using LAPS:
   `nxc winrm {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} --laps -X {{whoami}}`
nxc-wmi:
**`nxc-wmi`**: Pentest and exploit the Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).

4. Execute the specified command on the targeted host:
   `nxc wmi {{192.168.178.2}} {{[-u|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}} -x {{command}}`
nxc:

nxcdb:

nyxt:

oathtool:

oauth2c:

objdump:

obs:

oc:

**Examples:**

2. Synchronize a specific account:

ogr2ogr:
**`ogr2ogr`**: Convert geospatial vector data between file formats.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Shapefile into a GeoPackage:
   `ogr2ogr -f GPKG {{path/to/output.gpkg}} {{path/to/input.shp}}`
2. Reduce a GeoJSON to features matching a condition:
   `ogr2ogr -where '{{myProperty > 42}}' -f {{GeoJSON}} {{path/to/output.geojson}} {{path/to/input.geojson}}`
3. Change coordinate reference system of a GeoPackage from `EPSG:4326` to `EPSG:3857`:
   `ogr2ogr -s_srs {{EPSG:4326}} -t_srs {{EPSG:3857}} -f GPKG {{path/to/output.gpkg}} {{path/to/input.gpkg}}`
4. Convert a CSV file into a GeoPackage, specifying the names of the coordinate columns and assigning a coordinate reference system:
   `ogr2ogr -f GPKG {{path/to/output.gpkg}} {{path/to/input.csv}} -oo X_POSSIBLE_NAMES={{longitude}} -oo Y_POSSIBLE_NAMES={{latitude}} -a_srs {{EPSG:4326}}`
5. Load a GeoPackage into a PostGIS database:
   `ogr2ogr -f PostgreSQL PG:dbname="{{database_name}}" {{path/to/input.gpkg}}`
6. Clip layers of a GeoPackage file to the given bounding box:
   `ogr2ogr -spat {{min_x}} {{min_y}} {{max_x}} {{max_y}} -f GPKG {{path/to/output.gpkg}} {{path/to/input.gpkg}}`
ogrinfo:
**`ogrinfo`**: List information about an OGR-supported data source.

**Examples:**
1. List supported formats:
   `ogrinfo --formats`
2. List layers of a data source:
   `ogrinfo {{path/to/input.gpkg}}`
3. Get detailed information about a specific layer of a data source:
   `ogrinfo {{path/to/input.gpkg}} {{layer_name}}`
4. Show summary information about a specific layer of a data source:
   `ogrinfo -so {{path/to/input.gpkg}} {{layer_name}}`
5. Show summary of all layers of the data source:
   `ogrinfo -so -al {{path/to/input.gpkg}}`
6. Show detailed information of features matching a condition:
   `ogrinfo -where '{{attribute_name > 42}}' {{path/to/input.gpkg}} {{layer_name}}`
7. Update a layer in the data source with SQL:
   `ogrinfo {{path/to/input.geojson}} -dialect SQLite -sql "{{UPDATE input SET attribute_name = 'foo'}}"`

**`ogrmerge.py`**: Merge several vector datasets into a single one.

**Examples:**
1. Create a GeoPackage with a layer for each input Shapefile:
   `ogrmerge.py -f {{GPKG}} -o {{path/to/output.gpkg}} {{path/to/input1.shp path/to/input2.shp ...}}`
2. Create a virtual datasource (VRT) with a layer for each input GeoJSON:
   `ogrmerge.py -f {{VRT}} -o {{path/to/output.vrt}} {{path/to/input1.geojson path/to/input2.geojson ...}}`
3. Concatenate two vector datasets and store source name of dataset in attribute 'source_name':
   `ogrmerge.py -single -f {{GeoJSON}} -o {{path/to/output.geojson}} -src_layer_field_name country {{source_name}} {{path/to/input1.shp path/to/input2.shp ...}}`

   `sudo openconnect {{[-c|--certificate]}} {{path/to/certificate.pem}} {{vpn.example.org}}`
openocd:
**`openocd`**: Debug and program embedded systems with OpenOCD.

**Examples:**
1. Attach OpenOCD session to a board with a configuration file:
   `openocd {{[-f|--file]}} {{config_file.cfg}}`
2. Attach OpenOCD session to a board with multiple configuration files:
   `openocd {{[-f|--file]}} {{config_file1.cfg}} {{[-f|--file]}} {{config_file2.cfg}}`
3. Attach OpenOCD session to a board with configuration files and a list of commands to be executed on server startup:
   `openocd {{[-f|--file]}} {{config_file.cfg}} {{[-c|--command]}} "{{command}}"`
4. Use configuration files in the specified path:
   `openocd {{[-s|--search]}} {{path/to/search}} {{[-f|--file]}} {{config_file.cfg}}`
5. [Interactive] After OpenOCD startup, connect GDB to OpenOCD default port 3333:
   `target extended-remote localhost`
6. List site-wide script library:
   `ls /usr/local/share/openocd/scripts`
openrgb:
**`openrgb`**: Control RGB lighting.

**Examples:**
1. Start the OpenRGB GUI:
   `openrgb`
2. List devices supported by OpenRGB:
   `openrgb --noautoconnect {{[-l|--list-devices]}}`
3. Set the mode and color of a device:
   `openrgb {{[-m|--mode]}} {{off|static|breathing|rainbow|flashing|...}} {{[-c|--color]}} {{random|red|00AAFF|...}}`
4. Display help:
   `openrgb {{[-h|--help]}}`
openscad:
**`openscad`**: Software for creating solid 3D CAD objects.

**Examples:**
1. Open a file:
   `openscad {{path/to/button.scad}}`
2. Convert a file to STL:
   `openscad -o {{path/to/button.stl}} {{path/to/button.scad}}`
3. Render a file to PNG in a specific colorscheme:
   `openscad -o {{path/to/button.png}} --colorscheme {{Sunset}} {{path/to/button.scad}}`
openssl-dgst:
**`openssl-dgst`**: Generate digest values and perform signature operations.

**Examples:**
1. Calculate the SHA256 digest for a file, saving the result to a specific file:
   `openssl dgst -sha256 -binary -out {{output_file}} {{input_file}}`
2. Sign a file using an RSA key, saving the result to a specific file:
   `openssl dgst -sign {{private_key_file}} -sha256 -sigopt rsa_padding_mode:pss -out {{output_file}} {{input_file}}`
3. Verify an RSA signature:
   `openssl dgst -verify {{public_key_file}} -signature {{signature_file}} -sigopt rsa_padding_mode:pss {{signature_message_file}}`
4. Sign a file using and ECDSA key:
   `openssl dgst -sign {{private_key_file}} -sha256 -out {{output_file}} {{input_file}}`
5. Verify an ECDSA signature:
   `openssl dgst -verify {{public_key_file}} -signature {{signature_file}} {{signature_message_file}}`
openssl-genpkey:
**`openssl-genpkey`**: Generate asymmetric key pairs.

**Examples:**
1. Generate an RSA private key of 2048 bits, saving it to a specific file:
   `openssl genpkey -algorithm rsa -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:{{2048}} -out {{path/to/private.key}}`
2. Generate an elliptic curve private key using the curve `prime256v1`, saving it to a specific file:
   `openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:{{prime256v1}} -out {{path/to/private.key}}`
3. Generate an `ED25519` elliptic curve private key, saving it to a specific file:
   `openssl genpkey -algorithm {{ED25519}} -out {{path/to/private.key}}`
openssl-genrsa:
**`openssl-genrsa`**: Generate RSA private keys.

**Examples:**
1. Generate an RSA private key of 2048 bits to `stdout`:
   `openssl genrsa`
2. Save an RSA private key of an arbitrary number of bits to the output file:
   `openssl genrsa -out {{output_file.key}} {{1234}}`
3. Generate an RSA private key and encrypt it with AES256 (you will be prompted for a passphrase):
   `openssl genrsa {{-aes256}}`
openssl-prime:
**`openssl-prime`**: Compute prime numbers.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a 2048bit prime number and display it in hexadecimal:
   `openssl prime -generate -bits 2048 -hex`
2. Check if a given number is prime:
   `openssl prime {{number}}`
openssl-rand:
**`openssl-rand`**: Generate random bytes using a cryptographically secure PRNG.

**Examples:**
1. Generate an 8-byte (16 characters) hex string and write it to `stdout`:
   `openssl rand -hex 8`
2. Generate 20 random bytes encoded in base64:
   `openssl rand -base64 20`
3. Generate random bytes and write them to a file (without encoding):
   `openssl rand -out {{path/to/file}} {{length}}`
4. Generate 1 KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB random bytes encoded in hex/base64:
   `openssl rand -{{hex|base64}} 1{{K|M|G|T}}`
openssl-req:
**`openssl-req`**: Manage PKCS#10 Certificate Signing Requests.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a certificate signing request to be sent to a certificate authority:
   `openssl req -new -sha256 -key {{filename.key}} -out {{filename.csr}}`
2. Generate a self-signed certificate and a corresponding key-pair, storing both in a file:
   `openssl req -new -x509 -newkey {{rsa}}:{{4096}} -keyout {{filename.key}} -out {{filename.cert}} -subj "{{/C=XX/CN=foobar}}" -days {{365}}`
openssl-s_client:
**`openssl-s_client`**: Create TLS client connections.

**Examples:**
1. Display the start and expiry dates for a domain's certificate:
   `openssl s_client -connect {{host}}:{{port}} 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates`
2. Display the certificate presented by an SSL/TLS server:
   `openssl < /dev/null s_client -connect {{host}}:{{port}}`
3. Set the Server Name Indicator (SNI) when connecting to the SSL/TLS server:
   `openssl s_client -connect {{host}}:{{port}} -servername {{hostname}}`
4. Display the complete certificate chain of an HTTPS server:
   `openssl < /dev/null s_client -connect {{host}}:443 -showcerts`
openssl-speed:
**`openssl-speed`**: Benchmark OpenSSL algorithms.

**Examples:**
1. Benchmark all available algorithms:
   `openssl speed`
2. Benchmark the most common algorithms:
   `openssl speed {{md5 sha1 sha256 aes rsa}}`
3. Benchmark a specific EVP cipher:
   `openssl speed -evp {{aes-256-cbc}}`
4. Benchmark algorithms for a specific duration (in seconds):
   `openssl speed -seconds {{10}}`
5. Benchmark using wall-clock time instead of CPU user time:
   `openssl speed -elapsed`
6. Output in machine readable format:
   `openssl speed -mr`
7. Benchmark multiple algorithms in parallel using all available CPU cores:
   `openssl speed -multi $(nproc)`
openssl-ts:
**`openssl-ts`**: Generate and verify timestamps.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a SHA-512 timestamp request of a specific file and output to `file.tsq`:
   `openssl ts -query -data {{path/to/file}} -sha512 -out {{path/to/file.tsq}}`
2. Check the date and metadata of a specific timestamp response file:
   `openssl ts -reply -in {{path/to/file.tsr}} -text`
3. Verify a timestamp request file and a timestamp response file from the server with an SSL certificate file:
   `openssl ts -verify -in {{path/to/file.tsr}} -queryfile {{path/to/file.tsq}} -partial_chain -CAfile {{path/to/cert.pem}}`
4. Create a timestamp response for request using key and signing certificate and output it to `file.tsr`:
   `openssl ts -reply -queryfile {{path/to/file.tsq}} -inkey {{path/to/tsakey.pem}} -signer tsacert.pem -out {{path/to/file.tsr}}`
openssl-x509:
**`openssl-x509`**: Manage X.509 certificates.

**Examples:**
1. Display certificate information:
   `openssl x509 -in {{filename.crt}} -noout -text`
2. Display a certificate's expiration date:
   `openssl x509 -enddate -noout -in {{filename.pem}}`
3. Convert a certificate between binary DER encoding and textual PEM encoding:
   `openssl x509 -inform {{der}} -outform {{pem}} -in {{original_certificate_file}} -out {{converted_certificate_file}}`
4. Store a certificate's public key in a file:
   `openssl x509 -in {{certificate_file}} -noout -pubkey -out {{output_file}}`
openssl:
**`openssl`**: OpenSSL cryptographic toolkit.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a private key and encrypt the output file using AES-256:
   `openssl genpkey -algorithm {{rsa|ec}} -out {{path/to/private.key}} -aes256`
2. Generate the corresponding public key from the private key `private.key` using `rsa`:
   `openssl rsa -in {{path/to/private.key}} -pubout -out {{path/to/public.key}}`
3. Generate a self-signed certificate valid for a specified number of days (365):
   `openssl req -new -x509 -key {{path/to/private.key}} -out {{path/to/certificate.crt}} -days 365`
4. Convert a certificate to `.pem` or `.der` format:
   `openssl x509 -in {{path/to/certificate.crt}} -out {{path/to/certificate.pem|path/to/certificate.der}} -outform {{pem|der}}`
5. Check certificate details:
   `openssl x509 -in {{path/to/certificate.crt}} -text -noout`
6. Generate a certificate signing request (CSR):
   `openssl req -new -key {{path/to/private.key}} -out {{path/to/request.csr}}`
7. Display help:
   `openssl help`
8. Display version:
   `openssl version`
openstack-flavor:
**`openstack-flavor`**: Manage OpenStack instance flavors (virtual hardware templates).

**Examples:**
1. List all flavors:
   `openstack flavor list`
2. Show details of a flavor:
   `openstack flavor show {{flavor_id_or_name}}`
3. Create a new flavor with 2 vCPUs, 4GB RAM, and 20GB disk:
   `openstack flavor create {{flavor_name}} --vcpus 2 --ram 4096 --disk 20`
4. Delete a flavor:
   `openstack flavor delete {{flavor_id_or_name}}`
5. Create a flavor with 10GB ephemeral disk and 512MB swap space:
   `openstack flavor create {{flavor_name}} --vcpus 4 --ram 8192 --disk 40 --ephemeral 10 --swap 512`
openstack-help:
**`openstack-help`**: Display help information about the openstackclient cli.

**Examples:**
1. Display a description of a particular command:
   `openstack help {{command_name}}`
2. Get help for Identity v3:
   `openstack --os-identity-api-version 3 --help`

   `openstack --help`
openstack-image:
**`openstack-image`**: OpenStack Image service, aka OpenStack Glance, allows users to upload and discover data assets meant to be used with other services.

**Examples:**
1. List available images:
   `openstack image list {{--private|--shared|--all}}`
2. Display image details:
   `openstack image show --human-readable {{image_id}}`
3. Create/upload an image:
   `openstack image create --file {{path/to/file}} {{--private|--shared|--all}} {{image_name}}`
4. Delete image(s):
   `openstack image delete {{image_id1 image_id2 ...}}`
5. Save an image locally:
   `openstack image save --file {{filename}} {{image_id}}`
openstack-network:
**`openstack-network`**: Manage OpenStack network resources.

**Examples:**
1. List all networks:
   `openstack network list`
2. Show details of a network:
   `openstack network show {{network_id_or_name}}`
3. Create a new network with a given name:
   `openstack network create {{network_name}}`
4. Delete a network:
   `openstack network delete {{network_id_or_name}}`
5. Enable a network:
   `openstack network set --enable {{network_id_or_name}}`

   `openstack network set --disable {{network_id_or_name}}`
openstack-port:
**`openstack-port`**: Manage OpenStack network ports (virtual network interfaces).

**Examples:**
1. List all ports:
   `openstack port list`
2. Show detailed information about a specific port:
   `openstack port show {{port_id_or_name}}`
3. Create a port on a specific network:
   `openstack port create --network {{network_id_or_name}} {{port_name}}`
4. Create a port and assign it a fixed IP `192.168.1.50`:

5. Delete a port:

openstack-server:
**`openstack-server`**: Manage OpenStack virtual machines.

**Examples:**
1. List servers:
   `openstack server list`
2. Start server(s):
   `openstack server start {{instance_id1 instance_id2 ...}}`
3. Stop server:
   `openstack server stop {{instance_id1 instance_id2 ...}}`
4. Create new server:
   `openstack server create --image {{image_id}} --flavor {{flavor_id}} --network {{network_id}} --wait {{server_name}}`

7. Perform a soft or hard reset to the server:
   `openstack server reboot {{--soft|--hard}} --wait {{instance_id}}`
openstack-subnet:
**`openstack-subnet`**: Manage OpenStack subnets (IP address blocks within a network).

**Examples:**
1. List all subnets:
   `openstack subnet list`
2. Show details of a specific subnet:
   `openstack subnet show {{subnet_id_or_name}}`
3. List subnets associated with a network:
   `openstack subnet list --network {{network_id_or_name}}`
4. Create a subnet with subnet range `192.168.0.0/24` in a given network:
   `openstack subnet create --network {{network_id_or_name}} --subnet-range 192.168.0.0/24 {{subnet_name}}`

openstack-volume:
**`openstack-volume`**: Manage OpenStack volumes.

**Examples:**
1. List volumes:
   `openstack volume list --all-projects`
2. Show volume details:
   `openstack volume show {{volume_id}}`
3. Create new volume:
   `openstack volume create --size {{size_in_GB}} --image {{image_id}} --snapshot {{snapshot_id}} {{--bootable|--non-bootable}} {{volume_name}}`
4. Delete volumes(s):
   `openstack volume delete {{volume_id1 volume_id2 ...}}`
5. Migrate volume to a new host:
   `openstack volume migrate --host {{host_hostname}} {{instance_id}}`
6. Set volume properties:
   `openstack volume set --name {{volume_new_name}} --size {{volume_new_size}} {{--attached|--detached}} {{--bootable|--non-bootable}} {{volume_id}}`
openttd:
**`openttd`**: Open source clone of the Microprose game "Transport Tycoon Deluxe".

**Examples:**
1. Start a new game:
   `openttd -g`
2. Load save game at start:
   `openttd -g {{path/to/file}}`
3. Start with the specified window resolution:
   `openttd -r {{1920x1080}}`
4. Start with a custom configuration file:
   `openttd -c {{path/to/file}}`
5. Start with selected video, sound, and music drivers:
   `openttd -v {{video_driver}} -s {{sound_driver}} -m {{music_driver}}`
6. Start a dedicated server, forked in the background:
   `openttd -f -D {{host}}:{{port}}`
7. Join a server with a password:
   `openttd -n {{host}}:{{port}}#{{player_name}} -p {{password}}`
openvpn:
**`openvpn`**: OpenVPN client and daemon binary.

**Examples:**
1. Connect to server using a configuration file:
   `sudo openvpn {{path/to/client.conf}}`
2. Try to set up an insecure peer-to-peer tunnel on bob.example.com host:
   `sudo openvpn --remote {{alice.example.com}} --dev {{tun1}} --ifconfig {{10.4.0.1}} {{10.4.0.2}}`
3. Connect to the awaiting bob.example.com host without encryption:
   `sudo openvpn --remote {{bob.example.com}} --dev {{tun1}} --ifconfig {{10.4.0.2}} {{10.4.0.1}}`
4. Create a cryptographic key and save it to file:
   `openvpn --genkey secret {{path/to/key}}`
5. Try to set up a peer-to-peer tunnel on bob.example.com host with a static key:
   `sudo openvpn --remote {{alice.example.com}} --dev {{tun1}} --ifconfig {{10.4.0.1}} {{10.4.0.2}} --secret {{path/to/key}}`
6. Connect to the awaiting bob.example.com host with the same static key as on bob.example.com:
   `sudo openvpn --remote {{bob.example.com}} --dev {{tun1}} --ifconfig {{10.4.0.2}} {{10.4.0.1}} --secret {{path/to/key}}`
opera:
**`opera`**: This command is an alias of `chromium`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr chromium`
opt:
**`opt`**: Run optimizations and analyze LLVM source files.

**Examples:**
1. Run an optimization or analysis on a bitcode file:
   `opt -{{passname}} {{path/to/file.bc}} -S -o {{file_opt.bc}}`
2. Output the Control Flow Graph of a function to a `.dot` file:
   `opt {{-dot-cfg}} -S {{path/to/file.bc}} -disable-output`
3. Optimize the program at level 2 and output the result to another file:
   `opt -O2 {{path/to/file.bc}} -S -o {{path/to/output_file.bc}}`
optipng:
**`optipng`**: PNG file optimization utility.

**Examples:**
1. Compress a PNG with default settings:
   `optipng {{path/to/file.png}}`
2. Compress a PNG with the best compression:
   `optipng -o {{7}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
3. Compress a PNG with the fastest compression:
   `optipng -o {{0}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
4. Compress a PNG and add interlacing:
   `optipng -i {{1}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
5. Compress a PNG and preserve all metadata (including file timestamps):
   `optipng -preserve {{path/to/file.png}}`
6. Compress a PNG and remove all metadata:
   `optipng -strip all {{path/to/file.png}}`
opusenc:
**`opusenc`**: Convert WAV or FLAC audio to Opus.

**Examples:**
1. Convert WAV to Opus using default options:
   `opusenc {{path/to/input.wav}} {{path/to/output.opus}}`
2. Convert stereo audio at the highest quality level:
   `opusenc --bitrate {{512}} {{path/to/input.wav}} {{path/to/output.opus}}`
3. Convert 5.1 surround sound audio at the highest quality level:
   `opusenc --bitrate {{1536}} {{path/to/input.flac}} {{path/to/output.opus}}`
4. Convert speech audio at the lowest quality level:
   `opusenc {{path/to/input.wav}} --downmix-mono --bitrate {{6}} {{path/to/out.opus}}`
orca-c:
**`orca-c`**: A C-port of the ORCA live programming environment.

**Examples:**
1. Start ORCA with an empty workspace:
   `orca-c`
2. Start ORCA and open a specific file:
   `orca-c {{path/to/file.orca}}`
3. Start ORCA and set a specific tempo (defaults to 120):
   `orca-c --bpm {{beats_per_minute}}`

5. Start ORCA and set the maximum number of undo steps (defaults to 100):
   `orca-c --undo-limit {{limit}}`
6. Show the main menu inside of ORCA:
   `<F1>`
7. Show all shortcuts inside of ORCA:
   `<?>`
8. Show all ORCA operators inside of ORCA:
   `<Ctrl g>`
osage:
**`osage`**: Render an image of a `clustered` network graph from a `graphviz` file.

**Examples:**
1. Render a PNG image with a filename based on the input filename and output format (uppercase -O):
   `osage -T {{png}} -O {{path/to/input.gv}}`
2. Render a SVG image with the specified output filename (lowercase -o):
   `osage -T {{svg}} -o {{path/to/image.svg}} {{path/to/input.gv}}`
3. Render the output in PS, PDF, SVG, Fig, PNG, GIF, JPEG, JSON, or DOT format:
   `osage -T {{format}} -O {{path/to/input.gv}}`
4. Render a GIF image using `stdin` and `stdout`:

5. Display help:
   `osage -?`
osmium:
**`osmium`**: Multipurpose tool for handling OpenStreetMap (OSM) files.

**Examples:**
1. Show file information:
   `osmium fileinfo {{path/to/input.osm}}`
2. Display contents:
   `osmium show {{path/to/input.osm}}`
3. Convert file format from PBF into XML:
   `osmium cat {{path/to/input.osm.pbf}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.osm}}`
4. Extract a geographic region by the given [b]ounding box:
   `osmium extract {{[-b|--bbox]}} {{min_longitude}},{{min_latitude}},{{max_longitude}},{{max_latitude}} {{path/to/input.pbf}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pbf}}`
5. Extract a geographic region by a GeoJSON file:

   `osmium tags-filter {{path/to/input.pbf}} amenity=restaurant {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pbf}}`
7. Filter for "way" objects tagged as "highway":
   `osmium tags-filter {{path/to/input.pbf}} w/highway {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pbf}}`
8. Filter "way" and "relation" objects tagged as "building":
   `osmium tags-filter {{path/to/input.pbf}} wr/building {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pbf}}`
osv-scanner:
**`osv-scanner`**: Scan various mediums for dependencies and matches them against the OSV database.

**Examples:**
1. Scan a Docker image:
   `osv-scanner -D {{docker_image_name}}`
2. Scan a package lockfile:
   `osv-scanner -L {{path/to/lockfile}}`
3. Scan an SBOM file:

4. Scan multiple directories recursively:

5. Skip scanning Git repositories:
   `osv-scanner --skip-git {{-r|-D}} {{target}}`
6. Output result in JSON format:
   `osv-scanner --json {{-D|-L|-S|-r}} {{target}}`
ots:
**`ots`**: Share end-to-end encrypted secrets using a one-time-viewable URL.

1. Create new secret:

2. Create new secret and specify hours until expiry (default is 24):
   `ots new -x {{number_of_hours}}h`

   `ots new --region {{regional_server_id}}`
ouch:
**`ouch`**: Utility for compressing and decompressing files and directories.

**Examples:**
1. Decompress a specific file:
   `ouch decompress {{path/to/archive.tar.xz}}`
2. Decompress a file to a specific location:
   `ouch decompress {{path/to/archive.tar.xz}} --dir {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Decompress multiple files:
   `ouch decompress {{path/to/archive1.tar path/to/archive2.tar.gz ...}}`
4. Compress files:
   `ouch compress {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}} {{path/to/archive.zip}}`
oxipng:
**`oxipng`**: Losslessly improve compression of PNG files.

**Examples:**
1. Compress a PNG file (overwrites the file by default):
   `oxipng {{path/to/file.png}}`
2. Compress a PNG file and save the output to a new file:
   `oxipng --out {{path/to/output.png}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
3. Compress all PNG files in the current directory using multiple threads:
   `oxipng "*.png"`
4. Compress a file with a set optimization level (default is 2):
   `oxipng {{[-o|--opt]}} {{0|1|2|3|4|5|6|max}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
5. Set the PNG interlacing type (`off` removes interlacing, `on` applies Adam7 interlacing, `keep` preserves existing interlacing; default is `off`):
   `oxipng {{[-i|--interlace]}} {{off|on|keep}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
6. Perform additional optimization on images with an alpha channel:
   `oxipng {{[-a|--alpha]}} {{path/to/file.png}}`
7. Use the much slower but stronger Zopfli compressor with max optimization:
   `oxipng {{[-z|--zopfli]}} {{[-o|--opt]}} max {{path/to/file.png}}`
8. Strip all non-critical metadata chunks:
   `oxipng --strip all {{path/to/file.png}}`
p10k:
**`p10k`**: Manage configurations for powerlevel10k.

**Examples:**
1. Configure powerlevel10k interactively:
   `p10k configure`
2. Reload powerlevel10k:
   `p10k reload`
3. Display help:
   `p10k help`
p4:
**`p4`**: Perforce Version Control System.
