1. Log in to the Perforce service:
   `p4 login -a`
2. Create a client:
   `p4 client`
3. Copy files from depot into the client workspace:
   `p4 sync`
4. Create or edit changelist description:
   `p4 change`
5. Open a file to edit:
   `p4 edit -c {{changelist_number}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Open a new file to add it to the depot:
   `p4 add`
7. Display list of files modified by changelist:
   `p4 describe -c {{changelist_number}}`
8. Submit a changelist to the depot:
   `p4 submit -c {{changelist_number}}`
p5:
**`p5`**: Template builder and sketch manager for p5.js.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new p5 collection:
   `p5 new {{collection_name}}`
2. Generate a new p5 project (should be run from collection directory):
   `p5 generate {{project_name}}`
3. Run the p5 manager server:
   `p5 server`
4. Update libraries to their latest versions:
   `p5 update`
p7zip:
**`p7zip`**: Wrapper of 7-Zip file archiver with high compression ratio.

**Examples:**
1. Archive a file, replacing it with a 7zipped compressed version:
   `p7zip {{path/to/file}}`
2. Archive a file keeping the input file:
   `p7zip {{[-k|--keep]}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Decompress a file, replacing it with the original uncompressed version:
   `p7zip {{[-d|--decompress]}} {{compressed.ext}}.7z`
4. Decompress a file keeping the input file:
   `p7zip {{[-d|--decompress]}} {{[-k|--keep]}} {{compressed.ext}}.7z`
5. Skip some checks and force compression or decompression:
   `p7zip {{[-f|--force]}} {{path/to/file}}`
paci:
**`paci`**: A package manager for Bash scripts.

**Examples:**
1. Update the list of available packages and versions (it's recommended to run this before other `paci` commands):
   `paci refresh`
2. Configure its behavior:
   `paci configure`
3. Search for a given package:
   `paci search {{package}}`
4. Install a package:
   `paci install {{package}}`
5. Update a package:
   `paci update {{package}}`
packer:
**`packer`**: Build automated machine images.

**Examples:**
1. Build an image:
   `packer build {{path/to/config.json}}`
2. Check the syntax of a Packer image config:
   `packer validate {{path/to/config.json}}`
3. Format a Packer image config:
   `packer fmt {{path/to/config.pkr.hcl}}`
packtpub:
**`packtpub`**: Download freely offered books from packtpub.com.

**Examples:**
1. Download the daily offer book into the current directory with the specified book format (defaults to `pdf`):
   `packtpub download {{[-t|--type]}} {{pdf|ebup|mobi}}`
2. Download the daily offer book into the specified directory:
   `packtpub download {{[-d|--dir]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Start an interactive login to packtpub.com:
   `packtpub login`
4. Log out from packtpub.com:
   `packtpub logout`
5. Display the daily offer:
   `packtpub view-offer`
6. Open the daily offer in the default web browser:
   `packtpub view-offer`
7. Display the currently logged-in user:
   `packtpub whoami`
packwiz:
**`packwiz`**: Create, edit, and manage Minecraft modpacks.

**Examples:**
1. Interactively create a new modpack in the current directory:
   `packwiz init`
2. Add a mod from Modrinth or Curseforge:
   `packwiz {{modrinth|curseforge}} add {{url|slug|search_term}}`
3. List all mods in the modpack:
   `packwiz list`
4. Update `index.toml` after manually editing files:
   `packwiz refresh`
5. Export as a Modrinth (`.mrpack`) or Curseforge (Zip) file:
   `packwiz {{modrinth|curseforge}} export`
pactl:
**`pactl`**: Control a running PulseAudio sound server.

**Examples:**
1. Show information about the sound server:
   `pactl info`
2. List all sinks (or other types - sinks are outputs and sink-inputs are active audio streams):
   `pactl list {{sinks}} short`
3. Change the default sink (output) to 1 (the number can be retrieved via the `list` subcommand):
   `pactl set-default-sink {{1}}`
4. Move sink-input 627 to sink 1:
   `pactl move-sink-input {{627}} {{1}}`
5. Set the volume of sink 1 to 75%:
   `pactl set-sink-volume {{1}} {{0.75}}`
6. Toggle mute on the default sink (using the special name `@DEFAULT_SINK@`):
   `pactl set-sink-mute {{@DEFAULT_SINK@}} toggle`
pageres:
**`pageres`**: Capture screenshots of websites in various resolutions.

**Examples:**
1. Take multiple screenshots of multiple URLs at different resolutions:
   `pageres {{https://example.com/}} {{https://example2.com/}} {{1366x768}} {{1600x900}}`
2. Provide specific options for a URL, overriding global options:
   `pageres [{{https://example.com/}} {{1366x768}} --no-crop] [{{https://example2.com/}} {{1024x768}}] {{[-c|--crop]}}`
3. Provide a custom filename template:
   `pageres {{https://example.com/}} {{1024x768}} --filename='{{<%= date %> - <%= url %>}}'`
4. Capture a specific element on a page:
   `pageres {{https://example.com/}} {{1366x768}} --selector='{{.page-header}}'`
5. Hide a specific element:
   `pageres {{https://example.com/}} {{1366x768}} --hide='{{.page-header}}'`
6. Capture a screenshot of a local file:
   `pageres {{path/to/local_file.html}} {{1366x768}}`
pake:
**`pake`**: Turn any webpage into a desktop app with Rust/Tauri.

**Examples:**
1. Package a web page:
   `pake {{https://www.example.com/}}`
2. Package a web page with a specific window size:
   `pake --width {{800}} --height {{600}} {{https://www.example.com/}}`
3. Package a web page with a custom application name and icon:
   `pake --name {{application_name}} --icon {{path/to/icon.ico}} {{https://www.example.com/}}`
4. Package a web page with a non-resizable window:
   `pake --no-resizable {{https://www.example.com/}}`
5. Package a web page with fullscreen mode:
   `pake --fullscreen {{https://www.example.com/}}`
6. Package a web page with a transparent title bar:
   `pake --transparent {{https://www.example.com/}}`
palmtopnm:
**`palmtopnm`**: Convert a Palm bitmap file to a PNM image.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Palm bitmap to a PNM image:
   `palmtopnm {{path/to/file.palm}} > {{path/to/file.pnm}}`
2. Display information about the input file:
   `palmtopnm {{[-verb|-verbose]}} {{path/to/file.palm}} > {{path/to/file.pnm}}`
3. Convert the n'th rendition of the image contained in the input file:
   `palmtopnm {{[-r|-rendition]}} {{n}} {{path/to/file.palm}} > {{path/to/file.pnm}}`
4. Write a histogram of the colors in the input file to `stdout`:
   `palmtopnm {{[-s|-showhist]}} {{path/to/file.palm}} > {{path/to/file.pnm}}`
5. Output the transparent color of the input image if set:
   `palmtopnm {{[-t|-transparent]}} {{path/to/file.palm}}`
pamarith:
**`pamarith`**: Apply a binary function on two Netpbm images.

**Examples:**
1. Apply the specified binary function pixel-wise on the two specified images (which must be of the same size):
   `pamarith -{{add|subtract|multiply|divide|difference|minimum|maximum|...}} {{path/to/image1.pam|pbm|pgm|ppm}} {{path/to/image2.pam|pbm|pgm|ppm}}`
pambackground:
**`pambackground`**: Create a mask of the background in a PAM image.

**Examples:**
1. Create a mask of the background in a PAM image:
   `pambackground {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pambrighten:
**`pambrighten`**: Change a PAM image's saturation and value.

**Examples:**
1. Increase the saturation of each pixel by the specified percentage:
   `pambrighten {{[-s|-saturation]}} {{value_percent}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Increase the value (from the HSV color space) of each pixel by the specified percentage:
   `pambrighten {{[-va|-value]}} {{value_percent}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamcomp:
**`pamcomp`**: Overlay two PAM images.

**Examples:**
1. Overlay two images such with the overlay blocking parts of the underlay:
   `pamcomp {{path/to/overlay.pam}} {{path/to/underlay.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Set the horizontal alignment of the overlay:
   `pamcomp {{[-ali|-align]}} {{left|center|right|beyondleft|beyondright}} {{[-x|-xoff]}} {{x_offset}} {{path/to/overlay.pam}} {{path/to/underlay.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
3. Set the vertical alignment of the overlay:
   `pamcomp {{[-va|-valign]}} {{top|middle|bottom|above|below}} {{[-y|-yoff]}} {{y_offset}} {{path/to/overlay.pam}} {{path/to/underlay.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
4. Set the opacity of the overlay:
   `pamcomp {{[-o|-opacity]}} {{0.7}} {{path/to/overlay.pam}} {{path/to/underlay.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamcrater:
**`pamcrater`**: Create a PAM image of cratered terrain.

**Examples:**
1. Create an image of cratered terrain with the specified dimensions:
   `pamcrater {{[-h|-height]}} {{height}} {{[-w|-width]}} {{width}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Create an image containing the specified number of craters:
   `pamcrater {{[-n|-number]}} {{n_craters}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamcut:
**`pamcut`**: Cut out a rectangular region from a Netpbm image.

**Examples:**
1. Discard the specified number of columns/rows on each side of the image:
   `pamcut {{[-cropl|-cropleft]}} {{value}} {{[-cropr|-cropright]}} {{value}} {{[-cropt|-croptop]}} {{value}} {{[-cropb|-cropbottom]}} {{value}} {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
2. Keep only the columns between the specified columns (inclusively):
   `pamcut {{[-l|-left]}} {{value}} {{[-ri|-right]}} {{value}} {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
3. Fill missing areas with black pixels if the specified rectangle does not entirely lie within the input image:
   `pamcut {{[-t|-top]}} {{value}} {{[-b|-bottom]}} {{value}} -pad {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
pamdeinterlace:
**`pamdeinterlace`**: Remove every other row in a Netpbm image.

**Examples:**
1. Produce an image consisting of the input's even-numbered rows:
   `pamdeinterlace {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
2. Produce an image consisting of the input's odd-numbered rows:
   `pamdeinterlace {{[-takeo|-takeodd]}} {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
pamdepth:
**`pamdepth`**: Reduce the depth (i.e. color resolution) in an image.

**Examples:**
1. Read a PBM image, set its maxval and save it to a file:
   `pamdepth {{maxval}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
pamdice:
**`pamdice`**: Slice a Netpbm image vertically or horizontally.

**Examples:**
1. Slice a Netpbm image such that the resulting tiles have the specified height and width:
   `pamdice {{[-o|-outstem]}} {{path/to/filename_stem}} {{[-he|-height]}} {{value}} {{[-w|-width]}} {{value}} {{path/to/input.ppm}}`
2. Make the produced pieces overlap by the specified amount horizontally and vertically:
   `pamdice {{[-o|-outstem]}} {{path/to/filename_stem}} {{[-he|-height]}} {{value}} {{[-w|-width]}} {{value}} {{[-ho|-hoverlap]}} {{value}} {{[-vo|-voverlap]}} {{value}} {{path/to/input.ppm}}`
pamditherbw:
**`pamditherbw`**: Apply dithering to a greyscale image, i.e. turn it into a pattern of black and white pixels that look the same as the original greyscale.

**Examples:**
1. Read a PGM image, apply dithering and save it to a file:
   `pamditherbw {{path/to/image.pgm}} > {{path/to/file.pgm}}`
2. Use the specified quantization method:
   `pamditherbw -{{floyd|fs|atkinson|threshold|hilbert|...}} {{path/to/image.pgm}} > {{path/to/file.pgm}}`
3. Use the atkinson quantization method and the specified seed for a pseudo-random number generator:
   `pamditherbw {{[-a|-atkinson]}} {{[-r|-randomseed]}} {{1337}} {{path/to/image.pgm}} > {{path/to/file.pgm}}`
4. Specify the thresholding value for quantization methods that perform some sort of thresholding:
   `pamditherbw -{{fs|atkinson|thresholding}} {{[-va|-value]}} {{0.3}} {{path/to/image.pgm}} > {{path/to/file.pgm}}`
pamedge:
**`pamedge`**: Perform edge-detection on a Netpbm image.

**Examples:**
1. Perform edge-detection on a Netpbm image:
   `pamedge {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamenlarge:
**`pamenlarge`**: Enlarge a PAM image by duplicating pixels.

**Examples:**
1. Enlarge the specified image by the specified factor:
   `pamenlarge {{[-s|-scale]}} {{n}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Enlarge the specified image by the specified factors horizontally and vertically:
   `pamenlarge {{[-x|-xscale]}} {{xn}} {{[-y|-yscale]}} {{yn}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamexec:
**`pamexec`**: Execute a shell command on each image in a Netpbm file.

**Examples:**
1. Execute a shell command on each image in a Netpbm file:
   `pamexec {{command}} {{path/to/image.pam}}`
2. Stop processing if a command terminates with a nonzero exit status:
   `pamexec {{command}} {{path/to/image.pam}} {{[-c|-check]}}`
pamfile:
**`pamfile`**: Describe Netpbm (PAM or PNM) files.

**Examples:**
1. Describe the specified Netpbm files:
   `pamfile {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
2. Describe every image in each input file (as opposed to only the first image in each file) in a machine-readable format:
   `pamfile {{[-a|-allimages]}} -machine {{path/to/file}}`
3. Display a count on how many images the input files contain:
   `pamfile {{[-cou|-count]}} {{path/to/file}}`
pamfix:
**`pamfix`**: Fix errors in PAM, PBM, PGM, and PPM files.

**Examples:**
1. Fix a Netpbm file that is missing its last part:
   `pamfix {{[-t|-truncate]}} {{path/to/corrupted.ext}} > {{path/to/output.ext}}`
2. Fix a Netpbm file where pixel values exceed the image's `maxval` by lowering the offending pixels' values:
   `pamfix {{[-cl|-clip]}} {{path/to/corrupted.ext}} > {{path/to/output.ext}}`
3. Fix a Netpbm file where pixel values exceed the image's `maxval` by increasing it:
   `pamfix {{[-ch|-changemaxval]}} {{path/to/corrupted.pam|pbm|pgm|ppm}} > {{path/to/output.pam|pbm|pgm|ppm}}`
pamfixtrunc:
**`pamfixtrunc`**: This command has been superseded by `pamfix -truncate`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the current command:
   `tldr pamfix`
pamflip:
**`pamflip`**: Flip or rotate a PAM or PNM image.

**Examples:**
1. Rotate the input image counter-clockwise for a specific degree:
   `pamflip {{[-r|-rotate]}}{{90|180|270}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Flip left for right:
   `pamflip {{[-lr|-leftright]}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
3. Flip top for bottom:
   `pamflip {{[-tb|-topbottom]}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
4. Flip the input image on the main diagonal:
   `pamflip {{[-xy|-transpose]}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamfunc:
**`pamfunc`**: Apply a simple arithmetic function to a Netpbm image.

**Examples:**
1. Apply the specified arithmetic function with `n` as the second argument to each sample in the specified PAM image:
   `pamfunc -{{multiplier|divisor|adder|subtractor|min|max}} {{n}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Apply the specified bit string function with `n` as the second argument to each sample in the specified PAM image:
   `pamfunc -{{andmask|ormask|xormask|shiftleft|shiftright}} {{n}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamixer:
**`pamixer`**: A simple command-line mixer for PulseAudio.

**Examples:**
1. List all sinks and sources with their corresponding IDs:
   `pamixer --list-sinks --list-sources`
2. Set the volume to 75% on the default sink:
   `pamixer --set-volume {{75}}`
3. Toggle mute on a sink other than the default:
   `pamixer --toggle-mute --sink {{id}}`
4. Increase the volume on default sink by 5%:
   `pamixer {{[-i|--increase]}} {{5}}`
5. Decrease the volume on a source by 5%:
   `pamixer {{[-d|--decrease]}} {{5}} --source {{id}}`
6. Use the allow boost option to increase, decrease, or set the volume above 100%:
   `pamixer --set-volume {{105}} --allow-boost`
7. Mute the default sink (use `--unmute` instead to unmute):
   `pamixer {{[-m|--mute]}}`
pammixinterlace:
**`pammixinterlace`**: Merge each row in an image with its two neighbors.

**Examples:**
1. Merge each row in an image with its two neighbors:
   `pammixinterlace {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
2. Use the specified filtering mechanism:
   `pammixinterlace {{[-f|-filter]}} {{linear|fir|ffmpeg}} {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
3. Turn on adaptive filtering mode, i.e., only modify pixels that are obviously part of a comb pattern:
   `pammixinterlace {{[-a|-adaptive]}} {{path/to/image.ppm}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
pamnoraw:
**`pamnoraw`**: This command is an alias of `pamtopnm -plain`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr pamtopnm`
pamoil:
**`pamoil`**: Turn a PAM image into an oil painting.

**Examples:**
1. Turn a PAM image into an oil painting:
   `pamoil {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file.pam}}`
2. Consider a neighborhood of `n` pixels for the "smearing" effect:
   `pamoil -n {{n}} {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file.pam}}`
pampick:
**`pampick`**: Pick images out of a multi-image Netpbm stream.

**Examples:**
1. Execute a shell command on each image in a Netpbm file:
   `pampick < {{path/to/image.pam}} {{image_number1 image_number2 ...}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pampop9:
**`pampop9`**: Simulate a multi-lens camera such as the Pop9.

**Examples:**
1. Tile the input image xtiles by ytiles times, increasing the offset each time as determined by xdelta and ydelta:
   `pampop9 {{path/to/input.pam}} {{xtiles}} {{ytiles}} {{xdelta}} {{ydelta}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamrgbatopng:
**`pamrgbatopng`**: This command has been superseded by `pamtopng`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the current command:
   `tldr pamtopng`
pamscale:
**`pamscale`**: Scale a Netpbm image.

**Examples:**
1. Scale an image such that the result has the specified dimensions:
   `pamscale {{[-wid|-width]}} {{width}} {{[-h|-height]}} {{height}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Scale an image such that the result has the specified width, keeping the aspect ratio:
   `pamscale {{[-wid|-width]}} {{width}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
3. Scale an image such that its width and height is changed by the specified factors:
   `pamscale {{[-xsc|-xscale]}} {{x_factor}} {{[-ysc|-yscale]}} {{y_factor}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
4. Scale an image such that it fits into the specified bounding box while preserving its aspect ratio:
   `pamscale -xyfit {{bbox_width}} {{bbox_height}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
5. Scale an image such that it completely fills the specified box while preserving its aspect ratio:
   `pamscale -xyfill {{box_width}} {{box_height}} {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamshadedrelief:
**`pamshadedrelief`**: Generate a shaded relief from an elevation map.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a shaded relief image with the input image interpreted as an elevation map:
   `pamshadedrelief < {{path/to/input.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Gamma adjust the image by the specified factor:
   `pamshadedrelief < {{path/to/input.pam}} {{[-g|-gamma]}} {{factor}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamslice:
**`pamslice`**: Extract one line of values out of a PAM image.

**Examples:**
1. Print the values of the pixels in the n'th row in a table:
   `pamslice {{[-r|-row]}} {{n}} {{path/to/image.pam}}`
2. Print the values of the pixels in the n'th column in a table:
   `pamslice {{[-c|-column]}} {{n}} {{path/to/image.pam}}`
3. Consider the m'th plane of the input image only:
   `pamslice {{[-r|-row]}} {{n}} -plane {{m}} {{path/to/image.pam}}`
4. Produce output in a format suitable for input to an `xmgr` for visualisation:
   `pamslice {{[-r|-row]}} {{n}} {{[-x|-xmgr]}} {{path/to/image.pam}}`
pamsplit:
**`pamsplit`**: Split a multi-image Netpbm file into multiple single-image Netpbm files.

**Examples:**
1. Split a multi-image Netpbm file into multiple single-image Netpbm files:
   `pamsplit {{path/to/image.pam}}`
2. Specify a pattern for naming output files:
   `pamsplit {{path/to/image.pam}} {{file_%d.pam}}`
pamstack:
**`pamstack`**: Stack the planes of multiple PAM images into one PAM image.

**Examples:**
1. Stack the planes of the specified PAM images in the specified order:
   `pamstack {{path/to/image1.pam path/to/image2.pam ...}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Specify the tuple type name of the output PAM file (maximum of 255 characters):
   `pamstack {{[-t|-tupletype]}} {{tuple_type}} {{path/to/image1.pam path/to/image2.pam ...}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamstretch-gen:
**`pamstretch-gen`**: Scale up a PAM image by decimal values.

**Examples:**
1. Scale up a PAM image by the specified decimal factor:
   `pamstretch-gen {{n}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamstretch:
**`pamstretch`**: Scale up a PAM image by interpolating between pixels.

**Examples:**
1. Scale up a PAM image by an integer factor:
   `pamstretch {{n}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Scale up a PAM image by the specified factors in the horizontal and vertical directions:
   `pamstretch {{[-x|-xscale]}} {{xn}} {{[-y|-yscale]}} {{yn}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
pamtofits:
**`pamtofits`**: Convert a Netpbm image to the Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) format.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Netpbm image to the FITS format:
   `pamtofits {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.fits}}`
pamtogif:
**`pamtogif`**: Convert a Netpbm image into an unanimated GIF image.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Netpbm image into an unanimated GIF image:
   `pamtogif {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.gif}}`
2. Mark the specified color as transparent in the output GIF file:
   `pamtogif {{[-t|-transparent]}} {{color}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.gif}}`
3. Include the specified text as a comment in the output GIF file:
   `pamtogif {{[-c|-comment]}} "{{Hello World!}}" {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.gif}}`
pamtopam:
**`pamtopam`**: Copy a PAM image.

**Examples:**
1. Copy a PAM image (i.e. a PBM, PGM, PPM, or PAM image) from `stdin` to `stdout`:
   `pamtopam < {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Display version:
   `pamtopam {{[-v|-version]}}`
pamtopng:
**`pamtopng`**: Convert a PAM image to PNG.

**Examples:**
1. Convert the specified PAM image to PNG:
   `pamtopng {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`
2. Mark the specified color as transparent in the output image:
   `pamtopng {{[-t|-transparent]}} {{color}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`
3. Include the text in the specified file as tEXt chunks in the output:
   `pamtopng {{[-te|-text]}} {{path/to/file.txt}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`
4. Cause the output file to be interlaced in Adam7 format:
   `pamtopng {{[-in|-interlace]}} {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.png}}`
pamtopnm:
**`pamtopnm`**: Convert a PAM image to an equivalent PNM image.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a PAM image to an equivalent PNM image, i.e. a PBM, PGM, or PPM image:
   `pamtopnm {{path/to/image.pam}} > {{path/to/output.pbm|pgm|ppm}}`
2. Display version:
   `pamtopnm {{[-v|-version]}}`
pamtoqoi:
**`pamtoqoi`**: Convert a Netpbm image to a QOI image (Quite OK Image format).

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Netpbm image to the QOI format:
   `pamtoqoi {{path/to/image.pnm}} > {{path/to/output.qoi}}`
pamtosrf:
**`pamtosrf`**: Convert Netpbm images to SRF format.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Netpbm image or a stream of Netpbm images to SRF format:
   `pamtosrf {{path/to/file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.srf}}`
pamtotga:
**`pamtotga`**: Convert a Netpbm image to a TrueVision Targa file.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Netpbm image to a TrueVision Targa file:
   `pamtotga {{path/to/file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.tga}}`
2. Specify the color map of the output image:
   `pamtotga -{{cmap|cmap16|mono|rgb}} {{path/to/file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.tga}}`
3. Display version:
   `pamtotga {{[-v|-version]}}`
pamtotiff:
**`pamtotiff`**: Convert a PAM image to a TIFF file.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a PAM image to a TIFF image:
   `pamtotiff {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file.tiff}}`
2. Explicitly specify a compression method for the output file:
   `pamtotiff -{{none|packbits|lzw|g3|g4|flate|adobeflate}} {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file.tiff}}`
3. Always produce a color TIFF image, even if the input image is greyscale:
   `pamtotiff {{[-c|-color]}} {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file.tiff}}`
pamtouil:
**`pamtouil`**: Convert a PNM or PAM file into a Motif UIL icon file.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a PNM or PAM file into a Motif UIL icon file:
   `pamtouil {{path/to/input.pnm|pam}} > {{path/to/output.uil}}`
2. Specify a prefix string to be printed in the output UIL file:
   `pamtouil {{[-n|-name]}} {{uilname}} {{path/to/input.pnm|pam}} > {{path/to/output.uil}}`
pamtowinicon:
**`pamtowinicon`**: Convert a PAM image to a Windows ICO file.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a PAM image file to an ICO file:
   `pamtowinicon {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.ico}}`
2. Encode images with resolutions smaller than `t` in the BMP format and all other images in the PNG format:
   `pamtowinicon {{[-pn|-pngthreshold]}} {{t}} {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.ico}}`
3. Make all pixels outside the non-opaque area black:
   `pamtowinicon {{[-t|-truetransparent]}} {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output.ico}}`
pamtoxvmini:
**`pamtoxvmini`**: Convert a Netpbm image to an XV thumbnail picture.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a PAM image to an XV thumbnail picture:
   `pamtoxvmini {{path/to/input_file.pam}} > {{path/to/output_file}}`
pamundice:
**`pamundice`**: Combine a grid of Netpbm images into one.

**Examples:**
1. Combine the images whose names match the `printf`-style filename expression. Assume a grid with a specific size:
   `pamundice {{filename_%1d_%1a.ppm}} {{[-a|-across]}} {{grid_width}} {{[-d|-down]}} {{grid_height}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
2. Assume that the tiles overlap horizontally and vertically by the specified amount:
   `pamundice {{filename_%1d_%1a.ppm}} {{[-a|-across]}} {{x_value}} {{[-d|-down]}} {{y_value}} {{[-ho|-hoverlap]}} {{value}} {{[-vo|-voverlap]}} {{value}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
3. Specify the images to be combined through a text file containing one filename per line:
   `pamundice {{[-l|-listfile]}} {{path/to/file.txt}} {{[-a|-across]}} {{x_value}} {{[-d|-down]}} {{y_value}} > {{path/to/output.ppm}}`
pamvalidate:
**`pamvalidate`**: Validate PAM, PGM, PBM, and PPM files.

**Examples:**
1. Copy a Netpbm file from `stdin` to `stdout` if and only if it valid; fail otherwise:
   `{{command}} | pamvalidate > {{path/to/output.ext}}`
pandoc:
**`pandoc`**: Convert documents between various formats.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a Markdown file to PDF using `pdflatex` (the formats are determined by file extensions):
   `pandoc {{path/to/input.md}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pdf}}`
2. Convert the output from another command to PDF, using a specific PDF engine:
   `{{command}} | pandoc {{[-f|--from]}} {{input_format}} --pdf-engine {{tectonic|weasyprint|typst|...}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.pdf}}`
3. Convert to a standalone file with the appropriate headers/footers (for LaTeX, HTML, etc.):
   `pandoc {{path/to/input.md}} {{[-s|--standalone]}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output.html}}`
4. Manually specify formats (overriding automatic format detection using the filename extension, or when there is no extension):
   `pandoc {{[-f|--from]}} {{docx|...}} {{path/to/input}} {{[-t|--to]}} {{pdf|...}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output}}`
5. Transform a document using a Lua script (see <https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html> for more information):
   `pandoc {{path/to/input}} {{[-L|--lua-filter]}} {{path/to/filter.lua}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output}}`
6. Convert a remote HTML file to markdown and print the result to `stdout`:
   `pandoc {{[-f|--from]}} html {{[-t|--to]}} markdown {{https://example.com}}`
7. List all supported input formats:
   `pandoc --list-input-formats`
8. List all supported output formats:
   `pandoc --list-output-formats`
pangolin:
**`pangolin`**: Implements the dynamic nomenclature of SARS-CoV-2 lineages (Pango nomenclature).

**Examples:**
1. Run `pangolin` on the specified FASTA file:
   `pangolin {{path/to/file.fa}}`
2. Use the specified analysis engine:
   `pangolin --analysis-mode {{accurate|fast|pangolearn|usher}}`
pants:
**`pants`**: Fast, scalable, user-friendly, open-source build and developer workflow tool.

**Examples:**
1. List all targets:
   `pants list ::`
2. Run all tests:
   `pants test ::`
3. Fix, format, and lint only uncommitted files:
   `pants --changed-since=HEAD fix fmt lint`
4. Typecheck only uncommitted files and their dependents:
   `pants --changed-since=HEAD --changed-dependents=transitive check`
5. Create a distributable package for the specified target:
   `pants package {{path/to/directory:target-name}}`
6. Auto-generate BUILD file targets for new source files:
   `pants tailor ::`
7. Display help:
   `pants help`
paperkey:
**`paperkey`**: An OpenPGP key archiver.

**Examples:**
1. Take a specific secret key and generate a text file with the secret data:
   `paperkey --secret-key {{path/to/secret_key.gpg}} --output {{path/to/secret_data.txt}}`
2. Take the secret key data in `secret_data.txt` and combine it with the public key to reconstruct the secret key:
   `paperkey --pubring {{path/to/public_key.gpg}} --secrets {{path/to/secret_data.txt}} --output {{secret_key.gpg}}`
3. Export a specific secret key and generate a text file with the secret data:
   `gpg --export-secret-key {{key}} | paperkey --output {{path/to/secret_data.txt}}`
papermc:
**`papermc`**: Manage a Minecraft server.

**Examples:**
1. Start a server:
   `papermc start`
2. Stop a server:
   `papermc stop`
3. Restart a server:
   `papermc restart`
4. Backup a world:
   `papermc backup`
5. Restore world data from a backup:
   `papermc restore {{path/to/file}}`
6. Display help:
   `papermc`
par2:
**`par2`**: File verification and repair using PAR 2.0 compatible parity archives (.par2 files).

**Examples:**
1. Create a parity archive with a set percentage level of redundancy:
   `par2 create -r{{1..100}} -- {{path/to/file}}`
2. Create a parity archive with a chosen number of volume files (in addition to the index file):
   `par2 create -n{{1..32768}} -- {{path/to/file}}`
3. Verify a file with a parity archive:
   `par2 verify -- {{path/to/file.par2}}`
4. Repair a file with a parity archive:
   `par2 repair -- {{path/to/file.par2}}`
parallel-lint:
**`parallel-lint`**: Check the syntax of PHP files in parallel.

**Examples:**
1. Lint a specific directory:
   `parallel-lint {{path/to/directory}}`
2. Lint a directory using the specified number of parallel processes:
   `parallel-lint -j {{processes}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Lint a directory, excluding the specified directory:
   `parallel-lint --exclude {{path/to/excluded_directory}} {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Lint a directory of files using a comma-separated list of extension(s):
   `parallel-lint -e {{php,html,phpt}} {{path/to/directory}}`
5. Lint a directory and output the results as JSON:
   `parallel-lint --json {{path/to/directory}}`
6. Lint a directory and show Git Blame results for rows containing errors:
   `parallel-lint --blame {{path/to/directory}}`
parallel:
**`parallel`**: Run commands on multiple CPU cores.

**Examples:**
1. Gzip several files at once, using all cores:
   `parallel gzip ::: {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
2. Read arguments from `stdin`, run 4 jobs at once:
   `ls *.txt | parallel {{[-j|--jobs]}} 4 gzip`
3. Convert JPEG images to PNG using replacement strings:
   `parallel convert {} {.}.png ::: *.jpg`
4. Parallel xargs, cram as many args as possible onto one command:
   `{{args}} | parallel -X {{command}}`
5. Break `stdin` into ~1M blocks, feed each block to `stdin` of new command:
   `cat {{big_file.txt}} | parallel --pipe --block 1M {{command}}`
6. Run on multiple machines via SSH:
   `parallel {{[-S|--sshlogin]}} {{machine1}},{{machine2}} {{command}} ::: {{arg1}} {{arg2}}`
7. Download 4 files simultaneously from a text file containing links showing progress:
   `parallel {{[-j|--jobs]}} 4 --bar --eta curl {{[-sO|--silent --remote-name]}} {} :::: {{path/to/links.txt}}`
8. Print the jobs which `parallel` is running in `stderr`:
   `parallel {{[-t|--verbose]}} {{command}} ::: {{args}}`
parquet-tools:
**`parquet-tools`**: Show, inspect, and manipulate Parquet file.

**Examples:**
1. Display the content of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools cat {{path/to/parquet}}`
2. Display the first few lines of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools head {{path/to/parquet}}`
3. Print the schema of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools schema {{path/to/parquet}}`
4. Print the metadata of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools meta {{path/to/parquet}}`
5. Print the content and metadata of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools dump {{path/to/parquet}}`
6. Concatenate several Parquet files into the target one:
   `parquet-tools merge {{path/to/parquet1}} {{path/to/parquet2}} {{path/to/target_parquet}}`
7. Print the count of rows in a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools rowcount {{path/to/parquet}}`
8. Print the column and offset indexes of a Parquet file:
   `parquet-tools column-index {{path/to/parquet}}`
particle:
**`particle`**: Interact with Particle devices.

**Examples:**
1. Log in or create an account for the Particle CLI:
   `particle setup`
2. Display a list of devices:
   `particle list`
3. Create a new Particle project interactively:
   `particle project create`
4. Compile a Particle project:
   `particle compile {{device_type}} {{path/to/source_code.ino}}`
5. Update a device to use a specific app remotely:
   `particle flash {{device_name}} {{path/to/program.bin}}`
6. Update a device to use the latest firmware via serial:
   `particle flash --serial {{path/to/firmware.bin}}`
7. Execute a function on a device:
   `particle call {{device_name}} {{function_name}} {{function_arguments}}`
pass-otp:
**`pass-otp`**: A pass extension for managing one-time-password (OTP) tokens.

**Examples:**
1. Prompt for an otpauth URI token and create a new pass file:
   `pass otp insert {{path/to/pass}}`
2. Prompt for an otpauth URI token and append to an existing pass file:
   `pass otp append {{path/to/pass}}`
3. Print a 2FA code using the OTP token in a pass file:
   `pass otp {{path/to/pass}}`
4. Copy and don't print a 2FA code using the OTP token in a pass file:
   `pass otp {{[-c|--clip]}} {{path/to/pass}}`
5. Display a QR code using the OTP token stored in a pass file:
   `pass otp uri {{[-q|--qrcode]}} {{path/to/pass}}`
6. Prompt for an OTP secret value specifying issuer and account (at least one must be specified) and append to existing pass file:
   `pass otp append {{[-s|--secret]}} {{[-i|--issuer]}} {{issuer_name}} {{[-a|--account]}} {{account_name}} {{path/to/pass}}`
pass:
**`pass`**: Store and read passwords or other sensitive data.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize (or re-encrypt) the storage using one or more GPG IDs:
   `pass init {{gpg_id_1 gpg_id_2 ...}}`
2. Save a new password and additional information (press `<Ctrl d>` on a new line to complete):
   `pass insert {{[-m|--multiline]}} {{path/to/data}}`
3. Edit an entry:
   `pass edit {{path/to/data}}`
4. Copy a password (first line of the data file) to the clipboard:
   `pass {{[-c|--clip]}} {{path/to/data}}`
5. List the whole store tree:
   `pass`
6. Generate a new random password with a given length, and copy it to the clipboard:
   `pass generate {{[-c|--clip]}} {{path/to/data}} {{num}}`
7. Initialize a new Git repository (any changes done by pass will be committed automatically):
   `pass git init`
8. Run a Git command on behalf of the password storage:
   `pass git {{command}}`
passwd:
**`passwd`**: Change a user's password.

**Examples:**
1. Change the password of the current user interactively:
   `passwd`
2. Change the password of a specific user:
   `sudo passwd {{username}}`
3. Get the current status of the user:
   `passwd {{[-S|--status]}}`
4. Make the password of the account blank (it will set the named account passwordless):
   `passwd {{[-d|--delete]}}`
5. Set password programmatically (ideal for install scripts):
   `yes {{password}} | passwd`
paste:
**`paste`**: Merge lines of files.

**Examples:**
1. Join all the lines into a single line, using `TAB` as delimiter:
   `paste {{[-s|--serial]}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Join all the lines into a single line, using the specified delimiter:
   `paste {{[-s|--serial]}} {{[-d|--delimiters]}} {{delimiter}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Merge two files side by side, each in its column, using `TAB` as delimiter:
   `paste {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
4. Merge two files side by side, each in its column, using the specified delimiter:
   `paste {{[-d|--delimiters]}} {{delimiter}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
5. Merge two files, with lines added alternatively:
   `paste {{[-d|--delimiters]}} '\n' {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
pastel:
**`pastel`**: Generate, analyze, convert, and manipulate colors.

**Examples:**
1. Convert colors from one format to another. Here from RGB to HSL:
   `pastel format {{hsl}} {{ff8000}}`
2. Show and analyze colors on the terminal:
   `pastel color "{{rgb(255,50,127)}}"`
3. Pick a color from somewhere on the screen:
   `pastel pick`
4. Generate a set of `n` visually distinct colors:
   `pastel distinct {{n}}`
5. List all X11/CSS color names:
   `pastel list`
patator:
**`patator`**: A multi-purpose brute-forcer, with a modular design and a flexible usage.

**Examples:**
1. Brute force ssh login with rate limit and timeout options (successful login will show login banner or something similar):
   `patator ssh_login host={{ip_or_host}} user=FILE0 password=FILE1 0={{path/to/users.txt}} 1={{path/to/passwords.txt}} --rate_limit={{seconds}} --timeout={{seconds}} -x ignore:mesg='Authentication failed.'`
2. Brute force encrypted ZIP file:
   `patator unzip_pass zipfile={{path/to/file.zip}} password=FILE0 0={{path/to/passwords.txt}} -x ignore:code!=0`
3. Brute force http basic auth (payload file `userpass.txt` should be in the format `username:password`):
   `patator http_fuzz url={{http://host:port}} auth_type=basic user_pass=COMBO00:COMBO01 0={{path/to/userpass.txt}} -x ignore:code=401`
4. Brute force FTP/FTPS login:
   `patator ftp_login host={{ip_or_host}} user=FILE0 password=FILE1 0={{path/to/users.txt}} 1={{path/to/passwords.txt}} tls={{0|1}} -x ignore:mesg='Login incorrect.' -x ignore,reset,retry:code=500`
5. List all available modules:
   `patator --help`
6. Display help for a particular module:
   `patator {{module_name}} --help`
patch:
**`patch`**: Patch a file (or files) with a diff file.

**Examples:**
1. Apply a patch using a diff file (filenames must be included in the diff file):
   `patch {{[-i|--input]}} {{patch.diff}}`
2. Apply a patch to a specific file:
   `patch {{[-i|--input]}} {{patch.diff}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Patch a file writing the result to a different file:
   `patch {{[-i|--input]}} {{patch.diff}} {{path/to/input_file}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_file}}`
4. Apply a patch to the current directory:
   `patch {{[-i|--input]}} {{patch.diff}} {{[-p|--strip]}} 1`
5. Apply the reverse of a patch:
   `patch {{[-i|--input]}} {{patch.diff}} {{[-R|--reverse]}}`
patchwork:
**`patchwork`**: Render an image of a `squareified treemap` network graph from a `graphviz` file.

**Examples:**
1. Render a PNG image with a filename based on the input filename and output format (uppercase -O):
   `patchwork -T {{png}} -O {{path/to/input.gv}}`
2. Render a SVG image with the specified output filename (lowercase -o):
   `patchwork -T {{svg}} -o {{path/to/image.svg}} {{path/to/input.gv}}`
3. Render the output in PS, PDF, SVG, Fig, PNG, GIF, JPEG, JSON, or DOT format:
   `patchwork -T {{format}} -O {{path/to/input.gv}}`
4. Render a `gif` image using `stdin` and `stdout`:
   `echo "{{digraph {this -> that} }}" | patchwork -T {{gif}} > {{path/to/image.gif}}`
5. Display help:
   `patchwork -?`
pathchk:
**`pathchk`**: Check the validity and portability of pathnames.

**Examples:**
1. Check pathnames for validity in the current system:
   `pathchk {{path1 path2 ...}}`
2. Check pathnames for validity on a wider range of POSIX compliant systems:
   `pathchk -p {{path1 path2 ...}}`
3. Check pathnames for validity on all POSIX compliant systems:
   `pathchk {{[-p -P|--portability]}} {{path1 path2 ...}}`
4. Only check for empty pathnames or leading dashes (-):
   `pathchk -P {{path1 path2 ...}}`
pax:
**`pax`**: Archiving and copying utility.

**Examples:**
1. List the contents of an archive:
   `pax -f {{archive.tar}}`
2. List the contents of a `gzip` archive:
   `pax -zf {{archive.tar.gz}}`
3. Create an archive from files:
   `pax -wf {{target.tar}} {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
4. Create an archive from files, using output redirection:
   `pax -w {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}} > {{target.tar}}`
5. Extract an archive into the current directory:
   `pax -rf {{source.tar}}`
6. Copy to a directory, while keeping the original metadata; `target/` must exist:
   `pax -rw {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/directory1 path/to/directory2 ...}} {{target/}}`
pbmclean:
**`pbmclean`**: Clean up a PBM image by erasing isolated black and white pixels.

**Examples:**
1. Clean up a PBM image by erasing isolated black and white pixels:
   `pbmclean {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Clean up only black/white pixels:
   `pbmclean -{{black|white}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
3. Specify the minimum number of neighboring pixels of the same color in order for a pixel not to be considered isolated:
   `pbmclean {{[-m|-minneighbors]}} {{3}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
pbmlife:
**`pbmlife`**: Apply Conway's Rules of Life to a PBM image.

**Examples:**
1. Apply the Rules of Life to an input PBM image file for one generation and the output the result as a PBM image file:
   `pbmlife {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
2. Display version:
   `pbmlife {{[-v|-version]}}`
pbmmake:
**`pbmmake`**: Create a blank bitmap.

**Examples:**
1. Create a blank bitmap of the specified dimensions:
   `pbmmake {{width}} {{height}} > {{path/to/output_file.pbm}}`
2. Specify the color of the created bitmap:
   `pbmmake -{{white|black|grey}} {{width}} {{height}} > {{path/to/output_file.pbm}}`
pbmmask:
**`pbmmask`**: Create a mask bitmap from a regular bitmap.

**Examples:**
1. Create a mask bitmap separating background from foreground:
   `pbmmask {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Expand the generated mask by one pixel:
   `pbmmask {{[-r|-expand]}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
pbmnoise:
**`pbmnoise`**: Generate white noise.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a PGM image containing white noise:
   `pbmnoise {{width}} {{height}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Specify the seed for the pseudo-random number generator:
   `pbmnoise {{width}} {{height}} -randomseed {{value}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
3. Specify the desired rate of white to black pixels:
   `pbmnoise {{width}} {{height}} -ratio {{1/3}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
pbmpage:
**`pbmpage`**: Generate a test pattern for printing.

**Examples:**
1. Generate a test pattern for printing onto US standard paper:
   `pbmpage > {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
2. Generate a test pattern for printing onto A4 paper:
   `pbmpage -a4 > {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
3. Specify the pattern to use:
   `pbmpage {{1|2|3}} > {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
pbmpscale:
**`pbmpscale`**: Enlarge a PBM image with edge smoothing.

**Examples:**
1. Enlarge a PBM image by the specified factor with edge smoothing:
   `pbmpscale {{n}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/file.pbm}}`
pbmreduce:
**`pbmreduce`**: Proportionally reduce a PBM image.

**Examples:**
1. Reduce the specified image by the specified factor:
   `pbmreduce {{n}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Use simple thresholding when reducing:
   `pbmreduce {{[-t|-threshold]}} {{n}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
3. Use the specified threshold for all quantizations:
   `pbmreduce {{[-va|-value]}} {{0.6}} {{n}} {{path/to/image.pbm}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
pbmtext:
**`pbmtext`**: Render text as a PBM image.

**Examples:**
1. Render a single line of text as a PBM image:
   `pbmtext "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Render multiple lines of text as a PBM image:
   `echo "{{Hello\nWorld!}}" | pbmtext > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
3. Render text using a custom font supplied as a PBM file:
   `pbmtext {{[-f|-font]}} {{path/to/font.pbm}} "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
4. Specify the number of pixels between characters and lines:
   `echo "{{Hello\nWorld!}}" | pbmtext {{[-s|-space]}} {{3}} {{[-ls|-lspace]}} {{10}} > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
pbmtextps:
**`pbmtextps`**: Render text as a PBM image using PostScript.

**Examples:**
1. Render a single line of text as a PBM image:
   `pbmtextps "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
2. Specify the font and font size:
   `pbmtextps -font {{Times-Roman}} -fontsize {{30}} "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
3. Specify the desired left and top margins:
   `pbmtextps {{[-l|-leftmargin]}} {{70}} {{[-t|-topmargin]}} {{162}} "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.pbm}}`
4. Do not output the rendered text as a PBM image, but a PostScript program that would create this image:
   `pbmtextps {{[-du|-dump-ps]}} "{{Hello World!}}" > {{path/to/output.ps}}`
pbmto4425:

1. Merge two (or more) PDFs:
   `pdfjam {{path/to/file1.pdf path/to/file2.pdf ...}} {{[-o|--outfile]}} {{path/to/output_file.pdf}}`

   `pdfjam {{path/to/file1.pdf 1 path/to/file2.pdf 1 ...}} {{[-o|--outfile]}} {{path/to/output_file.pdf}}`
3. Merge subranges from two PDFs:
   `pdfjam {{path/to/file1.pdf 3-5,1}} {{path/to/file2.pdf 4-6}} {{[-o|--outfile]}} {{path/to/output_file.pdf}}`
4. Sign an A4 page (adjust delta to height for other formats) with a scanned signature by overlaying them:

5. Arrange the pages from the input file into a fancy 2x2 grid:

   `pdfjam {{path/to/file1.pdf last-1 path/to/file2.pdf last-1 ...}} --suffix {{reversed}}`

   `pdftk {{path/to/input}}.pdf burst output {{path/to/out_%d}}.pdf`
4. Rotate all pages by 180 degrees clockwise:
   `pdftk {{path/to/input}}.pdf cat 1-endsouth output {{path/to/output}}.pdf`
5. Rotate third page by 90 degrees clockwise and leave others unchanged:
   `pdftk {{path/to/input}}.pdf cat 1-2 3east 4-end output {{path/to/output}}.pdf`
6. Interleave two PDFs with one-sided scans of a two-sided document, where the backs were scanned back to front:

peco:

pee:

peerflix:

peerindex:
**`peerindex`**: Inspect MRT TABLE_DUMPV2 Peer Index Table.

2. Display all peers that have provided routing information:

peludna-prognoza:
**`peludna-prognoza`**: Fetch pollen measurement data for Croatian cities from your terminal using Pliva's allergies data API.

perl-rename:
**`perl-rename`**: This command is an alias of `rename`.

perl:
**`perl`**: The Perl 5 language interpreter.

**Examples:**
1. Print lines from `stdin` [m]atching `regex1` and case [i]nsensitive `regex2`:
   `perl -n -e 'print if m/regex1/ and m/regex2/i'`

perlbrew:

perldoc:
**`perldoc`**: Look up Perl documentation in `.pod` format.

pest:
**`pest`**: A PHP testing framework with a focus on simplicity.

pfetch:

pg_amcheck:
**`pg_amcheck`**: Check for corruption in one or more PostgreSQL databases.

**Examples:**
1. Check a specific database:
   `pg_amcheck {{dbname}}`
2. Check all databases:
   `pg_amcheck {{[-a|--all]}}`
3. Check databases matching the specified pattern:
   `pg_amcheck {{[-d|--database]}} {{pattern}}`
4. Check specific tables within a database:
   `pg_amcheck {{[-t|--table]}} {{pattern}} {{dbname}}`
5. Check specific schemas within a database:
   `pg_amcheck {{[-s|--schema]}} {{pattern}} {{dbname}}`
6. Display help:
   `pg_amcheck {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_archivecleanup:
**`pg_archivecleanup`**: Remove old WAL archive files in PostgreSQL.

**Examples:**
1. Clean an archive directory up to a given WAL file:
   `pg_archivecleanup {{path/to/archive}} {{path/to/walfile}}`
2. Perform a dry run (list files that would be removed without actually doing it):
   `pg_archivecleanup {{[-n|--dry-run]}} {{path/to/archive}} {{path/to/walfile}}`
3. Strip a file extension before deciding deletion:
   `pg_archivecleanup {{[-x|--strip-extension]}} {{extension}} {{path/to/archive}} {{path/to/walfile}}`
4. Remove backup history files too:
   `pg_archivecleanup {{[-b|--clean-backup-history]}} {{path/to/archive}} {{path/to/walfile}}`
5. Enable debug logging output:
   `pg_archivecleanup {{[-d|--debug]}} {{path/to/archive}} {{path/to/walfile}}`
pg_basebackup:
**`pg_basebackup`**: Take a base backup of a running PostgreSQL cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Take a base backup from a remote PostgreSQL server:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}}`
2. Take a backup with progress shown:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-P|--progress]}}`
3. Create a compressed backup (`gzip`) in tar format:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-F|--format]}} {{[t|tar]}} {{[-z|--gzip]}}`
4. Create an incremental backup using a previous manifest file:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-i|--incremental]}} {{path/to/old_manifest}}`
5. Write a recovery configuration for setting up a standby:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-R|--write-recovery-conf]}}`
6. Relocate a tablespace during backup:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-T|--tablespace-mapping]}} {{path/to/old_tablespace}}={{path/to/new_tablespace}}`
7. Limit transfer rate to reduce server load:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-r|--max-rate]}} {{100M}}`
8. Stream WAL logs while taking the backup:
   `pg_basebackup {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/backup_dir}} {{[-X|--wal-method]}} stream`
pg_checksums:
**`pg_checksums`**: Enable, disable, or check data checksums in a PostgreSQL database cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Check data checksums in a database cluster:
   `pg_checksums {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
2. Enable data checksums in a database cluster:
   `pg_checksums {{[-e|--enable]}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
3. Disable data checksums in a database cluster:
   `pg_checksums {{[-d|--disable]}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
4. Check data checksums with verbose output:
   `pg_checksums {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
5. Check data checksums showing progress:
   `pg_checksums {{[-P|--progress]}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
6. Display help:
   `pg_checksums {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_combinebackup:
**`pg_combinebackup`**: Reconstruct a full (synthetic) PostgreSQL backup from an incremental backup chain.

**Examples:**
1. Combine a full and incremental backup into one synthetic full backup:
   `pg_combinebackup {{path/to/full_backup}} {{path/to/incremental_backup}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
2. Perform a dry run to show what would be done, without creating files:
   `pg_combinebackup {{[-n|--dry-run]}} {{path/to/full_backup}} {{path/to/incremental_backup}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
3. Use hard links instead of copying files (faster, same filesystem required):
   `pg_combinebackup {{[-k|--link]}} {{path/to/full_backup}} {{path/to/incremental_backup}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
4. Use file cloning (reflinks) for efficient copy if supported:
   `pg_combinebackup --clone {{path/to/full_backup}} {{path/to/incremental_backup}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
5. Use the `copy_file_range` system call for efficient copying:
   `pg_combinebackup --copy-file-range {{path/to/full_backup}} {{path/to/incremental_backup}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
6. Relocate a tablespace during reconstruction:
   `pg_combinebackup {{path/to/backup1 path/to/backup2 ...}} {{[-T|--tablespace-mapping]}} /{{path/to/old_tablespace}}=/{{path/to/new_tablespace}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
7. Disable fsync for faster but unsafe writes (testing only):
   `pg_combinebackup {{[-N|--no-sync]}} {{path/to/backup1 path/to/backup2 ...}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
8. Show detailed debug output:
   `pg_combinebackup {{[-d|--debug]}} {{path/to/backup1 path/to/backup2 ...}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_directory}}`
pg_config:
**`pg_config`**: Display information about the installed PostgreSQL version.

**Examples:**

2. Show the directory for library files:

3. Show the directory for include files (C headers):

6. Display help:
   `pg_config {{[-?|--help]}}`
7. Display version:
   `pg_config --version`
pg_controldata:
**`pg_controldata`**: Display control information of a PostgreSQL database cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Display control information for a specific data directory:
   `pg_controldata {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
2. Display help:
   `pg_controldata {{[-?|--help]}}`
3. Display version:
   `pg_controldata {{[-V|--version]}}`
pg_createsubscriber:
**`pg_createsubscriber`**: Convert a physical replica into a new logical replica.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a physical replica to a logical replica for a specific database:
   `pg_createsubscriber {{[-d|--database]}} {{dbname}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-P|--publisher-server]}} {{connstr}}`
2. Perform a dry run without modifying the target directory:
   `pg_createsubscriber {{[-n|--dry-run]}} {{[-d|--database]}} {{dbname}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-P|--publisher-server]}} {{connstr}}`
3. Enable two-phase commit for the subscription:
   `pg_createsubscriber {{[-T|--enable-two-phase]}} {{[-d|--database]}} {{dbname}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-P|--publisher-server]}} {{connstr}}`
4. Convert with verbose output:
   `pg_createsubscriber {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{[-d|--database]}} {{dbname}} {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-P|--publisher-server]}} {{connstr}}`
5. Display help:
   `pg_createsubscriber {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_ctl:
**`pg_ctl`**: Utility for controlling a PostgreSQL server and database cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize a new PostgreSQL database cluster:
   `pg_ctl {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{data_directory}} init`
2. Start a PostgreSQL server:
   `pg_ctl {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{data_directory}} start`
3. Stop a PostgreSQL server:
   `pg_ctl {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{data_directory}} stop`
4. Restart a PostgreSQL server:
   `pg_ctl {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{data_directory}} restart`
5. Reload the PostgreSQL server configuration:
   `pg_ctl {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{data_directory}} reload`
pg_dump:
**`pg_dump`**: Extract a PostgreSQL database into a script file or other archive file.

**Examples:**
1. Dump database into an SQL-script file:
   `pg_dump {{db_name}} > {{output_file.sql}}`
2. Same as above, customize username:
   `pg_dump {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} {{db_name}} > {{output_file.sql}}`
3. Same as above, customize host and port:
   `pg_dump {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{db_name}} > {{output_file.sql}}`
4. Dump a database into a custom-format archive file:
   `pg_dump {{[-F|--format]}} {{[c|custom]}} {{db_name}} > {{output_file.dump}}`
5. Dump only database data into an SQL-script file:
   `pg_dump {{[-a|--data-only]}} {{db_name}} > {{path/to/output_file.sql}}`
6. Dump only schema (data definitions) into an SQL-script file:
   `pg_dump {{[-s|--schema-only]}} {{db_name}} > {{path/to/output_file.sql}}`
pg_dumpall:
**`pg_dumpall`**: Extract a PostgreSQL database cluster into a script file or other archive file.

**Examples:**
1. Dump all databases:
   `pg_dumpall > {{path/to/file.sql}}`
2. Dump all databases using a specific username:
   `pg_dumpall {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} > {{path/to/file.sql}}`
3. Same as above, customize host and port:
   `pg_dumpall {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} > {{output_file.sql}}`
4. Dump only database data into an SQL-script file:
   `pg_dumpall {{[-a|--data-only]}} > {{path/to/file.sql}}`
5. Dump only schema (data definitions) into an SQL-script file:
   `pg_dumpall {{[-s|--schema-only]}} > {{output_file.sql}}`
pg_isready:
**`pg_isready`**: Check the connection status of a PostgreSQL server.

**Examples:**
1. Check connection:
   `pg_isready`
2. Check connection with a specific hostname and port:
   `pg_isready {{[-h|--host]}} {{hostname}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}}`
3. Check connection displaying a message only when the connection fails:
   `pg_isready {{[-q|--quiet]}}`
pg_receivewal:
**`pg_receivewal`**: Stream the write-ahead log from a running PostgreSQL cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Stream WAL to a local directory (minimum required):
   `pg_receivewal {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}}`
2. Same as above, specify host, port, username including verbose output:
   `pg_receivewal {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}}`
3. Use replication slot (create-if-needed):
   `pg_receivewal {{[-S|--slot]}} {{slot_name}} --create-slot {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}}`
4. Stop at a given WAL position (LSN):
   `pg_receivewal {{[-E|--endpos]}} {{lsn}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}}`
5. Control looping on failure:
   `pg_receivewal {{[-n|--no-loop]}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}}`
6. Flush data synchronously (force WAL writes immediately):
   `pg_receivewal --synchronous {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}}`
7. Compress WAL output (`gzip`, level 0-9):
   `pg_receivewal {{[-Z|--compress]}} {{level|method}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}}`
8. Set status reporting interval:
   `pg_receivewal {{[-s|--status-interval]}} {{seconds}} {{[-D|--directory]}} {{directory}} {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}}`
pg_recvlogical:
**`pg_recvlogical`**: Control PostgreSQL logical decoding streams.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new logical replication slot:
   `pg_recvlogical {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{dbname}} {{[-S|--slot]}} {{slot_name}} --create-slot`
2. Start streaming changes from a logical replication slot to a file:
   `pg_recvlogical {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{dbname}} {{[-S|--slot]}} {{slot_name}} --start {{[-f|--file]}} {{filename}}`
3. Drop a logical replication slot:
   `pg_recvlogical {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{dbname}} {{[-S|--slot]}} {{slot_name}} --drop-slot`
4. Create a slot with two-phase commit enabled:
   `pg_recvlogical {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{dbname}} {{[-S|--slot]}} {{slot_name}} --create-slot {{[-t|--enable-two-phase]}}`
5. Display help:
   `pg_recvlogical {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_resetwal:
**`pg_resetwal`**: Reset the write-ahead log and other control information of a PostgreSQL database cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Reset the WAL and control information for a specific data directory:
   `pg_resetwal {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}}`
2. Perform a dry run:
   `pg_resetwal {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-n|--dry-run]}}`
3. Force the WAL and control information reset:
   `pg_resetwal {{[-D|--pgdata]}} {{path/to/data}} {{[-f|--force]}}`
4. Display help:
   `pg_resetwal {{[-?|--help]}}`
5. Display version:
   `pg_resetwal {{[-V|--version]}}`
pg_restore:
**`pg_restore`**: Restore a PostgreSQL database from an archive file created by pg_dump.

**Examples:**
1. Restore an archive into an existing database:
   `pg_restore {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{db_name}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
2. Same as above, customize username:
   `pg_restore {{[-U|--username]}} {{username}} {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{db_name}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
3. Same as above, customize host and port:
   `pg_restore {{[-h|--host]}} {{host}} {{[-p|--port]}} {{port}} {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{db_name}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
4. List database objects included in the archive:
   `pg_restore {{[-l|--list]}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
5. Clean database objects before creating them:
   `pg_restore {{[-c|--clean]}} {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{db_name}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
6. Use multiple jobs to do the restoring:
   `pg_restore {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{2}} {{[-d|--dbname]}} {{db_name}} {{archive_file.dump}}`
pg_rewind:
**`pg_rewind`**: Synchronize a PostgreSQL data directory with another data directory that was forked from it.

**Examples:**
1. Synchronize target directory with source directory:
   `pg_rewind {{[-D|--target-pgdata]}} {{path/to/target_data}} --source-pgdata {{path/to/source_data}}`
2. Synchronize target with source server using connection string:
   `pg_rewind {{[-D|--target-pgdata]}} {{path/to/target_data}} --source-server {{connstr}}`
3. Perform a dry run:
   `pg_rewind {{[-D|--target-pgdata]}} {{path/to/target_data}} --source-pgdata {{path/to/source_data}} {{[-n|--dry-run]}}`
4. Show progress during synchronization:
   `pg_rewind {{[-D|--target-pgdata]}} {{path/to/target_data}} --source-pgdata {{path/to/source_data}} {{[-P|--progress]}}`
5. Display help:
   `pg_rewind {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_test_fsync:
**`pg_test_fsync`**: Determine the fastest wal_sync_method on your system.

**Examples:**
1. Run the default fsync benchmark (5 seconds):
   `pg_test_fsync`
2. Specify a custom test duration:
   `pg_test_fsync {{[-s|--secs-per-test]}} {{seconds}}`
3. Use a specific filename (it must be in same filesystem that the pg_wal directory is or will be placed in):
   `pg_test_fsync {{[-f|--filename]}} {{path/to/file}}`
pg_test_timing:
**`pg_test_timing`**: Measure timing overhead on your system (ensure clock monotonicity).

**Examples:**
1. Run the default timing test (3 seconds):
   `pg_test_timing`
2. Run for a custom duration:
   `pg_test_timing {{[-d|--duration]}} {{seconds}}`
pg_upgrade:
**`pg_upgrade`**: Upgrade a PostgreSQL database cluster to a new major version.

**Examples:**
1. Check clusters before upgrading:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-c|--check]}} {{[-b|--old-bindir]}} {{path/to/old_bin}} {{[-B|--new-bindir]}} {{path/to/new_bin}} {{[-d|--old-datadir]}} {{path/to/old_data}} {{[-D|--new-datadir]}} {{path/to/new_data}}`
2. Perform the actual upgrade:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-b|--old-bindir]}} {{path/to/old_bin}} {{[-B|--new-bindir]}} {{path/to/new_bin}} {{[-d|--old-datadir]}} {{path/to/old_data}} {{[-D|--new-datadir]}} {{path/to/new_data}}`
3. Use multiple parallel jobs during the upgrade:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{njobs}} {{[-b|--old-bindir]}} {{path/to/old_bin}} {{[-B|--new-bindir]}} {{path/to/new_bin}} {{[-d|--old-datadir]}} {{path/to/old_data}} {{[-D|--new-datadir]}} {{path/to/new_data}}`
4. Specify the old and new PostgreSQL ports:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-p|--old-port]}} {{port}} {{[-P|--new-port]}} {{port}} {{[-b|--old-bindir]}} {{path/to/old_bin}} {{[-B|--new-bindir]}} {{path/to/new_bin}} {{[-d|--old-datadir]}} {{path/to/old_data}} {{[-D|--new-datadir]}} {{path/to/new_data}}`
5. Use hard links instead of copying files to the new cluster:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-k|--link]}} {{[-b|--old-bindir]}} {{path/to/old_bin}} {{[-B|--new-bindir]}} {{path/to/new_bin}} {{[-d|--old-datadir]}} {{path/to/old_data}} {{[-D|--new-datadir]}} {{path/to/new_data}}`
6. Display help:
   `pg_upgrade {{[-?|--help]}}`
pg_verifybackup:
**`pg_verifybackup`**: Verify the integrity of a base backup of a PostgreSQL cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Verify a backup stored in a specific directory:
   `pg_verifybackup {{path/to/backup}}`

piactl:

pic:

picard:

pickle:

pico:

picocom:

   `sudo picocom {{/dev/ttyXYZ}} {{[-b|--baud]}} {{baud_rate}}`
3. Map special characters (e.g. `LF` to `CRLF`):
   `sudo picocom {{/dev/ttyXYZ}} --imap {{lfcrlf}}`

5. Display help:
   `picocom {{[-h|--help]}}`
picom-trans:
**`picom-trans`**: Set the window opacity for the `picom` window compositor.

**Examples:**
1. Set the currently focused window opacity to a specific percentage:
   `picom-trans {{[-c|--current]}} {{[-o|--opacity]}} {{percentage}}`

   `picom-trans {{[-n|--name]}} {{Firefox}} {{[-o|--opacity]}} {{percentage}}`

   `picom-trans {{[-s|--select]}} {{[-o|--opacity]}} {{percentage}}`

picom:
**`picom`**: Standalone compositor for Xorg.

2. Start `picom` as a background process:
   `picom {{[-b|--daemon]}}`
3. Use a custom configuration file:
   `picom --config {{path/to/config_file}}`
picotool:
**`picotool`**: Manage Raspberry Pi Pico boards.

**Examples:**
1. Display information about the currently loaded program on a Pico:
   `picotool info`
2. Load a binary onto a Pico:
   `picotool load {{path/to/binary}}`
3. Convert an ELF or BIN file to UF2:

picttoppm:
**`picttoppm`**: Convert a Macintosh PICT file to a PPM image.

1. Convert a PICT file to a PPM image:
   `picttoppm {{path/to/file.pict}} > {{path/to/file.ppm}}`

pie:
**`pie`**: The PHP Installer for Extensions.

**Examples:**
1. Install or update an extension:

pigz:
**`pigz`**: Multithreaded zlib compression utility.

**Examples:**
1. Compress a file with default options:
   `pigz {{path/to/file}}`
2. Compress a file using the best compression method:
   `pigz {{[-9|--best]}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Compress a file using no compression and 4 processors:
   `pigz -0 {{[-p|--processes]}} {{4}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. Compress a directory using tar:
   `tar cf - {{path/to/directory}} | pigz > {{path/to/file.tar.gz}}`
5. Decompress a file:
   `pigz {{[-d|--decompress]}} {{archive.gz}}`
6. List the contents of an archive:
   `pigz {{[-l|--list]}} {{archive.tar.gz}}`
ping:
**`ping`**: Send ICMP ECHO_REQUEST packets to network hosts.

**Examples:**
1. Ping a host with IP `10.0.0.1` (Note: `10.0.0.1` can be shortened to `10.1`):
   `ping 10.0.0.1`
2. Ping a host only a specific number of times:
   `ping -c {{count}} {{host}}`
3. Ping host, specifying the interval in seconds between requests (default is 1 second):
   `ping -i {{seconds}} {{host}}`
4. Ping host without trying to lookup symbolic names for addresses:
   `ping -n {{host}}`
5. Ping host and ring the bell when a packet is received (if your terminal supports it):
   `ping -a {{host}}`
6. Also display a message if no response was received:
   `ping -O {{host}}`
7. Ping a host with specific [c]ount of pings, per-packet time to [W]ait for a response, and total [w]ait time limit of the entire ping run:
   `ping -c {{count}} -W {{seconds}} -w {{seconds}} {{host}}`
8. Ping all IPv6 local network hosts:
   `ping -6 ff02::1%{{eth0}}`
ping.py:
**`ping.py`**: Check if an IPv4 host is reachable using ICMP.

**Examples:**
1. Ping a host from a specified source IPv4 address:
   `ping.py {{source_ipv4}} {{destination_ipv4}}`
2. Ping 192.168.1.100 from 192.168.1.10:
   `ping.py 192.168.1.10 192.168.1.100`
ping6:
**`ping6`**: Send ICMP ECHO_REQUEST packets to network hosts via IPv6 address.

**Examples:**
1. Ping a host:
   `ping6 {{host}}`
2. Ping a host only a specific number of times:
   `ping6 -c {{count}} {{host}}`
3. Ping a host, specifying the interval in seconds between requests (default is 1 second):
   `ping6 -i {{seconds}} {{host}}`
4. Ping a host without trying to lookup symbolic names for addresses:
   `ping6 -n {{host}}`
5. Ping a host and ring the bell when a packet is received (if your terminal supports it):
   `ping6 -a {{host}}`
ping6.py:
**`ping6.py`**: Check if an IPv6 host is reachable using ICMPv6.

**Examples:**
1. Ping an IPv6 host from a specified source IPv6 address:
   `ping6.py {{source_ipv6}} {{destination_ipv6}}`
2. Ping 2001:db8::2 from 2001:db8::1:
   `ping6.py 2001:db8::1 2001:db8::2`
pinky:
**`pinky`**: Print user information using the `finger` protocol.

1. Display details about the current user:

   `pinky {{user}}`

   `pinky {{user}} -l`

pint:

pinta:
**`pinta`**: A free, open source program for drawing and image editing.

**Examples:**
1. Start Pinta:

pio-access:

pio-ci:

   `pnmpsnr {{path/to/file1.pnm}} {{path/to/file2.pnm}} -target {{n}}`

   `pnmpsnr {{path/to/file1.pnm}} {{path/to/file2.pnm}} -target1 {{threshold_Y}} -target2 {{threshold_Cb}} -target3 {{threshold_Cr}}`
