   `vagrant destroy {{[-g|--graceful]}}`
vagrant-global-status:
**`vagrant-global-status`**: Display the state of all Vagrant machines on the system.

**Examples:**
1. Display the state of all machines:
   `vagrant global-status`
2. Prune any stale entries from the output:
   `vagrant global-status --prune`
vagrant-halt:
**`vagrant-halt`**: Shuts down the running machine Vagrant is managing.

**Examples:**
1. Halt the currently running Vagrant machine gracefully:
   `vagrant halt`
2. Halt a specific machine by its ID or name gracefully:
   `vagrant halt {{id_or_name}}`
3. Forcefully halt the current running machine(s) (This can affect multiple running machines if they are part of the same Vagrant environment):
   `vagrant halt {{[-f|--force]}}`
4. Forcefully halt a specific machine by its ID or name:
   `vagrant halt {{[-f|--force]}} {{id_or_name}}`
vagrant-init:
**`vagrant-init`**: Initialize a Vagrant environment in the current directory by creating a `Vagrantfile`.

**Examples:**
1. Create a `Vagrantfile`:
   `vagrant init`
2. Create a `Vagrantfile` without instructional comments:
   `vagrant init {{[-m|--minimal]}}`
3. Specify the box name and URL:
   `vagrant init {{box_name}} {{box_url}}`
4. Create a `Vagrantfile` with a specific box version:
   `vagrant init --box-version {{version}} {{box_name}}`
5. Send the `Vagrantfile` to `stdout`:
   `vagrant init {{[-o|--output]}} -`
6. Overwrite an existing `Vagrantfile`:
   `vagrant init {{[-f|--force]}}`
7. Provide a custom ERB template for generating the `Vagrantfile`:
   `vagrant init --template {{path/to/file.erb}}`
vagrant-plugin:
**`vagrant-plugin`**: Manage Vagrant plugins.

**Examples:**
1. List all the plugins currently installed:
   `vagrant plugin list`
2. Install a plugin from remote repositories, usually RubyGems:
   `vagrant plugin install {{vagrant_vbguest}}`
3. Install a plugin from a local file source:
   `vagrant plugin install {{path/to/my_plugin.gem}}`
4. Update all installed plugins to their latest version:
   `vagrant plugin update`
5. Update a plugin to the latest version:
   `vagrant plugin update {{vagrant_vbguest}}`
6. Uninstall a specific plugin:
   `vagrant plugin uninstall {{vagrant_vbguest}}`
vagrant-port:
**`vagrant-port`**: List mappings between guest and host ports.

**Examples:**
1. List all port mappings of machine(s) running in the current directory:
   `vagrant port`
2. List mappings for a specific machine (if `Vagrantfile` is multi-machine):
   `vagrant port {{machine_name}}`
3. Display info for a specific guest port:
   `vagrant port --guest {{port_number}}`
4. Display machine-readable output:
   `vagrant port --machine-readable`
vagrant-reload:
**`vagrant-reload`**: Equivalent of running `halt` followed by `up`.

**Examples:**
1. Reload the currently running machine:
   `vagrant reload`
2. Target a machine by name or ID:
   `vagrant reload {{name|id}}`
3. Force the provisioners to run:
   `vagrant reload --provision`
vagrant-resume:
**`vagrant-resume`**: Resume a Vagrant managed machine that was previously suspended.

**Examples:**
1. Resume machine specified by name or id:
   `vagrant resume {{name|id}}`
2. Resume and run all configured provisioners:
   `vagrant resume {{name|id}} --provision`
3. Resume and specify which provisioners to re-run:
   `vagrant resume {{name|id}} --provision-with {{provisioner}}`
vagrant-snapshot:
**`vagrant-snapshot`**: Manage snapshots of Vagrant machines.

**Examples:**
1. Take a snapshot of the machine (running or stopped):
   `vagrant snapshot save {{snapshot_name}}`
2. Restore a snapshot and start the machine:
   `vagrant snapshot restore {{snapshot_name}}`
3. Restore a snapshot without starting the machine:
   `vagrant snapshot restore --no-start {{snapshot_name}}`
4. Delete a snapshot:
   `vagrant snapshot delete {{snapshot_name}}`
5. List available snapshots of the machine:
   `vagrant snapshot list`
vagrant-ssh-config:
**`vagrant-ssh-config`**: Display configuration to SSH into a Vagrant machine manually (instead of using `vagrant ssh`).

**Examples:**
1. Get SSH configuration for the machine running in the current directory:
   `vagrant ssh-config`
2. Target a machine by name or ID:
   `vagrant ssh-config {{name|id}}`
vagrant-ssh:
**`vagrant-ssh`**: SSH into a running Vagrant machine.

**Examples:**
1. SSH into the machine running in the current directory:
   `vagrant ssh`
2. Target a running machine by name or ID:
   `vagrant ssh {{name|id}}`
3. Execute an SSH command and exit:
   `vagrant ssh {{[-c|--command]}} {{ssh_command}}`
4. SSH without authentication, leaving authentication up to the user:
   `vagrant ssh {{[-p|--plain]}}`
vagrant-status:
**`vagrant-status`**: Display the state of machines in the current Vagrant environment.

**Examples:**
1. View status of the machines in the current directory:
   `vagrant status`
2. Target a machine by name or ID:
   `vagrant status {{name|id}}`
vagrant-suspend:
**`vagrant-suspend`**: Save the state of the guest machine rather than fully shutting it down.

**Examples:**
1. Suspend the currently running machine:
   `vagrant suspend`
2. Target a machine by name or ID:
   `vagrant suspend {{name|id}}`
vagrant-upload:
**`vagrant-upload`**: Upload files and directories from the host to the guest machine.

**Examples:**
1. Upload file or directory from the host to the guest machine:
   `vagrant upload {{path/to/source_file_or_directory}} {{path/to/destination_file_or_directory}} {{name|id}}`
2. Compress the file or directory before uploading to guest machine:
   `vagrant upload --compress {{path/to/source_file_or_directory}} {{path/to/destination_file_or_directory}} {{name|id}}`
3. Specify which type of compression to use. Default type is `zip`:
   `vagrant upload --compression-type {{tgz|zip}} {{path/to/source_file_or_directory}} {{path/to/destination_file_or_directory}} {{name|id}}`
4. Create a temporary location on the guest machine and upload files to that location:
   `vagrant upload --temporary {{path/to/source_file_or_directory}} {{path/to/destination_file_or_directory}} {{name|id}}`
vagrant-validate:
**`vagrant-validate`**: Check the validity of a Vagrantfile.

**Examples:**
1. Validate the syntax of the Vagrantfile to ensure it is correctly structured and free of errors:
   `vagrant validate`
2. Ensure that the Vagrantfile is correctly structured while ignoring provider-specific configuration options:
   `vagrant validate {{[-p|--ignore-provider]}} {{docker|hypervlibvirt|parallels|qemu|virtualbox|vmware_desktop}}`
vagrant-version:
**`vagrant-version`**: Display Vagrant version information.

**Examples:**
1. Display the currently installed version and latest version of Vagrant that is currently available:
   `vagrant version`
2. Display version:
   `vagrant --version`
vagrant:
**`vagrant`**: Manage lightweight, reproducible, and portable development environments.

**Examples:**
1. Create a `Vagrantfile` in the current directory with the base Vagrant box:
   `vagrant init`
2. Create a `Vagrantfile` with a box from the Vagrant Public Registry:
   `vagrant init {{ubuntu/focal64}}`
3. Start and provision the Vagrant environment:
   `vagrant up`
4. Suspend the machine:
   `vagrant suspend`
5. Halt the machine:
   `vagrant halt`
6. Connect to the machine via SSH:
   `vagrant ssh`
7. Output the SSH configuration file of the running Vagrant machine:
   `vagrant ssh-config`
8. List all local boxes:
   `vagrant box list`
vainfo:
**`vainfo`**: Display information from VA API driver.

**Examples:**
1. Show version and supported entrypoints:
   `vainfo`
2. Test a specific display protocol:
   `vainfo --display {{wayland|x11|drm|...}}`
3. Show available display protocols:
   `vainfo --display help`
4. Show all supported entrypoints:
   `vainfo {{[-a|--all]}}`
5. Display help:
   `vainfo --help`
vala:
**`vala`**: Vala code runner.

**Examples:**
1. Run a vala file, with gtk+:
   `vala {{path/to/file.vala}} --pkg {{gtk+-3.0}}`
2. Display help:
   `vala --help`
3. Display version:
   `vala --version`
valac:
**`valac`**: Vala code compiler.

**Examples:**
1. Compile a vala file, with gtk+:
   `valac {{path/to/file.vala}} --pkg {{gtk+-3.0}}`
2. Display help:
   `valac --help`
3. Display version:
   `valac --version`
vale:
**`vale`**: Extensible style checker that supports multiple markup formats, such as Markdown and AsciiDoc.

**Examples:**
1. Check the style of a file:
   `vale {{path/to/file}}`
2. Check the style of a file with a specified configuration:
   `vale --config='{{path/to/.vale.ini}}' {{path/to/file}}`
3. Output the results in JSON format:
   `vale --output=JSON {{path/to/file}}`
4. Check style issues at the specific severity and higher:
   `vale --minAlertLevel={{suggestion|warning|error}} {{path/to/file}}`
5. Check the style from `stdin`, specifying markup format:
   `cat {{file.md}} | vale --ext=.md`
6. List the current configuration:
   `vale ls-config`
valgrind:
**`valgrind`**: Wrapper for a set of expert tools for profiling, optimizing, and debugging programs.

**Examples:**
1. Use the (default) Memcheck tool to show a diagnostic of memory usage by `program`:
   `valgrind {{program}}`
2. Use Memcheck to report all possible memory leaks of `program` in full detail:
   `valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all {{program}}`
3. Use the Cachegrind tool to profile and log CPU cache operations of `program`:
   `valgrind --tool=cachegrind {{program}}`
4. Use the Massif tool to profile and log heap memory and stack usage of `program`:
   `valgrind --tool=massif --stacks=yes {{program}}`
valkey-cli:
**`valkey-cli`**: Open a connection to a Valkey server.

**Examples:**
1. Connect to the local server:
   `valkey-cli`
2. Connect to a remote server on the default port (6379):
   `valkey-cli -h {{host}}`
3. Connect to a remote server specifying a port number:
   `valkey-cli -h {{host}} -p {{port}}`
4. Connect to a remote server specifying a URI:
   `valkey-cli -u {{uri}}`
5. Specify a password:
   `valkey-cli -a {{password}}`
6. Execute valkey command:
   `valkey-cli {{valkey_command}}`
7. Connect to the local cluster:
   `valkey-cli -c`
var-dump-server:
**`var-dump-server`**: Symfony dump server.

**Examples:**
1. Start the server:
   `var-dump-server`
2. Dump the data in an HTML file:
   `var-dump-server --format=html > {{path/to/file.html}}`
3. Make the server listen on a specific address and port:
   `var-dump-server --host {{127.0.0.1:9912}}`
varnishlog:
**`varnishlog`**: Display Varnish logs.

**Examples:**
1. Display logs in real time:
   `varnishlog`
2. Only display requests to a specific domain:
   `varnishlog -q 'ReqHeader eq "Host: {{example.com}}"'`
3. Only display POST requests:
   `varnishlog -q 'ReqMethod eq "{{POST}}"'`
4. Only display requests to a specific path:
   `varnishlog -q 'ReqURL eq "/{{path}}"'`
5. Only display requests to paths matching a `regex`:
   `varnishlog -q 'ReqURL ~ "{{regex}}"'`
vault:
**`vault`**: Interact with HashiCorp Vault.

**Examples:**
1. Connect to a Vault server and initialize a new encrypted data store:
   `vault init`
2. Unseal (unlock) the vault, by providing one of the key shares needed to access the encrypted data store:
   `vault unseal {{key-share-x}}`
3. Authenticate the CLI client against the Vault server, using an authentication token:
   `vault auth {{authentication_token}}`
4. Store a new secret in the vault, using the generic back-end called "secret":
   `vault write secret/{{hello}} value={{world}}`
5. Read a value from the vault, using the generic back-end called "secret":
   `vault read secret/{{hello}}`
6. Read a specific field from the value:
   `vault read -field={{field_name}} secret/{{hello}}`
7. Seal (lock) the Vault server, by removing the encryption key of the data store from memory:
   `vault seal`
vboxmanage-clonevm:
**`vboxmanage-clonevm`**: Create a clone of an existing virtual machine (VM).

**Examples:**
1. Clone the specified VM:
   `VBoxManage clonevm {{vm_name}}`
2. Specify a new name for the new VM:
   `VBoxManage clonevm {{vm_name}} --name {{new_vm_name}}`
3. Indicate the folder where the new VM configuration is saved:
   `VBoxManage clonevm {{vm_name}} --basefolder {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Register the cloned VM in VirtualBox:
   `VBoxManage clonevm {{vm_name}} --register`
vboxmanage-cloud:
**`vboxmanage-cloud`**: VirtualBox command-line interface for managing cloud instances and images.

**Examples:**
1. List the instances in the specified state belonging to the specified compartment:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} list instances --state={{running|terminated|paused}} --compartment-id={{compartment_id}}`
2. Create a new instance:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} instance create --domain-name={{domain_name}} --image-id={{image_id}}`
3. Gather information about a particular instance:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} instance info --id={{unique_id}}`
4. Terminate an instance:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} instance terminate --id={{unique_id}}`
5. List images within a specific compartment and state:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} list images --compartment-id={{compartment_id}} --state={{state_name}}`
6. Create a new image:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} image create --instance-id={{instance_id}} --display-name={{display_name}} --compartment-id={{compartment_id}}`
7. Retrieve information about a particular image:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} image info --id={{unique_id}}`
8. Delete an image:
   `VBoxManage cloud --provider={{provider_name}} --profile={{profile_name}} image delete --id={{unique_id}}`
vboxmanage-controlvm:
**`vboxmanage-controlvm`**: Change the state and the settings of a currently running virtual machine.

**Examples:**
1. Temporarily stop the execution of a virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} pause`
2. Resume the execution of a paused virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} resume`
3. Perform a cold reset on the virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} reset`
4. Poweroff a virtual machine with the same effect as pulling the power cable of a computer:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} poweroff`
5. Shutdown the virtual machine and save its current state:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} savestate`
6. Send an ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) shutdown signal to the virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} acpipowerbutton`
7. Send command to reboot itself to the guest OS:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} reboot`
8. Shutdown down the virtual machine without saving its state:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{uuid|vm_name}} shutdown`
vboxmanage-createvm:
**`vboxmanage-createvm`**: Create a new virtual machine.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new VM with default settings:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}}`
2. Set the base folder where the VM configuration will be stored:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --basefolder {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Set the guest OS type (one of `VBoxManage list ostypes`) for the imported VM:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --ostype {{ostype}}`
4. Register the created VM in VirtualBox:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --register`
5. Set the VM to the specified groups:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --group {{group1,group2,...}}`
6. Set the Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) of the VM:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --uuid {{uuid}}`
7. Set the cipher to use for encryption:
   `VBoxManage createvm --name {{vm_name}} --cipher {{AES-128|AES-256}}`
vboxmanage-export:
**`vboxmanage-export`**: Export virtual machines to a virtual appliance (ISO) or a cloud service.

**Examples:**
1. Specify the target OVA file:
   `VBoxManage export --output {{path/to/file.ova}}`
2. Export in OVF 0.9 legacy mode:
   `VBoxManage export --legacy09`
3. Export in OVF (0.9|1.0|2.0) format:
   `VBoxManage export --{{ovf09|ovf10|ovf20}}`
4. Create manifest of the exported files:
   `VBoxManage export --manifest`
5. Specify a description of the VM:
   `VBoxManage export --description "{{vm_description}}"`
vboxmanage-extpack:
**`vboxmanage-extpack`**: Manage extension packs for Oracle VirtualBox.

**Examples:**
1. Install extension packs to VirtualBox (Note: You need to remove the existing version of the extension pack before installing a new version.):
   `VBoxManage extpack install {{path/to/file.vbox-extpack}}`
2. Remove the existing version of the VirtualBox extension pack:
   `VBoxManage extpack install --replace`
3. Uninstall extension packs from VirtualBox:
   `VBoxManage extpack uninstall {{extension_pack_name}}`
4. Uninstall extension packs and skip most uninstallation refusals:
   `VBoxManage extpack uninstall --force {{extension_pack_name}}`
5. Clean up temporary files and directories left by extension packs:
   `VBoxManage extpack cleanup`
vboxmanage-import:
**`vboxmanage-import`**: Import a previously exported virtual machine (VM).

**Examples:**
1. Import a VM from an OVF or OVA file:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}}`
2. Set the name of the imported VM:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --name {{vm_name}}`
3. Indicate the folder where the configuration of the imported VM will be stored:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --basefolder {{path/to/directory}}`
4. Register the imported VM in VirtualBox:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --register`
5. Perform a dry run to check the import without actually importing:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --dry-run`
6. Set the guest OS type (one of `VBoxManage list ostypes`) for the imported VM:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --ostype {{ostype}}`
7. Set the memory (in megabytes) for the imported VM:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --memory {{1}}`
8. Set the number of CPUs for the imported VM:
   `VBoxManage import {{path/to/file.ovf}} --cpus {{1}}`
vboxmanage-list:
**`vboxmanage-list`**: List information about the Oracle VM VirtualBox software and associated service.

**Examples:**
1. List all VirtualBox virtual machines:
   `VBoxManage list vms`
2. Show DHCP servers available on the host system:
   `VBoxManage list dhcpservers`
3. Show Oracle VM VirtualBox extension packs currently installed:
   `VBoxManage list extpacks`
4. Show all virtual machine groups:
   `VBoxManage list groups`
5. Show virtual disk settings that are currently in use by VirtualBox:
   `VBoxManage list hdds`
6. Show host-only network interfaces available on host system:
   `VBoxManage list hostonlyifs`
7. Show the list of currently running virtual machines:
   `VBoxManage list runningvms`
8. Show host system information:
   `VBoxManage list hostinfo`
vboxmanage-modifyvm:
**`vboxmanage-modifyvm`**: Change settings for a virtual machine that is stopped.

**Examples:**
1. Rename the VM:
   `VBoxManage modifyvm {{uuid|vm_name}} --name {{new_name}}`
2. Adjust memory and CPU:
   `VBoxManage modifyvm {{uuid|vm_name}} --memory {{2048}} --cpus {{2}}`
3. Enable Remote Display (VRDE):
   `VBoxManage modifyvm {{uuid|vm_name}} --vrde on`
4. Enable session recording:
   `VBoxManage modifyvm {{uuid|vm_name}} --recording on`
vboxmanage-movevm:
**`vboxmanage-movevm`**: Move a virtual machine (VM) to a new location on the host system.

**Examples:**
1. Move the specified virtual machine to the current location:
   `VBoxManage movevm {{vm_name}}`
2. Specify the new location (full or relative pathname) of the virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage movevm {{vm_name}} --folder {{path/to/new_location}}`
vboxmanage-registervm:
**`vboxmanage-registervm`**: Register a virtual machine (VM).

**Examples:**
1. Register an existing VM:
   `VBoxManage registervm {{path/to/file.vbox}}`
2. Supply the encryption password file of the VM:
   `VBoxManage registervm {{path/to/file.vbox}} --password {{path/to/password_file}}`
3. Prompt for the encryption password on the command-line:
   `VBoxManage registervm {{path/to/file.vbox}} --password -`
vboxmanage-showvminfo:
**`vboxmanage-showvminfo`**: Show information about registered virtual machine.

**Examples:**
1. Show information about a particular virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo {{vm_name|uuid}}`
2. Show more detailed information about a particular virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo --details {{vm_name|uuid}}`
3. Show information in a machine readable format:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo --machinereadable {{vm_name|uuid}}`
4. Specify password ID if the virtual machine is encrypted:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo --password-id {{password_id}} {{vm_name|uuid}}`
5. Specify the password file if the virtual machine is encrypted:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo --password {{path/to/password_file}} {{vm_name|uuid}}`
6. Show the logs of a specific virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo --log {{vm_name|uuid}}`
vboxmanage-startvm:
**`vboxmanage-startvm`**: Start a virtual machine.

**Examples:**
1. Start a virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{vm_name|uuid}}`
2. Start a virtual machine with the specified UI mode:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{vm_name|uuid}} --type {{headless|gui|sdl|separate}}`
3. Specify a password file to start an encrypted virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{vm_name|uuid}} --password {{path/to/password_file}}`
4. Specify a password ID to start an encrypted virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{vm_name|uuid}} --password-id {{password_id}}`
5. Start a virtual machine with an environment variable pair name value:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{vm_name|uuid}} {{[-E|--putenv]}} {{name}}={{value}}`
vboxmanage-unregistervm:
**`vboxmanage-unregistervm`**: Unregister a virtual machine (VM).

**Examples:**
1. Unregister an existing VM:
   `VBoxManage unregistervm {{uuid|vm_name}}`
2. Delete hard disk image files, all saved state files, VM logs, and XML VM machine files:
   `VBoxManage unregistervm {{uuid|vm_name}} --delete`
3. Delete all files from the VM:
   `VBoxManage unregistervm {{uuid|vm_name}} --delete-all`
vboxmanage:
**`vboxmanage`**: Interface with VirtualBox.

**Examples:**
1. List all VirtualBox virtual machines:
   `VBoxManage list vms`
2. Show information about a particular virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage showvminfo {{name|uuid}}`
3. Start a virtual machine:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{name|uuid}}`
4. Start a virtual machine in headless mode:
   `VBoxManage startvm {{name|uuid}} --type headless`
5. Shutdown the virtual machine and save its current state:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{name|uuid}} savestate`
6. Shutdown down the virtual machine without saving its state:
   `VBoxManage controlvm {{name|uuid}} poweroff`
7. Update VBox extension packs:
   `VBoxManage extpack install --replace {{VboxExtensionPackFileName}}`
8. Display help:
   `VBoxManage --help`
vc:
**`vc`**: This command is an alias of `vercel`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr vercel`
vcluster:
**`vcluster`**: Create and manage lightweight virtual Kubernetes clusters in namespaces.

**Examples:**
1. Create a virtual cluster in a specific namespace:
   `vcluster create {{vcluster_name}} {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}}`
2. Connect to a virtual cluster with a local port and insecure mode:
   `vcluster connect {{vcluster_name}} {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}} --local-port {{port}} --insecure`

   `vcluster list`

   `vcluster platform list`

   `vcluster platform create {{vcluster_name}} {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}}`
7. Connect to a platform-managed virtual cluster:
   `vcluster platform connect {{vcluster_name}} {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}}`
8. Delete a platform-managed virtual cluster:
   `vcluster platform delete {{vcluster_name}} {{[-n|--namespace]}} {{namespace}}`
vcpkg:
**`vcpkg`**: Package manager for C/C++ libraries.

**Examples:**
1. Build and add package `libcurl` to the `vcpkg` environment:
   `vcpkg install curl`
2. Build and add `zlib` using the `emscripten` toolchain:
   `vcpkg install --triplet=wasm32-emscripten zlib`
3. Search for a package:

   `watson start {{project}}`
2. Start monitoring time in project with tags:
   `watson start {{project}} +{{tag}}`
3. Stop monitoring time for the current project:
   `watson stop`
4. Display the latest working sessions:
   `watson log`
5. Edit most recent frame:
   `watson edit`
6. Remove most recent frame:
   `watson remove`
waybar:
**`waybar`**: Highly customizable Wayland bar for Sway and Wlroots based compositors.

**Examples:**
1. Start `waybar` with the default configuration and stylesheet:
   `waybar`
2. Use a different configuration file:
   `waybar {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.jsonc}}`
3. Use a different stylesheet file:
   `waybar {{[-s|--style]}} {{path/to/stylesheet.css}}`
4. Set the logging level:
   `waybar {{[-l|--log-level]}} {{trace|debug|info|warning|error|critical|off}}`
wayland-info:
**`wayland-info`**: Display information about a Wayland compositor and available protocols.

**Examples:**
1. Display information about the current Wayland compositor and available protocols:
   `wayland-info`
2. Display information for interfaces matching a specific name:
   `wayland-info {{[-i|--interface]}} {{wl_output}}`
3. Save the output to a file:
   `wayland-info > {{path/to/file.txt}}`
waymore:
**`waymore`**: Fetch URLs of a domain from Wayback Machine, Common Crawl, Alien Vault OTX, URLScan, and VirusTotal.

**Examples:**
1. Search for URLs of a domain (output will typically be in `~/.config/waymore/results/`):
   `waymore {{[-i|--input]}} {{example.com}}`
2. Limit search results to only include a list of URLs for a domain and store outputs to the specified file:
   `waymore -mode U {{[-oU|--output-urls]}} {{path/to/example.com-urls.txt}} {{[-i|--input]}} {{example.com}}`
3. Only output the content bodies of URLs and store outputs to the specified directory:
   `waymore -mode R {{[-oR|--output-responses]}} {{path/to/example.com-url-responses}} {{[-i|--input]}} {{example.com}}`
4. Filter the results by specifying date ranges:
   `waymore -from {{YYYYMMDD|YYYYMM|YYYY}} {{[-to|--to-date]}} {{YYYYMMDD|YYYYMM|YYYY}} {{[-i|--input]}} {{example.com}}`
wbmptopbm:
**`wbmptopbm`**: Convert a wireless bitmap file to a PBM image.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a WBMP file to a PBM image:
   `wbmptopbm {{path/to/input_file.wbpm}} > {{path/to/output_file.pbm}}`
wc:
**`wc`**: Count lines, words, and bytes.

**Examples:**
1. Count all lines in a file:
   `wc {{[-l|--lines]}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Count all words in a file:
   `wc {{[-w|--words]}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Count all bytes in a file:
   `wc {{[-c|--bytes]}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. Count all characters in a file (taking multi-byte characters into account):
   `wc {{[-m|--chars]}} {{path/to/file}}`
5. Count all lines, words, and bytes from `stdin`:
   `{{find .}} | wc`
6. Count the length of the longest line in number of characters:
   `wc {{[-L|--max-line-length]}} {{path/to/file}}`
wcurl:
**`wcurl`**: A simple wrapper around `curl` to easily download files.

**Examples:**
1. Download the contents of a URL to a file indicated by the URL (`index.html` in this case):
   `wcurl {{https://example.com/index.html}}`
2. Download the contents of a URL to a file with a specified name:
   `wcurl {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file}} {{https://example.com/index.html}}`
3. Download the contents of a URL, enabling progress bar and defaulting to HTTP/2:
   `wcurl --curl-options "--progress-bar --http2" {{https://example.com/index.html}}`
4. Resume from an interrupted download:
   `wcurl --curl-options "--clobber --continue-at -" {{https://example.com/index.html}}`
wdiff:
**`wdiff`**: Display word differences between text files.

**Examples:**
1. Compare two files:
   `wdiff {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
2. Ignore case when comparing:
   `wdiff {{[-i|--ignore-case]}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
3. Display how many words are deleted, inserted, or replaced:
   `wdiff {{[-s|--statistics]}} {{path/to/file1}} {{path/to/file2}}`
weasyprint:
**`weasyprint`**: Render HTML to PDF or PNG.

**Examples:**
1. Render an HTML file to PDF:
   `weasyprint {{path/to/input.html}} {{path/to/output.pdf}}`
2. Render an HTML file to PNG, including an additional user stylesheet:
   `weasyprint {{path/to/input.html}} {{path/to/output.png}} --stylesheet {{path/to/stylesheet.css}}`
3. Output additional debugging information when rendering:
   `weasyprint {{path/to/input.html}} {{path/to/output.pdf}} --verbose`
4. Specify a custom resolution when outputting to PNG:
   `weasyprint {{path/to/input.html}} {{path/to/output.png}} --resolution {{300}}`
5. Specify a base URL for relative URLs in the input HTML file:
   `weasyprint {{path/to/input.html}} {{path/to/output.png}} --base-url {{url_or_filename}}`
web-ext:
**`web-ext`**: Manage web extension development.

**Examples:**
1. Run the web extension in the current directory in Firefox:
   `web-ext run`
2. Run a web extension from a specific directory in Firefox:
   `web-ext run --source-dir {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Display verbose execution output:
   `web-ext run --verbose`
4. Run a web extension in Firefox Android:
   `web-ext run --target firefox-android`
5. Lint the manifest and source files for errors:
   `web-ext lint`
6. Build and package the extension:
   `web-ext build`
7. Display verbose build output:
   `web-ext build --verbose`
8. Sign a package for self-hosting:
   `web-ext sign --api-key {{api_key}} --api-secret {{api_secret}}`
webpack:
**`webpack`**: Bundle a web project's js files and other assets into a single output file.

**Examples:**
1. Create a single output file from an entry point file:
   `webpack {{app.js}} {{bundle.js}}`
2. Load CSS files too from the JavaScript file (this uses the CSS loader for CSS files):
   `webpack {{app.js}} {{bundle.js}} --module-bind '{{css=css}}'`
3. Pass a configuration file (with e.g. the entry script and the output filename) and show compilation progress:
   `webpack {{[-c|--config]}} {{webpack.config.js}} --progress`
4. Automatically recompile on changes to project files:
   `webpack {{[-w|--watch]}} {{app.js}} {{bundle.js}}`
webpmux:
**`webpmux`**: Create WebP animations.

**Examples:**
1. Create a two-frame animation:
   `webpmux -frame {{path/to/frame1.webp}} +{{500}} -frame {{path/to/frame2.webp}} +{{500}} -loop {{0}} -o {{path/to/output.webp}}`
webstorm:
**`webstorm`**: The JetBrains JavaScript IDE.

**Examples:**
1. Open the current directory in WebStorm:
   `webstorm`
2. Open a specific directory in WebStorm:
   `webstorm {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Open specific files in the LightEdit mode:
   `webstorm -e {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 ...}}`
4. Open and wait until done editing a specific file in the LightEdit mode:
   `webstorm --wait -e {{path/to/file}}`
5. Open a file with the cursor at the specific line:
   `webstorm --line {{line_number}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Open and compare files (supports up to 3 files):
   `webstorm diff {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 path/to/optional_file3}}`
7. Open and perform a three-way merge:
   `webstorm merge {{path/to/left_file}} {{path/to/right_file}} {{path/to/target_file}}`
webtorrent:
**`webtorrent`**: The interface for WebTorrent.

**Examples:**
1. Download a torrent:
   `webtorrent download "{{torrent_id}}"`
2. Stream a torrent to VLC media player:
   `webtorrent download "{{torrent_id}}" --vlc`
3. Stream a torrent to a Digital Living Network Alliance (DLNA) device:
   `webtorrent download "{{torrent_id}}" --dlna`
4. Display a list of files for a specific torrent:
   `webtorrent download "{{torrent_id}}" --select`
5. Specify a file index from the torrent to download:
   `webtorrent download "{{torrent_id}}" --select {{index}}`
6. Seed a specific file or directory:
   `webtorrent seed {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
7. Create a new torrent file for the specified file path:
   `webtorrent create {{path/to/file}}`
8. Display information for a magnet URI or `.torrent` file:
   `webtorrent info {{path/to/file_or_magnet}}`
weechat:
**`weechat`**: Internet relay chat client with various features.

**Examples:**
1. Start WeeChat:
   `weechat`
2. Do not load any plugin(s) on startup:
   `weechat --no-plugin`
3. Do not load any script(s) on startup:
   `weechat --no-script`
4. Do not connect to servers automatically:
   `weechat --no-connect`
5. Write default terminal colors to `stdout`:
   `weechat --colors`
wezterm-cli:
**`wezterm-cli`**: Interact with a running Wezterm GUI or multiplexer.

**Examples:**
1. List windows, tabs, and panes:
   `wezterm cli list`
2. Split the current pane and print the new pane's ID to `stdout`:
   `wezterm cli split-pane --{{left|right|top|bottom}} --{{cells|percent}} {{n}}`
3. Activate (focus) a pane:
   `wezterm cli activate-pane --pane-id {{id}}`
4. Kill a pane:
   `wezterm cli kill-pane --pane-id {{id}}`
wezterm:
**`wezterm`**: Wez's Terminal Emulator - a powerful cross-platform terminal emulator and multiplexer.

**Examples:**
1. Start a new Wezterm process and create a window:
   `wezterm`
2. Establish an `ssh` session in a new Wezterm window:
   `wezterm ssh {{user}}@{{host}}:{{port}}`
3. Connect to the multiplexer (`wezterm-mux-server`):
   `wezterm connect {{domain_name}}`
4. Output an image to the terminal:
   `wezterm imgcat {{path/to/image}}`
5. Record a terminal session as an asciicast (by default recordings are saved to `/tmp`):
   `wezterm record`
6. Replay an asciicast terminal session:
   `wezterm replay {{path/to/cast_file}}`
7. Specify the configuration file to use (overrides the normal configuration file resolution):
   `wezterm --config-file {{path/to/config_file}}`
8. Display help:
   `wezterm help`
wfuzz:
**`wfuzz`**: A web application bruteforcer.

**Examples:**
1. Directory and file bruteforce using the specified [w]ordlist and also [p]roxying the traffic:
   `wfuzz -w {{path/to/file}} -p {{127.0.0.1:8080:HTTP}} {{http://example.com/FUZZ}}`
2. Save the results to a [f]ile:
   `wfuzz -w {{path/to/file}} -f {{filename}} {{http://example.com/FUZZ}}`
3. Show [c]olorized output while only showing the declared response codes in the output:
   `wfuzz -c -w {{path/to/file}} --sc {{200,301,302}} {{http://example.com/FUZZ}}`
4. Use a custom [H]eader to fuzz subdomains while [h]iding specific response [c]odes and word counts. Increase the [t]hreads to 100 and include the target ip/domain:
   `wfuzz -w {{path/to/file}} -H "{{Host: FUZZ.example.com}}" --hc {{301}} --hw {{222}} -t {{100}} {{example.com}}`
5. Brute force Basic Authentication using a list of usernames and passwords from files for each FUZ[z] keyword, [h]iding response [c]odes of unsuccessful attempts:
   `wfuzz -c --hc {{401}} -s {{delay_between_requests_in_seconds}} -z file,{{path/to/usernames}} -z file,{{path/to/passwords}} --basic 'FUZZ:FUZ2Z' {{https://example.com}}`
6. Provide wordlist directly from the command-line and use POST request for fuzzing:
   `wfuzz -z list,{{word1-word2-...}} {{https://api.example.com}} -d "{{id=FUZZ&showwallet=true}}"`
7. Provide wordlists from a file applying Base64 and MD5 encoding on them (`wfuzz -e encoders` lists all available encoders):
   `wfuzz -z file,{{path/to/file}},none-base64-md5 {{https://example.com/FUZZ}}`
8. List available encoders/payloads/iterators/printers/scripts:
   `wfuzz -e {{encoders|payloads|iterators|printers|scripts}}`
wget:
**`wget`**: Download files from the Web.

**Examples:**
1. Download the contents of a URL to a file (named "foo" in this case):
   `wget {{https://example.com/foo}}`
2. Download the contents of a URL to a file (named "bar" in this case):
   `wget {{[-O|--output-document]}} {{bar}} {{https://example.com/foo}}`
3. Download a single web page and all its resources with 3-second intervals between requests (scripts, stylesheets, images, etc.):
   `wget {{[-pkw|--page-requisites --convert-links --wait]}} 3 {{https://example.com/some_page.html}}`
4. Download all listed files within a directory and its sub-directories (does not download embedded page elements):
   `wget {{[-mnp|--mirror --no-parent]}} {{https://example.com/some_path/}}`
5. Limit the download speed and the number of connection retries:
   `wget --limit-rate {{300k}} {{[-t|--tries]}} {{100}} {{https://example.com/some_path/}}`
6. Download a file from an HTTP server using Basic Auth (also works for FTP):
   `wget --user {{username}} --password {{password}} {{https://example.com}}`
7. Continue an incomplete download:
   `wget {{[-c|--continue]}} {{https://example.com}}`
8. Download all URLs stored in a text file to a specific directory:
   `wget {{[-P|--directory-prefix]}} {{path/to/directory}} {{[-i|--input-file]}} {{path/to/URLs.txt}}`
wget2:
**`wget2`**: An improved version of `wget` for downloading files from the web.

**Examples:**
1. Download the contents of a URL to a file using multiple threads (default behavior differs from `wget`):
   `wget2 {{https://example.com/resource}}`
2. Limit the number of threads used for downloading (default is 5 threads):
   `wget2 --max-threads {{10}} {{https://example.com/resource}}`
3. Download a single web page and all its resources (scripts, stylesheets, images, etc.):
   `wget2 {{[-p|--page-requisites]}} {{[-k|--convert-links]}} {{https://example.com/somepage.html}}`
4. Mirror a website, but do not ascend to the parent directory (does not download embedded page elements):
   `wget2 {{[-m|--mirror]}} {{[-np|--no-parent]}} {{https://example.com/somepath/}}`
5. Limit the download speed and the number of connection retries:
   `wget2 --limit-rate {{300k}} {{[-t|--tries]}} {{100}} {{https://example.com/somepath/}}`
6. Continue an incomplete download (behavior is consistent with `wget`):
   `wget2 {{[-c|--continue]}} {{https://example.com}}`
7. Download all URLs stored in a text file to a specific directory:
   `wget2 {{[-P|--directory-prefix]}} {{path/to/directory}} {{[-i|--input-file]}} {{URLs.txt}}`
8. Download a file from an HTTP server using Basic Auth (also works for HTTPS):
   `wget2 --user {{username}} --password {{password}} {{https://example.com}}`
whatwaf:
**`whatwaf`**: Detect and bypass web application firewalls and protection systems.

**Examples:**
1. Detect protection on a single URL, optionally use verbose output:
   `whatwaf {{[-u|--url]}} {{https://example.com}} --verbose`
2. Detect protection on a list of URLs in parallel from a file (one URL per line):
   `whatwaf {{[-t|--threads]}} {{number}} {{[-l|--list]}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Send requests through a proxy and use custom payload list from a file (one payload per line):
   `whatwaf --proxy {{http://127.0.0.1:8080}} --pl {{path/to/file}} {{[-u|--url]}} {{https://example.com}}`
4. Send requests through Tor (Tor must be installed) using custom payloads (comma-separated):
   `whatwaf --tor {{[-p|--payloads]}} '{{payload1,payload2,...}}' {{[-u|--url]}} {{https://example.com}}`
5. Use a random user-agent, set throttling and timeout, send a POST request, and force HTTPS connection:
   `whatwaf --ra --throttle {{seconds}} --timeout {{seconds}} {{[-P|--post]}} --force-ssl {{[-u|--url]}} {{http://example.com}}`
6. List all WAFs that can be detected:
   `whatwaf --wafs`
7. List all available tamper scripts:
   `whatwaf --tampers`
whatweb:
**`whatweb`**: Next-generation web scanner.

**Examples:**
1. Scan websites/targets for web technologies:
   `whatweb {{website1 website2 ...}}`
2. Read targets/websites from a file:
   `whatweb {{[-i|--input-file]}} {{targets_file}}`
3. Scan a website/target in verbose mode:
   `whatweb {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{example.com}}`
4. Run an aggressive scan on a website:
   `whatweb {{[-a|--aggression]}} 3 {{example.com}}`
5. Scan a network and suppress errors:
   `whatweb --no-errors {{192.168.0.0/24}}`
6. List plugins:
   `whatweb {{[-l|--list-plugins]}}`
7. List plugin details:
   `whatweb {{[-I|--info-plugins]}} {{plugin_name}}`
whence:
**`whence`**: A Zsh builtin to indicate how a command would be interpreted.

**Examples:**
1. Interpret `command`, with expansion if defined as an `alias` (similar to the `command -v` builtin):
   `whence "{{command}}"`
2. Display type of `command`, with location if defined as a function or binary (equivalent to the `type` and `command -V` builtins):
   `whence -v "{{command}}"`
3. Same as above, except display content of shell functions instead of location (equivalent to `which` builtin):
   `whence -c "{{command}}"`
4. Same as above, but show all occurrences on command path (equivalent to the `where` builtin):
   `whence -ca "{{command}}"`
5. Search only the `$PATH` for `command`, ignoring builtins, aliases, or shell functions (equivalent to the `where` command):
   `whence -p "{{command}}"`
where:
**`where`**: Report all known instances of a command.

**Examples:**
1. Find all instances of a command:
   `where {{command}}`
which:
**`which`**: Locate a program in the user's `$PATH`.

**Examples:**
1. Search the `$PATH` environment variable and display the location of any matching executables:
   `which {{executable}}`
2. If there are multiple executables which match, display all:
   `which {{[-a|--all]}} {{executable}}`
while:
**`while`**: Simple shell loop that repeats while the return value remains zero.

**Examples:**
1. Read `stdin` and perform an action on every line:
   `while read line; do {{echo "$line"}}; done`
2. Execute a command forever once every second:
   `while :; do {{command}}; sleep 1; done`
3. Execute a command until it fails:
   `while {{command}}; do :; done`
whisper:
**`whisper`**: Convert audio files to `txt`, `vtt`, `srt`, `tsv`, and `json`.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a specific audio file to all of the given file formats:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}}`
2. Convert an audio file specifying the output format of the converted file:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}} --output_format {{txt}}`
3. Convert an audio file using a specific model for conversion:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}} --model {{tiny.en,tiny,base.en,base,small.en,small,medium.en,medium,large-v1,large-v2,large}}`
4. Convert an audio file specifying which language the audio file is in to reduce conversion time:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}} --language {{english}}`
5. Convert an audio file and save it to a specific location:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}} --output_dir "{{path/to/output}}"`
6. Convert an audio file in quiet mode:
   `whisper {{path/to/audio.mp3}} --verbose {{False}}`
who:
**`who`**: Display who is logged in and related data (processes, boot time).

**Examples:**
1. Display the username, line, and time of all currently logged-in sessions:
   `who`
2. Display all available information:
   `who {{[-a|--all]}}`
3. Display all available information with table headers:
   `who {{[-aH|--all --heading]}}`
whoami:
**`whoami`**: This command is an alias of `id --user --name`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr id`
whois:
**`whois`**: Client for the WHOIS (RFC 3912) protocol.

**Examples:**
1. Get information about a domain name:
   `whois {{example.com}}`
2. Get information about an IP address:
   `whois {{8.8.8.8}}`
3. Get abuse contact for an IP address:
   `whois -b {{8.8.8.8}}`
wiggle:
**`wiggle`**: A patch application tool resolving conflicts in patches that `patch` cannot handle.

**Examples:**
1. Apply changes from the patch file to the original file:
   `wiggle {{path/to/file.patch}}`
2. Apply changes to the output file:
   `wiggle {{path/to/file.patch}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/output_file.txt}}`
3. Take any changes in `file.rej` that could not have been applied and merge them into a file:
   `wiggle {{[-r|--replace]}} {{path/to/file}} {{path/to/file.rej}}`
4. Extract one branch of a patch or merge file:
   `wiggle {{[-x|--extract]}} {{path/to/file.patch}}`
5. Apply a patch and save the compared words to the output file:
   `wiggle {{[-w|--words]}} {{path/to/my_word_patch.patch}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/word_patched_code.c}}`
6. Display help about the merge function:
   `wiggle {{[-m|--merge]}} {{[-h|--help]}}`
wikiman:
**`wikiman`**: Offline search engine for documentation.

**Examples:**
1. Search for a specific topic in all installed sources:
   `wikiman {{search_term}}`
2. Search for a topic in a specific [s]ource:
   `wikiman -s {{source}} {{search_term}}`
3. Search for a topic in two or more specific [s]ources:
   `wikiman -s {{source1,source2,...}} {{search_term}}`
4. List existing [S]ources:
   `wikiman -S`
5. Display [h]elp:
   `wikiman -h`
wikit:
**`wikit`**: Easily get Wikipedia summaries.

**Examples:**
1. Show a short summary of a specific topic on Wikipedia:
   `wikit {{topic}}`
2. Specify a language (ISO 639-1 language code):
   `wikit {{topic}} {{[-l|--lang]}} {{language_code}}`
3. Open the full Wikipedia article in the default browser:
   `wikit {{topic}} -b`
4. Open a disambiguation menu:
   `wikit {{topic}} -d`
winicontopam:
**`winicontopam`**: Convert a Windows ICO file to a PAM file.

**Examples:**
1. Read an ICO file and convert the best quality image contained therein to the PAM format:
   `winicontopam {{path/to/input_file.ico}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
2. Convert all images in the input file to PAM:
   `winicontopam {{[-al|-allimages]}} {{path/to/input_file.ico}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
3. Convert the n'th image in the input file to PAM:
   `winicontopam {{[-i|-image]}} {{n}} {{path/to/input_file.ico}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
4. If the image(s) to be extracted contain graded transparency data and an AND mask, write the AND mask into the fifth channel of the output PAM file:
   `winicontopam {{[-an|-andmasks]}} {{path/to/input_file.ico}} > {{path/to/output.pam}}`
winicontoppm:
**`winicontoppm`**: This command has been superseded by `winicontopam`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the current command:
   `tldr winicontopam`
wipeclean:
**`wipeclean`**: Clear the terminal screen using an animated wiper.

**Examples:**
1. Clear the terminal screen:
   `wipeclean`
2. Set the animation speed in frames per second (defaults to 150):
   `wipeclean {{[-s|--speed]}} {{speed}}`
wishlist:
**`wishlist`**: SSH directory and multiplexer.

**Examples:**
1. Explore SSH servers listed in your `~/.ssh/config` file (local mode):
   `wishlist`
2. Start Wishlist in server mode to provide remote access:
   `wishlist {{[s|serve]}}`
3. Use a custom configuration file:
   `wishlist {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.yaml}}`
4. Discover SSH endpoints using Zeroconf (mDNS/Bonjour):
   `wishlist --zeroconf.enabled`
5. Discover SSH nodes from DNS SRV records:
   `wishlist --srv.domain {{example.com}}`
6. Discover SSH nodes from a Tailscale tailnet:
   `wishlist --tailscale.net={{tailnet_name}} --tailscale.key={{tskey-api-abc123}}`
wkhtmltopdf:
**`wkhtmltopdf`**: Convert HTML documents or web pages into PDF files.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a HTML document into PDF:
   `wkhtmltopdf {{input.html}} {{output.pdf}}`
2. Specify the PDF page size (please see `PaperSize` of `QPrinter` for supported sizes):
   `wkhtmltopdf --page-size {{A4}} {{input.html}} {{output.pdf}}`
3. Set the PDF page margins:
   `wkhtmltopdf --margin-{{top|bottom|left|right}} {{10mm}} {{input.html}} {{output.pdf}}`
4. Set the PDF page orientation:
   `wkhtmltopdf --orientation {{Landscape|Portrait}} {{input.html}} {{output.pdf}}`
5. Generate a greyscale version of the PDF document:
   `wkhtmltopdf --grayscale {{input.html}} {{output.pdf}}`
wlc:
**`wlc`**: Manage localization projects on a Weblate instance.

**Examples:**
1. List projects using a configuration file:
   `wlc {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/file}} list-projects`

xml-c14n:

xml-canonic:

xml-edit:

xml-elements:

   `xzgrep {{--context|--before-context|--after-context}} 3 "{{search_pattern}}" {{path/to/file}}`
5. Print file name and line number for each match with color output:
   `xzgrep {{[-H|--with-filename]}} {{[-n|--line-number]}} --color=always "{{search_pattern}}" {{path/to/file}}`
6. Search for lines matching a pattern, printing only the matched text:
   `xzgrep {{[-o|--only-matching]}} "{{search_pattern}}" {{path/to/file}}`
7. Use extended `regex` (supports `?`, `+`, `{}`, `()`, and `|`), in case-insensitive mode:
   `xzgrep {{[-E|--extended-regexp]}} {{[-i|--ignore-case]}} "{{search_pattern}}" {{path/to/file}}`
xzless:
**`xzless`**: Display text from `xz` and `lzma` compressed files.

**Examples:**
1. View a compressed file:
   `xzless {{path/to/file}}`
2. View a compressed file and display line numbers:
   `xzless --LINE-NUMBERS {{path/to/file}}`
3. View a compressed file and quit if the entire file can be displayed on the first screen:
   `xzless --quit-if-one-screen {{path/to/file}}`
xzmore:
**`xzmore`**: Display text from `xz` or `lzma` compressed files.

**Examples:**
1. View a compressed file:
   `xzmore {{path/to/file}}`
ya:
**`ya`**: Manage Yazi plugins and flavors, publish or subscribe to DDS messages.

**Examples:**
1. Add a package:
   `ya pkg add {{package}}`
2. Delete a package:
   `ya pkg delete {{package}}`
3. Upgrade all packages:
   `ya pkg upgrade`
4. List all packages:
   `ya pkg list`
5. Emit a command to be executed by the current instance:
   `ya emit {{command}} {{arguments}}`
6. Emit commands to a specific remote instance:
   `ya emit-to {{receiver}} {{command}} {{arguments}}`
7. Publish a message to the current instance with string body:
   `ya pub --str {{string_message}}`
8. Subscribe to a specific kind of message from a remote instance:
   `ya sub {{message_kind}}`
yacas:
**`yacas`**: Yet Another Computer Algebra System.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive `yacas` session:
   `yacas`
2. [Interactive] While in a `yacas` session, execute a statement:
   `{{Integrate(x)Cos(x)}};`
3. [Interactive] While in a `yacas` session, display an example:
   `Example();`
4. [Interactive] Quit from a `yacas` session:

yacc:
**`yacc`**: Generate an LALR parser (in C) with a formal grammar specification file.

**Examples:**
1. Create a file `y.tab.c` containing the C parser code and compile the grammar file with all necessary constant declarations for values. (Constant declarations file `y.tab.h` is created only when the `-d` flag is used):
   `yacc -d {{path/to/grammar_file.y}}`
2. Compile a grammar file containing the description of the parser and a report of conflicts generated by ambiguities in the grammar:
   `yacc -d {{path/to/grammar_file.y}} -v`
3. Compile a grammar file, and prefix output filenames with `prefix` instead of `y`:
   `yacc -d {{path/to/grammar_file.y}} -v -b {{prefix}}`
yadm-alt:
**`yadm-alt`**: Create symbolic links and process templates for any managed files.

**Examples:**
1. Create symbolic links between alternate files manually:
   `yadm alt`
yadm-bootstrap:
**`yadm-bootstrap`**: Execute Yadm's bootstrap file.

**Examples:**
1. Execute bootstrap executable:
   `yadm bootstrap`
yadm-clone:
**`yadm-clone`**: Works just like `git clone`. In addition you can pass extra flags to configure your repository.

**Examples:**
1. Clone an existing repository:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}}`
2. Clone an existing repository, then execute the bootstrap file:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}} --bootstrap`
3. Clone an existing repository and after cloning, do not execute the bootstrap file:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}} --no-bootstrap`
4. Change the worktree that yadm will use during cloning:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}} --w {{worktree_file}}`
5. Change the branch that yadm gets files from:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}} -b {{branch}}`
6. Override an existing repository local branch:
   `yadm clone {{remote_repository_location}} -f`
yadm-config:
**`yadm-config`**: Pass options to yadm's config file. Change the `.config` of the repository managed by yadm.

**Examples:**
1. Set or update a yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm config {{key.inner-key}} {{value}}`
2. Get a value from yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm config --get {{key}}`
3. Unset a value in yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm config --unset {{key}}`
4. List all values in yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm config --list`
yadm-decrypt:
**`yadm-decrypt`**: Decrypt files that were encrypted by yadm.

**Examples:**
1. Decrypt files:
   `yadm decrypt`
yadm-encrypt:
**`yadm-encrypt`**: Encrypt files listed in the designated encrypt file.

**Examples:**
1. Encrypt files listed in the designated encrypt file:
   `yadm encrypt`
2. Create the necessary files and folders for encryption:
   `touch {{path/to/encrypt_file}} && mkdir {{path/to/archive_folder}}`
yadm-enter:
**`yadm-enter`**: Run a sub-shell with all Git variables set. This sub-shell can be used to easily interact with the local yadm repository using Git commands.

**Examples:**
1. Run a sub-shell with all Git variables set:
   `yadm enter`
2. Exit the sub-shell:
   `exit`
yadm-git-crypt:
**`yadm-git-crypt`**: Git Crypt enables transparent encryption and decryption of files in a Git repository.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize repo to use Git Crypt:
   `yadm git-crypt init`
2. Share the repository using GPG:
   `yadm git-crypt add-gpg-user {{user_id}}`
3. After cloning a repository with encrypted files, unlock them:
   `yadm git-crypt unlock`
4. Export a symmetric secret key:
   `yadm git-crypt export-key {{path/to/key_file}}`
yadm-gitconfig:
**`yadm-gitconfig`**: Pass options to `git config`. Change the `.gitconfig` of the repository managed by yadm.

**Examples:**
1. Update or set a Git configuration value:
   `yadm gitconfig {{key.inner-key}} {{value}}`
2. Get a value from yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm gitconfig --get {{key}}`
3. Unset a value in yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm gitconfig --unset {{key}}`
4. List all values in yadm's Git configuration:
   `yadm gitconfig --list`
yadm-init:
**`yadm-init`**: Initialize a new, empty repository for tracking dotfiles.

**Examples:**
1. Execute:
   `yadm init`
2. Override the worktree:
   `yadm init -w {{path/to/worktree_folder}}`
3. Overwrite an existing repository:
   `yadm init -f {{path/to/local_repository}}`
yadm-introspect:
**`yadm-introspect`**: Look at data that is managed by yadm.

**Examples:**
1. Output commands:
   `yadm introspect commands`
2. Output configs:
   `yadm introspect configs`
3. Output switches for the main yadm command:
   `yadm introspect switches`
4. Output repo:
   `yadm introspect repo`
yadm-list:
**`yadm-list`**: Print a list of files managed by yadm.

**Examples:**
1. Print a list of files managed by yadm in the current directory:
   `yadm list`
2. List all files managed by yadm completely:
   `yadm list -a`
yadm-perms:
**`yadm-perms`**: Update permissions.

**Examples:**
1. Change file permissions:
   `yadm perms`
yadm-transcrypt:
**`yadm-transcrypt`**: If `transcrypt` is installed, allows you to pass options directly to `transcrypt`.

**Examples:**
1. Set the symmetric cipher to utilize for encryption:
   `yadm transcrypt {{[-c|--cipher]}} {{cipher}}`
2. Pass the password to derive the key from:
   `yadm transcrypt {{[-p|--password]}} {{password}}`
3. Assume yes and accept defaults for non-specified options:
   `yadm transcrypt {{[-y|--yes]}}`
4. Display the current repository's cipher and password:
   `yadm transcrypt {{[-d|--display]}}`
5. Re -encrypt all encrypted files using new credentials:
   `yadm transcrypt {{[-r|--rekey]}}`
yadm-upgrade:
**`yadm-upgrade`**: Upgrade yadm to the latest version.

**Examples:**
1. Upgrade yadm to the latest version:
   `yadm upgrade`
2. Force the upgrade regardless of changes:
   `yadm upgrade -f`
yadm:
**`yadm`**: A dotfiles manager that works by using `git`.

**Examples:**
1. Override yadm's configuration directory:
   `yadm --yadm-dir`
2. Override yadm's data directory. yadm stores its data relative to this directory:
   `yadm --yadm-data`
3. Override the location of the yadm repository:
   `yadm --yadm-repo`
4. Override the location of yadm's main configuration file:
   `yadm --yadm-config`
5. Override the location of the yadm encryption configuration:
   `yadm --yadm-encrypt`
6. Override the location of the yadm encrypted files archive:
   `yadm --yadm-archive`
7. Override the location of the yadm bootstrap program:
   `yadm --yadm-bootstrap`
yamllint:
**`yamllint`**: A linter for YAML files.

**Examples:**
1. Lint a file:
   `yamllint {{path/to/file.yaml}}`
2. Lint all YAML files in a directory recursively:
   `yamllint {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Lint a file with a specific config file:
   `yamllint {{[-c|--config-file]}} {{path/to/config.yaml}} {{path/to/file.yaml}}`
4. Lint a file using a preset config (`default` or `relaxed`):
   `yamllint {{[-d|--config-data]}} "{{extends: relaxed}}" {{path/to/file.yaml}}`
5. Output in a parsable format (for CI integration):
   `yamllint {{[-f|--format]}} parsable {{path/to/file.yaml}}`
6. Lint a file with strict mode (return 2 for warnings):
   `yamllint {{[-s|--strict]}} {{path/to/file.yaml}}`
7. Read from `stdin`:

8. Display help:
   `yamllint {{[-h|--help]}}`
yank:
**`yank`**: Read input from `stdin` and display a selection interface that allows a field to be selected and copied to the clipboard.

**Examples:**
1. Yank using the default delimiters (\f, \n, \r, \s, \t):
   `{{sudo dmesg}} | yank`
2. Yank an entire line:
   `{{sudo dmesg}} | yank -l`
3. Yank using a specific delimiter:
   `{{echo hello=world}} | yank -d {{=}}`
4. Only yank fields matching a specific pattern:
   `{{ps ux}} | yank -g "{{[0-9]+}}"`
yapf:
**`yapf`**: Python style guide checker.

**Examples:**
1. Display a diff of the changes that would be made, without making them (dry-run):
   `yapf {{[-d|--diff]}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Recursively format all Python files in a directory, concurrently:
   `yapf {{[-ri|--recursive --in-place]}} --style {{pep8}} {{[-p|--parallel]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
yara:
**`yara`**: Pattern matching tool for identifying and classifying malware.

**Examples:**
1. Scan a specific file with a rule file:
   `yara {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Recursively scan a directory and subdirectories containing possible threats:
   `yara {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{[-r|--recursive]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
3. Scan a running process by its PID using multiple rules:
   `yara {{path/to/rule1.yar path/to/rule2.yar ...}} {{pid}}`
4. Print metadata associated with the matching rules:
   `yara {{[-m|--print-meta]}} {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/file}}`
5. Print the strings that caused the rule to match:
   `yara {{[-s|--print-strings]}} {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Use a specific number of threads for parallel scanning:
   `yara {{[-p|--threads]}} {{number_of_threads}} {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/directory}}`
7. Use compiled YARA rules file to scan a directory recursively:
   `yara {{[-C|--compiled-rules]}} {{path/to/rules.bin}} {{[-r|--recursive]}} {{path/to/directory}}`
yarac:
**`yarac`**: Compile YARA rule source files into a binary format for faster loading.

**Examples:**
1. Compile a specific rule file:
   `yarac {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/rule.bin}}`
2. Compile multiple rule files into a single binary:
   `yarac {{path/to/rule1.yar path/to/rule2.yar ...}} {{path/to/rules.bin}}`
3. Define an external variable during compilation:
   `yarac -d {{identifier}}={{value}} {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/rule.bin}}`
4. Disable warnings during compilation:
   `yarac {{[-w|--no-warnings]}} {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/rule.bin}}`
5. Fail compilation on any warnings (do not use along with `--no-warnings`):
   `yarac --fail-on-warnings {{path/to/rule.yar}} {{path/to/rule.bin}}`
yard:
**`yard`**: Documentation tool for Ruby.

**Examples:**
1. Create the documentation:

2. Create the documentation and save it to one file:
   `yard --one-file`
3. List all undocumented objects:
   `yard stats --list-undoc`
yarn-why:
**`yarn-why`**: Identifies why a Yarn package has been installed.

**Examples:**
1. Show why a Yarn package is installed:
   `yarn-why {{package}}`
yarn:
**`yarn`**: JavaScript and Node.js package manager alternative.

**Examples:**
1. Install a module globally:
   `yarn global add {{module_name}}`
2. Install all dependencies referenced in the `package.json` file (the `install` is optional):
   `yarn install`
3. Install a module and save it as a dependency to the `package.json` file (add `--dev` to save as a dev dependency):
   `yarn add {{module_name}}@{{version}}`
4. Uninstall a module and remove it from the `package.json` file:
   `yarn remove {{module_name}}`
5. Interactively create a `package.json` file:

6. Identify whether a module is a dependency and list other modules that depend upon it:
   `yarn why {{module_name}}`
yazi:
**`yazi`**: Blazing fast terminal file manager written in Rust.

**Examples:**
1. Launch Yazi from the current directory:

2. Print debug information:
   `yazi --debug`
3. Write the current working directory on exit to the file:
   `yazi --cwd-file {{path/to/cwd_file}}`
4. Clear the cache directory:
   `yazi --clear-cache`
ybacklight:
**`ybacklight`**: Manage screen backlight brightness.

**Examples:**
1. Print current brightness and maximal brightness, shortened and separated by a slash:
   `ybacklight Sc/Sm`
2. Specify the brightness:
   `ybacklight s{{420}}`
3. Increase the brightness by 42 big steps (4200 by default):
   `ybacklight Si42`
4. Decrease the brightness by 300:
   `ybacklight d300`
ybmtopbm:
**`ybmtopbm`**: Convert a Bennet Yee "face" file to PBM.

**Examples:**
1. Convert a YBM image file to PBM:
   `ybmtopbm {{path/to/input_file.ybm}} > {{path/to/output_file.pbm}}`
yek:
**`yek`**: Serialize a repository or directory into an LLM-friendly single file (fast Rust-based repomapper).

**Examples:**
1. Serialize the current directory and write the output to a temp file (prints path):
   `yek`
2. Serialize specific directories and write output to a directory:
   `yek {{path/to/directory1 path/to/directory2 ...}} --output-dir {{path/to/output_directory}}`
3. Process multiple files or use glob patterns (quote globs to avoid shell expansion):
   `yek "{{path/to/directory/**/*.rs}}" "{{path/to/directory/**/*.md}}"`
4. Cap the token-based output size to 128k tokens:
   `yek {{path/to/directory}} --tokens 128k`
5. Cap the byte-based max output size and set an explicit output file name:
   `yek {{path/to/directory}} --max-size {{100KB}} --output-name {{yek-output.txt}}`
6. Stream JSON output:
   `yek {{path/to/directory}} --json`
7. Include a directory tree header in the output:
   `yek {{path/to/directory}} --tree-header`
yes:
**`yes`**: Output something repeatedly.

**Examples:**
1. Repeatedly output `y`:
   `yes`
2. Repeatedly output a specified value:
   `yes {{value}}`
3. Accept everything prompted by the `apt-get` command:
   `yes | sudo apt-get install {{program}}`
4. Repeatedly output a newline to always accept the default option of a prompt:
   `yes ''`
yesod:
**`yesod`**: Helper tool for Yesod, a Haskell-based web framework.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new scaffolded site, with SQLite as backend, in the `my-project` directory:
   `stack new {{my-project}} {{yesod-sqlite}}`

3. Start development server:
   `stack exec -- yesod devel`

   `stack exec -- yesod touch`

   `stack exec -- yesod keter`
yj:
**`yj`**: Convert between YAML, TOML, JSON, and HCL, preserving map order.

ykinfo:
**`ykinfo`**: Get basic information from a YubiKey.

1. Display all information from YubiKey:
   `ykinfo -a`
2. Get only serial in decimal from YubiKey:
   `ykinfo -s -q`

   `ykinfo -c`
ykman-config:
**`ykman-config`**: Enable or disable YubiKey applications.

**Examples:**
1. Enable an application over USB or NFC (`--enable` can be used multiple times to specify more applications):
   `ykman config {{usb|nfc}} {{[-e|--enable]}} {{otp|u2f|fido2|oath|piv|openpgp|hsmauth}}`

   `ykman config {{usb|nfc}} {{[-d|--disable]}} {{otp|u2f|fido2|oath|piv|openpgp|hsmauth}}`
3. Disable all applications over NFC:
   `ykman config nfc {{[-D|--disable-all]}}`
ykman-fido:
**`ykman-fido`**: Manage YubiKey FIDO applications.

**Examples:**
1. Display general information about the FIDO2 application:
   `ykman fido info`
2. Change the FIDO pin:
   `ykman fido access change-pin`
3. List resident credentials stored on the YubiKey:
   `ykman fido credentials list`
4. Delete a resident credential from the YubiKey:
   `ykman fido credentials delete {{id}}`
5. List fingerprints stored on the YubiKey (requires a key with a fingerprint sensor):
   `ykman fido fingerprints list`
6. Add a new fingerprint to the YubiKey:
   `ykman fido fingerprints add {{name}}`
7. Delete a fingerprint from the YubiKey:
   `ykman fido fingerprints delete {{name}}`
8. Wipe all FIDO credentials (you have to do this after exceeding the number of PIN retry attempts):
   `ykman fido reset`
ykman-oath:
**`ykman-oath`**: Manage the OATH YubiKey application.

**Examples:**
1. Display general information about the OATH application:
   `ykman oath info`
2. Change the password used to protect OATH accounts (add `--clear` to remove it):
   `ykman oath access change`
3. Add a new account (the issuer is optional):
   `ykman oath accounts add {{[-i|--issuer]}} {{issuer}} {{name}}`
4. List all accounts (with their issuers):
   `ykman oath accounts list`
5. List all accounts with their current TOTP/HOTP codes (optionally filtering the list with a keyword):
   `ykman oath accounts code {{keyword}}`
6. Rename an account:
   `ykman oath accounts rename {{keyword}} {{issuer:name|name}}`
7. Delete an account:
   `ykman oath accounts delete {{keyword}}`
8. Delete all accounts and restore factory settings:
   `ykman oath reset`
ykman-openpgp:
**`ykman-openpgp`**: Manage the OpenPGP YubiKey application.

**Examples:**
1. Display general information about the OpenPGP application:
   `ykman openpgp info`

   `ykman openpgp access change-{{pin|reset-code|admin-pin}}`
4. Factory reset the OpenPGP application (you have to do this after exceeding the number of Admin PIN retry attempts):
   `ykman openpgp reset`
ykman:
**`ykman`**: YubiKey Manager - configure YubiKeys.

**Examples:**
1. Display general information about a YubiKey (serial number, firmware version, capabilities, etc.):
   `ykman info`
2. List connected YubiKeys with short, one-line descriptions (including the serial number):
   `ykman list`
3. View documentation for enabling and disabling applications:
   `tldr ykman config`
4. View documentation for managing the FIDO applications:
   `tldr ykman fido`
5. View documentation for managing the OATH application:
   `tldr ykman oath`
6. View documentation for managing the OpenPGP application:
   `tldr ykman openpgp`
yolo:
**`yolo`**: Train, validate, or infer models on various tasks and versions.

**Examples:**
1. Create a copy of the default configuration in your current working directory:
   `yolo task=init`
2. Train the object detection, instance segment, or classification model with the specified configuration file:
   `yolo task={{detect|segment|classify}} mode=train cfg={{path/to/config.yaml}}`
you-get:
**`you-get`**: Download media contents (videos, audios, images) from the Web.

**Examples:**
1. Print media information about a specific media on the web:
   `you-get {{[-i|--info]}} {{https://example.com/video?id=value}}`
2. Download a media from a specific URL:
   `you-get {{https://example.com/video?id=value}}`
3. Search on Google Videos and download:
   `you-get {{keywords}}`
4. Download a media to a specific location:
   `you-get {{[-o|--output-dir]}} {{path/to/directory}} {{[-O|--output-filename]}} {{filename}} {{https://example.com/watch?v=value}}`
5. Download a media using a proxy:
   `you-get {{[-x|--http-proxy]}} {{proxy_server}} {{https://example.com/watch?v=value}}`
youtube-dl:
**`youtube-dl`**: Download videos from YouTube and other websites.

**Examples:**
1. Download a video or playlist:
   `youtube-dl '{{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oHg5SJYRHA0}}'`
2. List all formats that a video or playlist is available in:
   `youtube-dl {{[-F|--list-formats]}} '{{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mwa0_nE9H7A}}'`
3. Download a video or playlist at a specific quality:
   `youtube-dl {{[-f|--format]}} "{{best[height<=480]}}" '{{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oHg5SJYRHA0}}'`
4. Download the audio from a video and convert it to an MP3:
   `youtube-dl {{[-x|--extract-audio]}} --audio-format {{mp3}} '{{url}}'`
5. Download the best quality audio and video and merge them:
   `youtube-dl {{[-f|--format]}} bestvideo+bestaudio '{{url}}'`
6. Download video(s) as MP4 files with custom filenames:
   `youtube-dl {{[-f|--format]}} {{mp4}} {{[-o|--output]}} "{{%(playlist_index)s-%(title)s by %(uploader)s on %(upload_date)s in %(playlist)s.%(ext)s}}" '{{url}}'`
7. Download a particular language's subtitles along with the video:
   `youtube-dl --sub-lang {{en}} --write-sub '{{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mwa0_nE9H7A}}'`
8. Download a playlist and extract MP3s from it:
   `youtube-dl {{[-f|--format]}} "bestaudio" {{[-c|--continue]}} {{[-w|--no-overwrites]}} {{[-i|--ignore-errors]}} {{[-x|--extract-audio]}} --audio-format mp3 {{[-o|--output]}} "%(title)s.%(ext)s" '{{url_to_playlist}}'`
youtube-viewer:
**`youtube-viewer`**: Search and play videos from YouTube.

**Examples:**
1. Search for a video:
   `youtube-viewer {{search_term}}`
2. Log in to your YouTube account:
   `youtube-viewer --login`
3. Watch a video with a specific URL in VLC:

zeroclaw-onboard:

zeroclaw-service:

zeroclaw-skills:
**`zeroclaw-skills`**: Manage user-defined skills for ZeroClaw.

zeroclaw-status:

   `zeroclaw status {{[-h|--help]}}`
zeroclaw:
**`zeroclaw`**: Fast, small, and fully autonomous AI assistant infrastructure.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize workspace and configuration (quick setup):
   `zeroclaw onboard --api-key {{api_key}} --provider {{openrouter|anthropic|openai|...}}`
