   `rpcclient {{[-U|--user]}} {{domain}}\{{username}}%{{password}} {{[-c|--command]}} {{semicolon_separated_commands}} {{ip_address}}`
5. [Interactive] Display domain users:
   `enumdomusers`
6. [Interactive] Display privileges:
   `enumprivs`
7. [Interactive] Display information about a specific user:
   `queryuser {{username|rid}}`
8. [Interactive] Create a new user in the domain:
   `createdomuser {{username}}`
rpcinfo:
**`rpcinfo`**: Make an RPC call to an RPC server and reports what it finds.

**Examples:**
1. Show full table of all RPC services registered on localhost:
   `rpcinfo`
2. Show concise table of all RPC services registered on localhost:
   `rpcinfo -s localhost`
3. Display table of statistics of rpcbind operations on localhost:
   `rpcinfo -m`
4. Display list of entries of given service name (mountd) and version number (2) on a remote nfs share:
   `rpcinfo -l {{remote_nfs_server_ip}} {{mountd}} {{2}}`
5. Delete the registration for version 1 of the mountd service for all transports:
   `rpcinfo -d {{mountd}} {{1}}`
rpi-eeprom-update:
**`rpi-eeprom-update`**: Update EEPROM and view other EEPROM information.

**Examples:**
1. Print information about the current raspberry pi EEPROM installed:
   `sudo rpi-eeprom-update`
2. Update a raspberry pi EEPROM:
   `sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a`
3. Cancel the pending update:
   `sudo rpi-eeprom-update -r`
4. Display help:
   `rpi-eeprom-update -h`
rpi-otp-private-key:
**`rpi-otp-private-key`**: Display the One-Time Programmable (OTP) private key of a Raspberry Pi.

**Examples:**
1. Read the OTP private key:
   `rpi-otp-private-key`
rpicam-hello:
**`rpicam-hello`**: View a live camera stream using a Raspberry Pi camera.

**Examples:**
1. Display a camera preview stream for a specific amount of time (in milliseconds):
   `rpicam-hello {{[-t|--timeout]}} {{time}}`
2. Tune the configuration for a particular camera sensor:
   `rpicam-hello --tuning-file {{/usr/share/libcamera/ipa/rpi/path/to/config.json}}`
rpicam-jpeg:
**`rpicam-jpeg`**: Capture and store a JPEG image using a Raspberry Pi camera.

**Examples:**
1. Capture an image and name the file:
   `rpicam-jpeg {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.jpg}}`
2. Capture an image with set dimensions:
   `rpicam-jpeg {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.jpg}} --width {{1920}} --height {{1080}}`
3. Capture an image with an exposure of 20 seconds and a gain of 150%:
   `rpicam-jpeg {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.jpg}} --shutter 20000 --gain 1.5`
rpicam-raw:
**`rpicam-raw`**: Capture a raw video on a Raspberry Pi camera.

**Examples:**
1. Capture a video for a specific amount of seconds:
   `rpicam-raw {{[-t|--timeout]}} {{2000}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.raw}}`
2. Change video dimensions and framerate:
   `rpicam-raw {{[-t|--timeout]}} {{5000}} --width {{4056}} --height {{3040}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.raw}} --framerate {{8}}`
rpicam-still:
**`rpicam-still`**: Capture and store a photo using a Raspberry Pi camera with legacy features missing from `rpicam-jpeg`.

**Examples:**
1. Capture a photo with different encoding:
   `rpicam-still {{[-e|--encoding]}} {{bmp|png|rgb|yuv420}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.[bmp|png|rgb|yuv420]}}`
2. Capture a raw image:
   `rpicam-still {{[-r|--raw]}} {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.jpg}}`
3. Capture a 100 second exposure image:
   `rpicam-still {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.jpg}} --shutter 100000`
rpicam-vid:
**`rpicam-vid`**: Capture a video using a Raspberry Pi camera.

**Examples:**
1. Capture a 10 second video:
   `rpicam-vid {{[-t|--timeout]}} 10000 {{[-o|--output]}} {{path/to/file.h264}}`
rpm-ostree:
**`rpm-ostree`**: A hybrid image/package system.

**Examples:**
1. Show rpm-ostree deployments in the order they will appear in the bootloader:
   `rpm-ostree status`
2. Show packages which are outdated and can be updated:
   `rpm-ostree upgrade --preview`
3. Prepare a new ostree deployment with upgraded packages and reboot into it:
   `rpm-ostree upgrade {{[-r|--reboot]}}`
4. Reboot into the previous ostree deployment:
   `rpm-ostree rollback {{[-r|--reboot]}}`
5. Install a package into a new ostree deployment and reboot into it:
   `rpm-ostree install {{package}} {{[-r|--reboot]}}`
rpm:
**`rpm`**: RPM Package Manager.

**Examples:**
1. Show version of httpd package:
   `rpm {{[-q|--query]}} httpd`
2. List versions of all matching packages:
   `rpm {{[-qa|--query --all]}} '{{mariadb*}}'`
3. Forcibly install a package regardless of currently installed versions:
   `rpm {{[-U|--upgrade]}} {{path/to/package.rpm}} --force`
4. Identify owner of a file and show version of the package:
   `rpm {{[-qf|--query --file]}} {{/etc/postfix/main.cf}}`
5. List package-owned files:
   `rpm {{[-ql|--query --list]}} {{kernel}}`
6. Show scriptlets from an RPM file:
   `rpm {{[-qp|--query --package]}} --scripts {{package.rpm}}`
7. Show changed, missing and/or incorrectly installed files of matching packages:
   `rpm {{[-Va|--verify --all]}} '{{php-*}}'`
8. Display the changelog of a specific package:
   `rpm {{[-q|--query]}} --changelog {{package}}`
rpm2cpio:
**`rpm2cpio`**: Convert an RPM package to a `cpio` archive.

**Examples:**
1. Convert an RPM package to a `cpio` archive and save it as `file.cpio` in the current directory:
   `rpm2cpio {{path/to/file.rpm}}`
rpmbuild:
**`rpmbuild`**: RPM Package Build tool.

**Examples:**
1. Build binary and source packages:
   `rpmbuild -ba {{path/to/spec_file}}`
2. Build a binary package without source package:
   `rpmbuild -bb {{path/to/spec_file}}`
3. Specify additional variables when building a package:
   `rpmbuild -bb {{path/to/spec_file}} --define "{{variable1}} {{value1}}" --define "{{variable2}} {{value2}}"`
rpmconf:
**`rpmconf`**: Handle `.rpmnew`, `.rpmsave`, and `.rpmorig` files left over by package upgrades.

**Examples:**
1. List leftover files and interactively choose what to do with each of them:
   `sudo rpmconf {{[-a|--all]}}`
2. Delete orphaned `.rpmnew` and `.rpmsave` files:
   `sudo rpmconf {{[-a|--all]}} {{[-c|--clean]}}`
rpmkeys:
**`rpmkeys`**: Tool to import and remove RPM keys for RPM repositories.

**Examples:**
1. List all imported RPM keys. Also outputs its Key ID needed for deleting an imported RPM key:
   `sudo rpmkeys --list`
2. Remove/Delete a previously imported RPM key, given by its 16-Number/Letters Key ID:
   `sudo rpmkeys --delete {{5a278d9c-5bbc73cb}}`
3. Import an RPM key of repository:
   `sudo rpmkeys --import {{path/to/rpm_key}}`
rpmspec:
**`rpmspec`**: Query a RPM spec file.

**Examples:**
1. List binary packages which would be generated from a RPM spec file:
   `rpmspec --query {{path/to/rpm.spec}}`
2. List all options for `--queryformat`:
   `rpmspec --querytags`
3. Get summary information for single binary packages generated from a RPM spec file:
   `rpmspec --query --queryformat "{{%{name}: %{summary}\n}}" {{path/to/rpm.spec}}`
4. Get the source package which would be generated from a RPM spec file:
   `rpmspec --query --srpm {{path/to/rpm.spec}}`
5. Parse a RPM spec file to `stdout`:
   `rpmspec --parse {{path/to/rpm.spec}}`
rsh:
**`rsh`**: Execute commands on a remote host.

**Examples:**
1. Execute a command on a remote host:
   `rsh {{remote_host}} {{ls -l}}`
2. Execute a command on a remote host with a specific username:
   `rsh {{remote_host}} {{[-l|--user]}} {{username}} {{ls -l}}`
3. Redirect `stdin` to `/dev/null` when executing a command on a remote host:
   `rsh {{remote_host}} --no-err {{ls -l}}`
rspamc:
**`rspamc`**: Client for `rspamd` servers.

**Examples:**
1. Train the bayesian filter to recognise an email as spam:
   `rspamc learn_spam {{path/to/email_file}}`
2. Train the bayesian filter to recognize an email as ham:
   `rspamc learn_ham {{path/to/email_file}}`
3. Generate a manual report on an email:
   `rspamc symbols {{path/to/email_file}}`
4. Show server statistics:
   `rspamc stat`
rtcwake:
**`rtcwake`**: Enter a system sleep state until specified wakeup time relative to your BIOS clock.

**Examples:**
1. Show whether an alarm is set or not:
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} show {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
2. Suspend to RAM and wakeup after 10 seconds:
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} mem {{[-s|--seconds]}} {{10}}`
3. Suspend to disk (higher power saving) and wakeup 15 minutes later:
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} disk --date +{{15}}min`
4. Freeze the system (more efficient than suspend-to-RAM but version 3.9 or newer of the Linux kernel is required) and wakeup at a given date and time:
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} freeze --date {{YYYYMMDDhhmm}}`
5. Disable a previously set alarm:
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} disable`
6. Perform a dry run to wakeup the computer at a given time. (Press `<Ctrl c>` to abort):
   `sudo rtcwake {{[-m|--mode]}} on --date {{hh:ss}}`
rtmon:
**`rtmon`**: Save network state changes to a file.

**Examples:**
1. Save all network state changes to a file:
   `sudo rtmon {{[f|file]}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Specify the type of change to log:
   `sudo rtmon {{[f|file]}} {{link|address|route}}`
rtorrent:
**`rtorrent`**: Download torrents.

**Examples:**
1. Add a torrent file or magnet to be downloaded:
   `rtorrent {{torrent_or_magnet}}`
2. Start the download:
   `<Ctrl s>`
3. View details about downloading torrent:
   `<ArrowRight>`
4. Close rtorrent safely:
   `<Ctrl q>`
ruget:
**`ruget`**: Alternative to wget written in Rust.

**Examples:**
1. Download the contents of a URL to a file:
   `ruget {{https://example.com/file}}`
2. Download the contents of a URL to a specified output file:
   `ruget {{[-o|--output]}} {{file_name}} {{https://example.com/file}}`
run-mailcap:
**`run-mailcap`**: Execute programs via entries in the mailcap file.

**Examples:**
1. Compose any existing file or new on default `mailcap` edit tool:
   `run-mailcap --action=compose {{path/to/file}}`
2. View any file on default `mailcap` explorer:
   `run-mailcap --action=edit {{path/to/file}}`
3. Print a file using the default `mailcap` print tool:
   `run-mailcap --action=print {{path/to/file}}`
4. View any file (usually image) on default `mailcap` explorer:
   `run-mailcap --action=view {{path/to/file}}`
5. Invoke individual actions/programs on run-mailcap:
   `run-mailcap --action={{view|cat|compose|composetyped|edit|print}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Turn on extra information:
   `run-mailcap --action={{action}} --debug {{path/to/file}}`
7. Ignore any "copiousoutput" directive and forward output to `stdout`:
   `run-mailcap --action={{action}} --nopager {{path/to/file}}`
8. Display the found command without actually executing it:
   `run-mailcap --action={{action}} --norun {{path/to/file}}`
run0:
**`run0`**: Elevate privileges interactively.

**Examples:**
1. Run a command as root:
   `run0 {{command}}`
2. Run a command as another user and/or group:
   `run0 {{[-u|--user]}} {{username|uid}} {{[-g|--group]}} {{group_name|gid}} {{command}}`
run_init:
**`run_init`**: Run init scripts in the proper SELinux context.

**Examples:**
1. Run a script in the init script context:
   `sudo run_init {{path/to/script}}`
2. Run a script with arguments:
   `sudo run_init {{path/to/script}} {{start|stop|restart}}`
3. Run a script and specify the init script context explicitly:
   `sudo run_init {{[-t|--type]}} {{context_type}} {{path/to/script}}`
4. Display the context that would be used without running the script:
   `sudo run_init {{[-n|--dry-run]}} {{path/to/script}}`
runcon:
**`runcon`**: Run a program in a different SELinux security context.

**Examples:**
1. Print the security context of the current execution context:
   `runcon`
2. Specify the domain to run a command in:
   `runcon {{[-t|--type]}} {{domain}}_t {{command}}`
3. Specify the context role to run a command with:
   `runcon {{[-r|--role]}} {{role}}_r {{command}}`
4. Specify the full context to run a command with:
   `runcon {{user}}_u:{{role}}_r:{{domain}}_t {{command}}`
runlevel:
**`runlevel`**: SysV runlevel utility.

**Examples:**
1. Return previous and current SysV runlevel:
   `runlevel`
2. Display help:
   `runlevel --help`
runlim:
**`runlim`**: Sample and limit time and memory usage of a program and its child processes using the proc filesystem on Linux.

**Examples:**
1. Print the time and memory usage of a command:
   `runlim {{command}} {{command_arguments}}`
2. Log statistics to a file instead of `stdout`:
   `runlim --output-file={{path/to/file}} {{command}} {{command_arguments}}`
3. Limit time to an upper bound (in seconds):
   `runlim --time-limit={{number}} {{command}} {{command_arguments}}`
4. Limit real-time to an upper bound (in seconds):
   `runlim --real-time-limit={{number}} {{command}} {{command_arguments}}`
5. Limit space to an upper bound (in MB):
   `runlim --space-limit={{number}} {{command}} {{command_arguments}}`
runuser:
**`runuser`**: Run commands as a user and group without asking for password.

**Examples:**
1. Run command as a different user:
   `sudo runuser {{user}} {{[-c|--command]}} '{{command}}'`
2. Run command as a different user and group:
   `sudo runuser {{user}} {{[-g|--group]}} {{group}} {{[-c|--command]}} '{{command}}'`
3. Start a login shell as a specific user:
   `sudo runuser {{user}} {{[-l|--login]}}`
4. Specify a shell for running instead of the default shell (also works for login):
   `sudo runuser {{user}} {{[-s|--shell]}} {{/bin/sh}}`
5. Preserve the entire environment of root (only if `--login` is not specified):
   `sudo runuser {{user}} {{[-p|--preserve-environment]}} {{[-c|--command]}} '{{command}}'`
rusnapshot:
**`rusnapshot`**: BTRFS snapshotting utility written in Rust.

**Examples:**
1. Create a snapshot using a configuration file:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} --cr`
2. List created snapshots:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} {{[-l|--list]}}`
3. Delete a snapshot by ID or the name of the snapshot:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} --del --id {{snapshot_id}}`
4. Delete all `hourly` snapshots:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-k|--keep]}} {{0}} --clean --kind {{hourly}}`
5. Create a read-write snapshot:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} --cr {{[-r|--rw]}}`
6. Restore a snapshot:
   `sudo rusnapshot {{[-c|--config]}} {{path/to/config.toml}} --id {{snapshot_id}} {{[-r|--restore]}}`
sa:
**`sa`**: Summarize accounting information about commands called by users, including basic information on CPU time spent processing and I/O rates.

**Examples:**
1. Display executable invocations per user (username not displayed):
   `sudo sa`
2. Display executable invocations per user, showing responsible usernames:
   `sudo sa --print-users`
3. List resources used recently per user:
   `sudo sa --user-summary`
sacct:
**`sacct`**: Display accounting data from the Slurm service.

**Examples:**
1. Display job ID, job name, partition, account, number of allocated cpus, job state, and job exit codes for recent jobs:
   `sacct`
2. Display job ID, job state, job exit code for recent jobs:
   `sacct {{[-b|--brief]}}`
3. Display the allocations of a job:
   `sacct {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{job_id}} {{[-X|--allocations]}}`
4. Display elapsed time, job name, number of requested CPUs, and memory requested of a job:
   `sacct {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{job_id}} {{[-o|--format]}} Elapsed,JobName,ReqCPUS,ReqMem`
5. Display recent jobs that occurred from one week ago up to the present day:
   `sacct {{[-S|--starttime]}} $(date {{[-d|--date]}} "1 week ago" +'%F')`
6. Output a larger number of characters for an attribute:
   `sacct {{[-o|--format]}} JobID,JobName%100`
sacctmgr:
**`sacctmgr`**: View, setup, and manage Slurm accounts.

**Examples:**
1. Show current configuration:
   `sacctmgr show configuration`
2. Add a cluster to the slurm database:
   `sacctmgr add cluster {{cluster_name}}`
3. Add an account to the slurm database:
   `sacctmgr add account {{account_name}} cluster={{cluster_of_account}}`
4. Show details of user/association/cluster/account using a specific format:
   `sacctmgr show {{user|association|cluster|account}} format="Account%10" format="GrpTRES%30"`
salloc:
**`salloc`**: Start an interactive shell session or execute a command by allocating one or more nodes in a cluster.

**Examples:**
1. Start an interactive shell session on a node in the cluster:
   `salloc`
2. Execute the specified command synchronously on a node in the cluster:
   `salloc {{ls --all}}`
3. Only allocate nodes fulfilling the specified constraints:
   `salloc {{[-C|--constraint]}} {{(amd|intel)&gpu}}`
sam:
**`sam`**: AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) CLI.

**Examples:**
1. Initialize a serverless application:
   `sam init`
2. Initialize a serverless application with a specific runtime:
   `sam init {{[-r|--runtime]}} {{python3.7}}`
3. Package a SAM application:
   `sam package`
4. Build your Lambda function code:
   `sam build`
5. Run your serverless application locally:
   `sam local start-api`
6. Deploy an AWS SAM application:
   `sam deploy`
sar:
**`sar`**: Monitor performance of various Linux subsystems.

**Examples:**
1. Report I/O and transfer rate issued to physical devices, one per second (press `<Ctrl c>` to quit):
   `sar -b {{1}}`
2. Report a total of 10 network device statistics, one per 2 seconds:
   `sar -n DEV {{2}} {{10}}`
3. Report CPU utilization, one per 2 seconds:
   `sar -u ALL {{2}}`
4. Report a total of 20 memory utilization statistics, one per second:
   `sar -r ALL {{1}} {{20}}`
5. Report the run queue length and load averages, one per second:
   `sar -q {{1}}`
6. Report paging statistics, one per 5 seconds:
   `sar -B {{5}}`
sattach:
**`sattach`**: Attach to a Slurm job step.

**Examples:**
1. Redirect the IO streams (`stdout`, `stderr`, and `stdin`) of a Slurm job step to the current terminal:
   `sattach {{jobid}}.{{stepid}}`
2. Use the current console's input as `stdin` to the specified task:
   `sattach --input-filter {{task_number}}`
3. Only redirect `stdin`/`stderr` of the specified task:
   `sattach --{{output|error}}-filter {{task_number}}`
sbatch:
**`sbatch`**: Submit a batch job to the SLURM scheduler.

**Examples:**
1. Submit a batch job:
   `sbatch {{path/to/job.sh}}`
2. Submit a batch job with a custom name:
   `sbatch --job-name={{myjob}} {{path/to/job.sh}}`
3. Submit a batch job with a time limit of 30 minutes:
   `sbatch --time={{00:30:00}} {{path/to/job.sh}}`
4. Submit a job and request multiple nodes:
   `sbatch --nodes={{3}} {{path/to/job.sh}}`
sbcast:
**`sbcast`**: Send a file to a job's allocated nodes.

**Examples:**
1. Send a file to all nodes allocated to the current job:
   `sbcast {{path/to/file}} {{path/to/destination}}`
2. Autodetect shared libraries the transmitted file depends upon and transmit them as well:
   `sbcast --send-libs={{yes}} {{path/to/executable}} {{path/to/destination}}`
sbctl:
**`sbctl`**: A user-friendly secure boot key manager.

**Examples:**
1. Show the current secure boot status:
   `sbctl status`
2. Create custom secure boot keys (by default, everything is stored in `/var/lib/sbctl`):
   `sbctl create-keys`
3. Enroll the custom secure boot keys and Microsoft's UEFI vendor certificates:
   `sbctl enroll-keys {{[-m|--microsoft]}}`
4. Automatically run `create-keys` and `enroll-keys` based on the settings in `/etc/sbctl/sbctl.conf`:
   `sbctl setup --setup`
5. Sign an EFI binary with the created key and save the file to the database:
   `sbctl sign {{[-s|--save]}} {{path/to/efi_binary}}`
6. Re-sign all the saved files:
   `sbctl sign-all`
7. Verify that all EFI executables on the EFI system partition have been signed:
   `sbctl verify`
scancel:
**`scancel`**: Cancel a Slurm job.

**Examples:**
1. Cancel a job using its ID:
   `scancel {{job_id}}`
2. Cancel all jobs from a user:
   `scancel {{user_name}}`
scanimage:
**`scanimage`**: Scan images with the Scanner Access Now Easy API.

**Examples:**
1. List available scanners to ensure the target device is connected and recognized:
   `scanimage {{[-L|--list-devices]}}`
2. Scan an image and save it to a file:
   `scanimage --format {{pnm|tiff|png|jpeg|pdf|...}} > {{path/to/new_image}}`
3. Specify the device to scan from:
   `scanimage {{[-d|--device]}} {{device_name}} > {{path/to/new_image}}`
4. Specify resolution for the scanned image (default resolution is 75dpi):
   `scanimage --resolution {{300}} > {{path/to/new_image}}`
schroot:
**`schroot`**: Run a command or start an interactive shell with a different root directory. More customizable than `chroot`.

**Examples:**
1. List available chroots:
   `schroot --list`
2. Run a command in a specific chroot:
   `schroot --chroot {{chroot}} {{command}}`
3. Run a command with options in a specific chroot:
   `schroot --chroot {{chroot}} {{command}} -- {{command_options}}`
4. Run a command in all available chroots:
   `schroot --all {{command}}`
5. Start an interactive shell within a specific chroot as a specific user:
   `schroot --chroot {{chroot}} --user {{user}}`
6. Begin a new session (a unique session ID is returned on `stdout`):
   `schroot --begin-session --chroot {{chroot}}`
7. Connect to an existing session:
   `schroot --run-session --chroot {{session_id}}`
8. End an existing session:
   `schroot --end-session --chroot {{session_id}}`
scontrol:
**`scontrol`**: View information about and modify jobs.

**Examples:**
1. Show information for job:
   `scontrol show job {{job_id}}`
2. Suspend a comma-separated list of running jobs:
   `scontrol suspend {{job_id1,job_id2,...}}`
3. Resume a comma-separated list of suspended jobs:
   `scontrol resume {{job_id1,job_id2,...}}`
4. Hold a comma-separated list of queued jobs (Use `release` command to permit the jobs to be scheduled):
   `scontrol hold {{job_id1,job_id2,...}}`
5. Release a comma-separated list of suspended job:
   `scontrol release {{job_id1,job_id2,...}}`
screenkey:
**`screenkey`**: A screencast tool to display keys pressed.

**Examples:**
1. Display keys which are currently being pressed on the screen:
   `screenkey`
2. Display keys and mouse buttons which are currently being pressed on the screen:
   `screenkey {{[-M|--mouse]}}`
3. Launch the settings menu of screenkey:
   `screenkey --show-settings`
4. Launch screenkey at a specific position:
   `screenkey {{[-p|--position]}} {{top|center|bottom|fixed}}`
5. Change the format of the key modifiers displayed on screen:
   `screenkey --mods-mode {{normal|emacs|mac|win|tux}}`
6. Change the appearance of screenkey:
   `screenkey --bg-color "{{#a1b2c3}}" {{[-f|--font]}} {{Hack}} --font-color {{yellow}} --opacity {{0.8}}`
7. Drag and select a window on screen to display screenkey:
   `screenkey {{[-p|--position]}} fixed {{[-g|--geometry]}} {{$(slop --nodecorations --format '%g')}}`
script:
**`script`**: Record all terminal output to a typescript file.

**Examples:**
1. Record a new session to a file named `typescript` in the current directory:
   `script`
2. Stop recording:
   `exit`
3. Record a new session to a custom filepath:
   `script {{path/to/session.out}}`
4. Append to an existing file:
   `script {{[-a|--append]}} {{logfile.log}}`
5. Record timing information (data is outputted to `stderr`):
   `script {{[-t|--timing]}} 2> {{path/to/timing_file}}`
6. Write out data as soon as it happens:
   `script {{[-f|--flush]}} {{path/to/file}}`
7. Execute quietly without start and done messages:
   `script {{[-q|--quiet]}} {{logfile.log}}`
8. Display help:
   `script {{[-h|--help]}}`
scriptlive:
**`scriptlive`**: Execute a typescript created by the `script` command in real-time.

**Examples:**
1. Execute a typescript in real-time:
   `scriptlive {{path/to/timing_file}} {{path/to/typescript}}`
2. Execute a typescript at double the original speed:
   `scriptlive {{path/to/timing_file}} {{path/to/typescript}} --divisor 2`
3. Execute a typescript created using `--log-in` option of `script`:
   `scriptlive --log-in {{path/to/stdin_log_file}} {{path/to/typescript}}`
4. Execute a typescript waiting at most 2 seconds between each command:
   `scriptlive {{path/to/timing_file}} {{path/to/typescript}} --maxdelay 2`
scriptreplay:
**`scriptreplay`**: Replay a typescript created by the `script` command to `stdout`.

**Examples:**
1. Replay a typescript at the speed it was recorded:
   `scriptreplay {{path/to/timing_file}} {{path/to/typescript}}`
2. Replay a typescript at double the original speed:
   `scriptreplay {{path/to/timingfile}} {{path/to/typescript}} 2`
3. Replay a typescript at half the original speed:
   `scriptreplay {{path/to/timingfile}} {{path/to/typescript}} 0.5`
scrontab:
**`scrontab`**: Manage Slurm crontab files.

**Examples:**
1. Install a new crontab from the specified file:
   `scrontab {{path/to/file}}`
2. [e]dit the crontab of the current user:
   `scrontab -e`
3. [e]dit the crontab of the specified user:
   `scrontab --user={{user_id}} -e`
4. [r]emove the current crontab:
   `scrontab -r`
5. Print the crontab of the current user to `stdout`:
   `scrontab -l`
scrot:
**`scrot`**: Screen capture utility.

**Examples:**
1. Capture a screenshot and save it to the current directory with the current date as the filename:
   `scrot`
2. Capture a screenshot and save it as `capture.png`:
   `scrot capture.png`
3. Capture a screenshot interactively:
   `scrot {{[-s|--select]}}`
4. Capture a screenshot interactively without exiting on keyboard input, press `<Esc>` to exit:
   `scrot {{[-is|--ignorekeyboard --select]}}`
5. Capture a screenshot interactively delimiting the region with a colored line:
   `scrot {{[-s|--select]}} {{[-l|--line]}} color={{x11_color|rgb_color}}`
6. Capture a screenshot from the currently focused window:
   `scrot {{[-u|--focused]}}`
7. Display a countdown of 10 seconds before taking a screenshot:
   `scrot {{[-c|--count]}} {{[-d|--delay]}} 10`
scrun:
**`scrun`**: An OCI runtime proxy for Slurm that runs containers as jobs.

**Examples:**
1. Create a new container with a specific ID:
   `scrun create {{container_id}}`
2. Start a previously created container:
   `scrun start {{container_id}}`
3. Query the state of a container:
   `scrun state {{container_id}}`
4. Send a signal to a container (default: SIGTERM):
   `scrun kill {{container_id}}`
5. Send a specific signal to a container:
   `scrun kill {{container_id}} {{SIGKILL}}`
6. Delete a container and release its resources:
   `scrun delete {{container_id}}`
7. Enable debug logging:
   `scrun {{create|start|kill|delete}} {{container_id}} --debug`
8. Display version:
   `scrun --version`
sdiag:
**`sdiag`**: Show information about the execution of `slurmctld`.

**Examples:**
1. Show all performance counters related to the execution of `slurmctld`:
   `sdiag {{[-a|--all]}}`
2. Reset performance counters related to the execution of `slurmctld`:
   `sdiag {{[-r|--reset]}}`
3. Specify the output format:
   `sdiag {{[-a|--all]}} --{{json|yaml}}`
4. Specify the cluster to send commands to:
   `sdiag {{[-a|--all]}} {{[-M|--cluster]}} {{cluster_name}}`
sealert:
**`sealert`**: Analyze and explain SELinux AVC denial messages.

**Examples:**
1. Analyze all recent SELinux denials:
   `sudo sealert {{[-a|--analyze]}} {{/var/log/audit/audit.log}}`
2. Analyze a specific alert ID from system logs:
   `sudo sealert {{[-l|--lookupid]}} {{alert_id}}`
3. Display a summary of recent SELinux alerts:
   `sudo sealert {{[-b|--browser]}}`
4. Monitor audit log in real-time for new alerts:
   `sudo tail {{[-f|--follow]}} {{/var/log/audit/audit.log}} | sealert {{[-l|--lookupid]}} -`
secon:
**`secon`**: Get the SELinux security context of a file, pid, current execution context, or a context specification.

**Examples:**
1. Get the security context of the current execution context:
   `secon`
2. Get the current security context of a process:
   `secon --pid {{1}}`
3. Get the current security context of a file, resolving all intermediate symlinks:
   `secon --file {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
4. Get the current security context of a symlink itself (i.e. do not resolve):
   `secon --link {{path/to/symlink}}`
5. Parse and explain a context specification:
   `secon {{system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c899,c900}}`
secret-tool:
**`secret-tool`**: Store and retrieve passwords, part of the `libsecret` package.

**Examples:**
1. Store a secret with an optional label:
   `secret-tool store --label={{label}} {{key}} {{value}}`
2. Retrieve a secret:
   `secret-tool lookup key {{key}}`
3. Get more information about a secret:
   `secret-tool search key {{key}}`
4. Delete a stored secret:
   `secret-tool clear key {{key}}`
see:
**`see`**: This command is an alias of `run-mailcap --action=view`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr run-mailcap`
selinuxenabled:
**`selinuxenabled`**: Check whether SELinux is enabled.

**Examples:**
1. Check if SELinux is enabled (no output; check exit code with `echo $?`):
   `selinuxenabled`
2. Check if SELinux is enabled and print the result:
   `selinuxenabled && echo "SELinux is enabled" || echo "SELinux is disabled"`
3. Use in a shell script to conditionally execute commands:
   `if selinuxenabled; then echo "SELinux is running"; fi`
semanage-boolean:
**`semanage-boolean`**: Manage persistent SELinux boolean settings.

**Examples:**
1. List all booleans settings:
   `sudo semanage boolean {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. List all user-defined boolean settings without headings:
   `sudo semanage boolean {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-C|--locallist]}} {{[-n|--noheading]}}`
3. Set or unset a boolean persistently:
   `sudo semanage boolean {{[-m|--modify]}} {{-1|--on|-0|--off}} {{haproxy_connect_any}}`
semanage-fcontext:
**`semanage-fcontext`**: Manage persistent SELinux security context rules on files/directories.

**Examples:**
1. List all file labelling rules:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. List all user-defined file labelling rules without headings:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-lCn|--list --locallist --noheading]}}`
3. Add a user-defined rule that labels any path which matches a PCRE `regex`:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{samba_share_t}} '{{/mnt/share(/.*)?}}'`
4. Add a user-defined rule that creates a labeling equivalence between two subpaths:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-e|--equal]}} /{{path/to/ref}} /{{path/to/target}}`
5. Delete a user-defined rule using its PCRE `regex`:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-d|--delete]}} '{{/mnt/share(/.*)?}}'`
6. Relabel a directory recursively by applying the new rules:
   `restorecon -Rv {{path/to/directory}}`
semanage-interface:
**`semanage-interface`**: Manage SELinux network interface type definitions.

**Examples:**
1. List all interface type definitions:
   `sudo semanage interface {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. Add a network interface type definition:
   `sudo semanage interface {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{type_name}} {{interface_name}}`
3. Delete a network interface type definition:
   `sudo semanage interface {{[-d|--delete]}} {{interface_name}}`
4. Modify a network interface type definition:
   `sudo semanage interface {{[-m|--modify]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{type_name}} {{interface_name}}`
5. List interface type definitions in a customized format:
   `sudo semanage interface {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-C|--locallist]}}`
semanage-login:
**`semanage-login`**: Manage SELinux login mappings between Linux users and SELinux users.

**Examples:**
1. List all login mappings:
   `sudo semanage login {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. Add a login mapping (map Linux user to SELinux user):
   `sudo semanage login {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-s|--seuser]}} {{selinux_user}} {{linux_username}}`
3. Delete a login mapping:
   `sudo semanage login {{[-d|--delete]}} {{linux_username}}`
4. Modify an existing login mapping:
   `sudo semanage login {{[-m|--modify]}} {{[-s|--seuser]}} {{selinux_user}} {{linux_username}}`
5. Add a login mapping with a specific MLS/MCS range:
   `sudo semanage login {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-s|--seuser]}} {{user_u}} {{[-r|--range]}} {{s0-s0:c0.c1023}} {{linux_username}}`
6. List only customized login mappings:
   `sudo semanage login {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-C|--locallist]}}`
semanage-permissive:
**`semanage-permissive`**: Manage persistent SELinux permissive domains.

**Examples:**
1. List all process types (a.k.a domains) that are in permissive mode:
   `sudo semanage permissive {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. Set permissive mode for a domain:
   `sudo semanage permissive {{[-a|--add]}} {{httpd_t}}`
3. Unset permissive mode for a domain:
   `sudo semanage permissive {{[-d|--delete]}} {{httpd_t}}`
semanage-port:
**`semanage-port`**: Manage persistent SELinux port definitions.

**Examples:**
1. List all port labeling rules:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. List all user-defined port labeling rules without headings:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-C|--locallist]}} {{[-n|--noheading]}}`
3. Add a user-defined rule that assigns a label to a protocol-port pair:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{ssh_port_t}} {{[-p|--proto]}} {{tcp}} {{22000}}`
4. Add a user-defined rule that assigns a label to a protocol-port-range pair:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{http_port_t}} {{[-p|--proto]}} {{tcp}} {{80-88}}`
5. Delete a user-defined rule using its protocol-port pair:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-d|--delete]}} {{[-p|--proto]}} {{udp}} {{11940}}`
semanage-user:
**`semanage-user`**: Manage SELinux user mappings.

**Examples:**
1. List all SELinux users:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. Add a new SELinux user:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-R|--roles]}} {{role_name}} {{selinux_user}}`
3. Delete a SELinux user:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-d|--delete]}} {{selinux_user}}`
4. Modify an existing SELinux user's roles:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-m|--modify]}} {{[-R|--roles]}} {{role_name}} {{selinux_user}}`
5. Add a SELinux user with a specific default level:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-R|--roles]}} {{role_name}} {{[-L|--level]}} {{s0}} {{selinux_user}}`
6. Add a SELinux user with a specific MLS/MCS range:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-R|--roles]}} {{role_name}} {{[-r|--range]}} {{s0-s0:c0.c1023}} {{selinux_user}}`
7. List only customized SELinux users:
   `sudo semanage user {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-C|--locallist]}}`
semanage:
**`semanage`**: SELinux persistent policy management tool.

**Examples:**
1. Set or unset a SELinux boolean. Booleans allow the administrator to customize how policy rules affect confined process types (a.k.a domains):
   `sudo semanage boolean {{[-m|--modify]}} {{--on|--off}} {{haproxy_connect_any}}`
2. Add a user-defined file context labeling rule. File contexts define what files confined domains are allowed to access:
   `sudo semanage fcontext {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{samba_share_t}} '/mnt/share(/.*)?'`
3. Add a user-defined port labeling rule. Port labels define what ports confined domains are allowed to listen on:
   `sudo semanage port {{[-a|--add]}} {{[-t|--type]}} {{ssh_port_t}} {{[-p|--proto]}} {{tcp}} {{22000}}`
4. Set or unset permissive mode for a confined domain. Per-domain permissive mode allows more granular control compared to `setenforce`:
   `sudo semanage permissive {{--add|--delete}} {{httpd_t}}`
5. Output local customizations in the default store:
   `sudo semanage export {{[-f|--output_file]}} {{path/to/file}}`
6. Import a file generated by `semanage export` into local customizations (CAREFUL: may remove current customizations!):
   `sudo semanage import {{[-f|--input_file]}} {{path/to/file}}`
semodule:
**`semodule`**: Manage SELinux policy modules.

**Examples:**
1. List all installed policy modules:
   `sudo semodule {{[-l|--list]}}`
2. Install a new policy module:
   `sudo semodule {{[-i|--install]}} {{path/to/module.pp}}`
3. Remove a policy module:
   `sudo semodule {{[-r|--remove]}} {{module_name}}`
4. Enable a policy module:
   `sudo semodule {{[-e|--enable]}} {{module_name}}`
5. Disable a policy module:
   `sudo semodule {{[-d|--disable]}} {{module_name}}`
6. Reload all policy modules:
   `sudo semodule {{[-R|--reload]}}`
7. Display the version of installed policy modules:
   `sudo semodule {{[-l|--list]}} {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
sensible-browser:
**`sensible-browser`**: Open the default browser.

**Examples:**
1. Open a new window of the default browser:
   `sensible-browser`
2. Open a URL in the default browser:
   `sensible-browser {{url}}`
sensible-editor:
**`sensible-editor`**: Open the default editor.

**Examples:**
1. Open a file in the default editor:
   `sensible-editor {{path/to/file}}`
2. Open a file in the default editor, with the cursor at the end of the file:
   `sensible-editor + {{path/to/file}}`
3. Open a file in the default editor, with the cursor at the beginning of line 10:
   `sensible-editor +10 {{path/to/file}}`
4. Open 3 files in vertically split editor windows at the same time:
   `sensible-editor -O3 {{path/to/file1 path/to/file2 path/to/file3}}`
sensors:
**`sensors`**: Report sensors information.

**Examples:**
1. Show the current readings of all sensor chips:
   `sensors`
2. Show temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit:
   `sensors --fahrenheit`
service:
**`service`**: Manage services by running init scripts.

**Examples:**
1. List the name and status of all services:
   `service --status-all`
2. Start/Stop/Restart/Reload service (start/stop should always be available):
   `service {{service_name}} {{start|stop|restart|reload}}`
3. Do a full restart (runs script twice with start and stop):
   `service {{service_name}} --full-restart`
4. Show the current status of a service:
   `service {{service_name}} status`
sesearch:
**`sesearch`**: Search SELinux policy rules.

**Examples:**
1. Search for all allow rules:
   `sesearch --allow`
2. Search for rules related to a specific type:
   `sesearch --allow {{[-t|--target]}} {{type_name}}`
3. Search for rules related to a specific source type:
   `sesearch --allow {{[-s|--source]}} {{source_type}}`
4. Search for rules that allow a specific class and permission:
   `sesearch --allow {{[-c|--class]}} {{class_name}} {{[-p|--perm]}} {{permission}}`
5. Search for rules with a specific target type and class:
   `sesearch --allow {{[-t|--target]}} {{type_name}} {{[-c|--class]}} {{class_name}}`
6. Display more detailed information about matched rules:
   `sesearch --allow {{[-t|--target]}} {{type_name}} {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
sestatus:
**`sestatus`**: Print the current SELinux status.

**Examples:**
1. Print the current status:
   `sestatus`
2. Print the current states of all policy booleans:
   `sestatus -b`
3. Print the current file and process contexts:
   `sestatus -v`
setarch:
**`setarch`**: Change the reported architecture for a program's execution, primarily used to modify how programs behave based on system architecture.

**Examples:**
1. Run a command as if the machine architecture is `i686` (useful for running 32-bit apps on a 64-bit kernel):
   `setarch i686 {{command}}`
2. Run a shell with the `x86_64` architecture:
   `setarch x86_64 {{bash}}`
3. Disable randomization of the virtual address space:
   `setarch {{linux32}} {{[-R|--addr-no-randomize]}} {{command}}`
4. List supported architectures:
   `setarch --list`
5. Display help:
   `setarch {{[-h|--help]}}`
setcap:
**`setcap`**: Set capabilities of specified file.

**Examples:**
1. Set capability `cap_net_raw` (to use RAW and PACKET sockets) for a given file:
   `setcap 'cap_net_raw' {{path/to/file}}`
2. Set multiple capabilities on a file (`ep` behind the capability means "effective permitted"):
   `setcap '{{cap_dac_read_search,cap_sys_tty_config+ep}}' {{path/to/file}}`
3. Remove all capabilities from a file:
   `setcap -r {{path/to/file}}`
4. Verify that the specified capabilities are currently associated with the specified file:
   `setcap -v '{{cap_net_raw}}' {{path/to/file}}`
5. The optional `-n root_uid` argument can be used to set the file capability for use only in a user namespace with this root user ID owner:
   `setcap -n {{root_uid}} '{{cap_net_admin}}' {{path/to/file}}`
setenforce:
**`setenforce`**: Toggle SELinux between enforcing and permissive modes.

**Examples:**
1. Put SELinux in enforcing mode:
   `setenforce {{1|Enforcing}}`
2. Put SELinux in permissive mode:
   `setenforce {{0|Permissive}}`
setfacl:
**`setfacl`**: Set file access control lists (ACL).

**Examples:**
1. Modify ACL of a file for user with read and write access:
   `setfacl {{[-m|--modify]}} u:{{username}}:rw {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
2. Modify default ACL of a file for all users:
   `setfacl {{[-d|--default]}} {{[-m|--modify]}} u::rw {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
3. Remove ACL of a file for a user:
   `setfacl {{[-x|--remove]}} u:{{username}} {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
4. Remove all ACL entries of a file:
   `setfacl {{[-b|--remove-all]}} {{path/to/file_or_directory}}`
setfattr:
**`setfattr`**: Set extended file attributes.

**Examples:**
1. Set name of attribute for file:
   `setfattr {{[-n|--name]}} user.{{attribute_name}} {{path/to/file}}`
2. Set a user-defined value of an extended attribute on a file:
   `setfattr {{[-n|--name]}} user.{{attribute_name}} {{[-v|--value]}} "{{value}}" {{path/to/file}}`
3. Remove a specific attribute of a file:
   `setfattr {{[-x|--remove]}} user.{{attribute_name}} {{path/to/file}}`
setfiles:
**`setfiles`**: Set SELinux file security contexts based on policy rules.

**Examples:**
1. Set file contexts according to the default policy file:
   `sudo setfiles /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts {{path/to/directory}}`
2. Set file contexts recursively and show changes:
   `sudo setfiles /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts {{path/to/directory}} {{[-v|--verbose]}}`
3. Preview what would be changed without actually modifying contexts:
   `sudo setfiles /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts {{path/to/directory}} {{[-n|--nochange]}}`
4. Set file contexts and verify them:
   `sudo setfiles /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts {{path/to/directory}} {{[-v|--verbose]}} {{[-F|--force]}}`
5. Use a specific root path for context matching:
   `sudo setfiles /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts {{path/to/new_directory}} {{[-r|--rootpath]}} {{path/to/old_directory}}`
setfont:
**`setfont`**: Set the terminal font for TTYs.

**Examples:**
1. Change the terminal font:
   `setfont {{font}}.gz`
2. Change the terminal font by specifying a path:
   `setfont /usr/share/kbd/{{mapping}}/{{font.ext}}`
3. Double font size:
   `setfont {{[-d|--double]}}`
4. Reset to the default font:
   `setfont`
setsebool:
**`setsebool`**: Set SELinux boolean value.

**Examples:**
1. Show the current setting of [a]ll booleans:
   `getsebool -a`
2. Set or unset a boolean temporarily (non-persistent across reboot):
   `sudo setsebool {{httpd_can_network_connect}} {{1|true|on|0|false|off}}`
3. Set or unset a boolean [P]ersistently:
   `sudo setsebool -P {{container_use_devices}} {{1|true|on|0|false|off}}`
4. Set or unset multiple booleans at once [P]ersistently:
   `sudo setsebool -P {{key1 1 key2 0 ...}}`
5. Set or unset a boolean persistently (alternative method using `semanage-boolean`):
   `sudo semanage boolean {{[-m|--modify]}} {{-1|--on|-0|--off}} {{haproxy_connect_any}}`
setserial:
**`setserial`**: Read and modify serial port information.

**Examples:**
1. Print all information about a specific serial device:
   `setserial -a {{/dev/cuaN}}`
2. Print the configuration summary of a specific serial device (useful for printing during bootup process):
   `setserial -b {{device}}`
3. Set a specific configuration parameter to a device:
   `sudo setserial {{device}} {{parameter}}`
4. Print the configuration of a list of devices:
   `setserial -g {{device1 device2 ...}}`
setsid:
**`setsid`**: Run a program in a new session if the calling process is not a process group leader.

**Examples:**
1. Run a program in a new session:
   `setsid {{program}}`
2. Run a program in a new session discarding the resulting output and error:
   `setsid {{program}} > /dev/null 2>&1`
3. Run a program creating a new process:
   `setsid {{[-f|--fork]}} {{program}}`
4. Return the exit code of a program as the exit code of setsid when the program exits:
   `setsid {{[-w|--wait]}} {{program}}`
5. Run a program in a new session setting the current terminal as the controlling terminal:
   `setsid {{[-c|--ctty]}} {{program}}`
setup-alpine:
**`setup-alpine`**: Install Alpine Linux.

**Examples:**
1. Run the full setup:
   `setup-alpine`
2. Use default configurations:
   `setup-alpine -q`
setxkbmap:
**`setxkbmap`**: Set the keyboard using the X Keyboard Extension.

**Examples:**
1. Set the keyboard in French AZERTY:
   `setxkbmap {{fr}}`
2. Set multiple keyboard layouts, their variants and switching option:
   `setxkbmap -layout {{us,de}} -variant {{,qwerty}} -option '{{grp:alt_caps_toggle}}'`
3. List all layouts:
   `localectl list-x11-keymap-layouts`
4. List variants for the layout:
   `localectl list-x11-keymap-variants {{de}}`
5. List available switching options:
   `localectl list-x11-keymap-options | grep grp:`
6. Display help:
   `setxkbmap -help`
sfdisk:
**`sfdisk`**: Display or manipulate a disk partition table.

**Examples:**
1. Back up the partition layout to a file:
   `sudo sfdisk {{[-d|--dump]}} {{/dev/sdX}} > {{path/to/file.dump}}`
2. Restore a partition layout:
   `sudo sfdisk < {{path/to/file.dump}} {{/dev/sdX}}`
3. Set the type of a partition:
   `sudo sfdisk --part-type {{/dev/sdX}} {{partition_number}} {{swap}}`
4. Delete a partition:
   `sudo sfdisk --delete {{/dev/sdX}} {{partition_number}}`
5. Display help:
   `sfdisk {{[-h|--help]}}`
sfill:
**`sfill`**: Securely overwrite the free space and inodes of the partition where the specified directory resides.

**Examples:**
1. Overwrite free space and inodes of a disk with 38 writes (slow but secure):
   `sfill /{{path/to/mounted_disk_directory}}`
2. Overwrite free space and inodes of a disk with 6 writes (fast but [l]ess secure) and show status ([v]erbose):
   `sfill -l -v /{{path/to/mounted_disk_directory}}`
3. Overwrite free space and inodes of a disk with 1 write (very fast but [l]ess secure [v]erbose) and show status:
   `sfill -ll -v /{{path/to/mounted_disk_directory}}`
4. Overwrite only free space of a d[I]sk:
   `sfill -I /{{path/to/mounted_disk_directory}}`
5. Overwrite only free [i]nodes of a disk:
   `sfill -i /{{path/to/mounted_disk_directory}}`
sh5util:
**`sh5util`**: Merge HDF5 files produced by the `sacct_gather_profile` plugin.

**Examples:**
1. Merge HDF5 files produced on each allocated node for the specified job or step:
   `sh5util {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{job_id|job_id.step_id}}`
2. Extract one or more data series from a merged job file:
   `sh5util {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{job_id|job_id.step_id}} {{[-E|--extract]}} {{[-i|--input]}} {{path/to/file.h5}} {{[-s|--series]}} {{Energy|Filesystem|Network|Task}}`
3. Extract one data item from all nodes in a merged job file:
   `sh5util {{[-j|--jobs]}} {{job_id|job_id.step_id}} {{[-I|--item-extract]}} {{[-s|--series]}} {{Energy|Filesystem|Network|Task}} {{[-d|--data]}} {{data_item}}`
shiny-mirrors:
**`shiny-mirrors`**: Generate a `pacman` mirror list for Manjaro Linux.

**Examples:**
1. Get the status of the current mirrors:
   `shiny-mirrors status`
2. Generate a mirror list using the default behavior:
   `sudo shiny-mirrors refresh`
3. Display the current configuration file:
   `shiny-mirrors config show`
4. Switch to a different branch interactively:
   `sudo shiny-mirrors config --branch`
shnsplit:
**`shnsplit`**: Splits audio files according to a `.cue` file.

**Examples:**
1. Split a `.wav` + `.cue` file into multiple files:
   `shnsplit -f {{path/to/file.cue}} {{path/to/file.wav}}`
2. Show supported formats:
   `shnsplit -a`
3. Split a `.flac` file into multiple files:
   `shnsplit -f {{path/to/file.cue}} -o flac {{path/to/file.flac}}`
4. Split a `.wav` file into files of the form "track-number - album - title":
   `shnsplit -f {{path/to/file.cue}} {{path/to/file.wav}} -t "%n - %a - %t"`
shntool-split:
**`shntool-split`**: This command is an alias of `shnsplit`.

**Examples:**
1. View documentation for the original command:
   `tldr shnsplit`
showkey:
**`showkey`**: Display the keycode of pressed keys on the keyboard, helpful for debugging keyboard-related issues and key remapping.

**Examples:**
1. View keycodes in decimal:
   `sudo showkey`
2. Display scancodes in hexadecimal:
   `sudo showkey {{[-s|--scancodes]}}`
3. Display keycodes in decimal (default):
   `sudo showkey {{[-k|--keycodes]}}`
4. Display keycodes in ASCII, decimal, and hexadecimal:
   `sudo showkey {{[-a|--ascii]}}`
5. Exit the program:
   `<Ctrl d>`
shutdown:
**`shutdown`**: Shutdown and reboot the system.

**Examples:**
1. Power off ([h]alt) immediately:
   `shutdown -h now`
2. Reboot immediately:
   `shutdown {{[-r|--reboot]}} now`
3. Reboot in 5 minutes:
   `shutdown {{[-r|--reboot]}} +5 &`
4. Shutdown at 1:00 pm (Uses 24h clock):
   `shutdown -h 13:00`
5. [c]ancel a pending shutdown/reboot operation:
   `shutdown -c`
sic:
**`sic`**: Simple IRC client.

**Examples:**
1. Connect to the default host (irc.ofct.net) with the nickname set in the `$USER` environment variable:
   `sic`
2. Connect to a given host, using a given nickname:
   `sic -h {{host}} -n {{nickname}}`
3. Connect to a given host, using a given nickname and password:
   `sic -h {{host}} -n {{nickname}} -k {{password}}`
4. Join a channel:
   `:j #{{channel}}<Enter>`
5. Send a message to a channel or user:
   `:m #{{channel|user}}<Enter>`
6. Set default channel or user:
   `:s #{{channel|user}}<Enter>`
silentcast:
**`silentcast`**: Silent screencast creator. Saves in `.mkv` and animated GIF formats.

**Examples:**
1. Launch silentcast:
   `silentcast`
2. Launch silentcast on a specific display:
   `silentcast --display={{display}}`
sinfo:
**`sinfo`**: View information about Slurm nodes and partitions.

**Examples:**
1. Show a quick summary overview of the cluster:
   `sinfo {{[-s|--summarize]}}`
2. View the detailed status of all partitions across the entire cluster:
   `sinfo`
3. View the detailed status of a specific partition:
   `sinfo {{[-p|--partition]}} {{partition_name}}`
4. View information about idle nodes:
   `sinfo {{[-t|--states]}} {{idle}}`
5. Summarise dead nodes:
   `sinfo {{[-d|--dead]}}`
6. List dead nodes and the reasons why:
   `sinfo {{[-R|--list-reasons]}}`
size:
**`size`**: Display the sizes of sections inside binary files.

**Examples:**
1. Display the size of sections in a given object or executable file:
   `size {{path/to/file}}`
2. Display the size of sections in a given object or executable file in [o]ctal:
   `size {{[-o|--radix=8]}} {{path/to/file}}`
3. Display the size of sections in a given object or executable file in [d]ecimal:
   `size {{[-d|--radix=10]}} {{path/to/file}}`
4. Display the size of sections in a given object or executable file in he[x]adecimal:
   `size {{[-x|--radix=16]}} {{path/to/file}}`
slabtop:
**`slabtop`**: Display kernel slab cache information in real time.

**Examples:**
1. Start `slabtop`:
   `sudo slabtop`
2. Sort by [c]ache size:
   `sudo slabtop {{[-s|--sort]}} c`
3. Sort by number of [o]bjects:
   `sudo slabtop {{[-s|--sort]}} o`
4. Sort by object [s]ize:
   `sudo slabtop {{[-s|--sort]}} s`
5. Display once and then exit:
   `sudo slabtop {{[-o|--once]}}`
6. Display help:
   `slabtop {{[-h|--help]}}`
slapt-get:
**`slapt-get`**: An `apt` like system for Slackware package management.

**Examples:**
1. Update the list of available packages and versions:
   `slapt-get --update`
2. Install a package, or update it to the latest available version:
   `slapt-get --install {{package}}`
3. Remove a package:
   `slapt-get --remove {{package}}`
4. Upgrade all installed packages to their latest available versions:
   `slapt-get --upgrade`
5. Locate packages by the package name, disk set, or version:
   `slapt-get --search {{query}}`
6. Show information about a package:
   `slapt-get --show {{package}}`
slapt-src:
**`slapt-src`**: A utility to automate building of slackbuilds.

**Examples:**
1. Update the list of available slackbuilds and versions:
   `slapt-src {{[-u|--update]}}`
2. List all available slackbuilds:
   `slapt-src {{[-l|--list]}}`
3. Fetch, build, and install the specified slackbuild(s):
   `slapt-src {{[-i|--install]}} {{slackbuild_name}}`
4. Locate slackbuilds by their name or description:
   `slapt-src {{[-s|--search]}} {{search_term}}`
5. Display information about a slackbuild:
   `slapt-src {{[-w|--show]}} {{slackbuild_name}}`
slop:
**`slop`**: Get a selection of the screen.

**Examples:**
1. Wait for the user to make a selection and output its geometry to `stdout`:
   `slop`
2. Double click, rather than click and drag, to draw a selection:
   `slop {{[-D|--nodrag]}}`
3. Highlight the selection rather than outlining it:
   `slop {{[-l|--highlight]}}`
4. Specify the output format:
   `slop {{[-f|--format]}} {{format_string}}`
5. Specify the selection rectangle's color:
   `slop {{[-c|--color]}} {{red}},{{green}},{{blue}},{{alpha}}`
slurmctld:
**`slurmctld`**: Monitor all other Slurm daemons and resources, accept work (jobs), and allocate resources to those jobs.

**Examples:**
1. Clear all previous `slurmctld` states from its last checkpoint:
   `slurmctld -c`
2. Set the daemon's nice value to the specified value, typically a negative number:
   `slurmctld -n {{value}}`
3. Write log messages to the specified file:
   `slurmctld -L {{path/to/output_file}}`
4. Display help:
   `slurmctld -h`
5. Display version:
   `slurmctld -V`
slurmd:
**`slurmd`**: Monitors all tasks running on the compute node, accepts tasks, launches tasks, and kills running tasks upon request.

**Examples:**
1. Report node rebooted when daemon restarted (Used for testing purposes):
   `slurmd -b`
2. Run the daemon with the given nodename:
   `slurmd -N {{nodename}}`
3. Write log messages to the specified file:
   `slurmd -L {{path/to/output_file}}`
4. Read configuration from the specified file:
   `slurmd -f {{path/to/file}}`
5. Display help:
   `slurmd -h`
slurmdbd:
**`slurmdbd`**: A secure enterprise-wide interface to a database for Slurm.

**Examples:**
1. Set the daemon's nice value to the specified value, typically a negative number:
   `slurmdbd -n {{value}}`
2. Change the working directory of `slurmdbd` to the LogFile path or to `/var/tmp`:
   `slurmdbd -s`
3. Display help:
   `slurmdbd -h`
4. Display version:
   `slurmdbd -V`
slurmrestd:
**`slurmrestd`**: Interface to Slurm via REST API.

**Examples:**
1. Change the [g]roup ID (and drop supplemental groups) before processing client requests:
   `slurmrestd -g {{group_id}} {{[host]:port|unix:/path/to/socket}}`
2. Comma-delimited list of [a]uthentication plugins to load:
   `slurmrestd -a {{authentication_plugins}} {{[host]:port|unix:/path/to/socket}}`
3. Read Slurm configuration from the specified [f]ile:
   `slurmrestd -f {{path/to/file}}`
4. Change [u]ser ID before processing client request:
   `slurmrestd -u {{user_id}}`
5. Display [h]elp:
   `slurmrestd -h`
6. Display [V]ersion:
   `slurmrestd -V`
slurmstepd:
**`slurmstepd`**: Slurm daemon for managing and monitoring individual job steps within a multi-step job.

**Examples:**
1. Start the daemon:
   `slurmstepd`
slurp:
**`slurp`**: Select a region in a Wayland compositor.

**Examples:**
1. Select a region and print it to `stdout`:
   `slurp`
2. Select a region and print it to `stdout`, while displaying the dimensions of the selection:
   `slurp -d`
3. Select a single point instead of a region:
   `slurp -p`

   `slurp -o -f '%o'`

sm:
**`sm`**: Display a short message fullscreen.

**Examples:**
1. Display a message in full-screen:
   `sm "{{Hello World!}}"`
2. Display a message with inverted colors:
   `sm {{[-i|--invert]}} "{{Hello World!}}"`
3. Display a message with a custom foreground color:
   `sm {{[-f|--foreground]}} {{blue}} "{{Hello World!}}"`

   `sm {{[-b|--background]}} {{#008888}} "{{Hello World!}}"`

   `sm {{[-r|--rotate]}} {{3}} "{{Hello World!}}"`

smbcacls:
**`smbcacls`**: View and manipulate Windows ACLs on SMB shares.

   `smbcacls //{{server}}/{{share}} {{path/to/file}} --user {{username}} --workgroup {{workgroup}}`
smbget:
**`smbget`**: `wget`-like utility for downloading files from SMB servers.

   `smbget {{smb://server/share/file}}`
2. Download a share or directory recursively:

smbnetfs:

1. Make shares available at `mountpoint`:

smbpasswd:

   `smbpasswd`

   `sudo smbpasswd {{username}}`
4. Delete a Samba user (use `pdbedit` instead if the Unix account has been deleted):
   `sudo smbpasswd -x {{username}}`
smem:
**`smem`**: Print memory usage for programs.

**Examples:**
1. Print memory usage for current processes:
   `smem`
2. Print memory usage for current processes for every user on a system:
   `smem --users`
3. Print memory usage for current processes for a specified user:
   `smem --userfilter {{username}}`
4. Print system memory information:

snake4:
**`snake4`**: Snake game in the terminal.

1. Start a snake game:
   `snake4`

   `{{<1>|<2>|<3>|<4>|<5>}}`

   `sudo systemctl start stratisd`
2. Create a storage pool from one or more devices:
   `sudo stratis pool create {{pool_name}} {{/dev/sdX /dev/sdY ...}}`
3. Create a filesystem (volume) in a pool:
   `sudo stratis filesystem create {{pool_name}} {{volume_name}}`
4. List all Stratis filesystems:
   `sudo stratis filesystem list`
5. Format and mount a Stratis volume manually:
   `sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/stratis/{{pool_name}}/{{volume_name}} && sudo mount /dev/stratis/{{pool_name}}/{{volume_name}} {{/mnt/target}}`
6. Add a volume to `/etc/fstab` for mounting at boot:
   `echo /dev/stratis/{{pool_name}}/{{volume_name}} {{/mnt/target}} xfs defaults,x-systemd.requires=stratisd.service 0 0 | sudo tee {{[-a|--append]}} /etc/fstab`
7. Extend an existing pool by adding a new device:
   `sudo stratis pool add-data {{pool_name}} {{/dev/sdZ}}`
8. Delete a volume:
   `sudo stratis filesystem destroy {{pool_name}} {{volume_name}}`
stress:
**`stress`**: Stress test CPU, memory, and IO on a Linux system.

**Examples:**
1. Spawn 4 workers to stress test CPU:
   `stress {{[-c|--cpu]}} {{4}}`
2. Spawn 2 workers to stress test IO and timeout after 5 seconds:
   `stress {{[-i|--io]}} {{2}} {{[-t|--timeout]}} {{5}}`
3. Spawn 2 workers to stress test memory (each worker allocates 256M bytes):
   `stress {{[-m|--vm]}} {{2}} --vm-bytes {{256M}}`
4. Spawn 2 workers spinning on write()/unlink() (each worker writes 1G bytes):
   `stress {{[-d|--hdd]}} {{2}} --hdd-bytes {{1GB}}`
strigger:
**`strigger`**: View or modify Slurm trigger information.

**Examples:**
1. Register a new trigger. Execute the specified program when the specified event occurs:
   `strigger --set --{{primary_database_failure|primary_slurmdbd_failure|primary_slurmctld_acct_buffer_full|primary_slurmctld_failure|...}} {{[-p|--program]}} {{path/to/executable}}`
2. Execute the specified program when the specified job terminated:
   `strigger --set {{[-j|--jobid]}} {{job_id}} {{[-f|--fini]}} {{[-p|--program]}} "{{path/to/executable}} {{argument1 argument2 ...}}"`
3. View active triggers:
   `strigger --get`
4. View active triggers regarding the specified job:
   `strigger --get {{[-j|--jobid]}} {{job_id}}`
5. Clear the specified trigger:
   `strigger --clear {{trigger_id}}`
strip:
**`strip`**: Discard symbols from executables or object files.

**Examples:**
1. Replace the input file with its stripped version:
   `strip {{path/to/file}}`
2. Strip symbols from a file, saving the output to a specific file:
   `strip {{path/to/input_file}} -o {{path/to/output_file}}`
3. Strip debug symbols only:
   `strip {{[-d|--strip-debug]}} {{path/to/file.o}}`
su:
**`su`**: Switch shell to another user.

**Examples:**
1. Switch to superuser (requires the root password):
   `su`
2. Switch to a given user (requires the user's password):
   `su {{username}}`
3. Switch to a given user and simulate a full login shell:
   `su - {{username}}`

7. Display version:
   `su {{[-V|--version]}}`
sulogin:
**`sulogin`**: Log in as root during single-user mode.

**Examples:**
1. Start `sulogin` on the default console:
   `sudo sulogin`
2. Start `sulogin` on a specific TTY device:
   `sudo sulogin {{/dev/ttyX}}`
3. Set a maximum timeout(in seconds) for entering the root password before continuing normal boot:
   `sudo sulogin {{[-t|--timeout]}} {{timeout}}`
4. Start root's shell as a login shell:
   `sudo sulogin {{[-p|--login-shell]}}`
5. Force a root shell without asking for a password when default methods of obtaining the password fail:
   `sudo sulogin {{[-e|--force]}}`
sview:
**`sview`**: Start a GUI to view and modify the state of Slurm.

**Examples:**
1. Start a GUI to view and modify the state of Slurm:
   `sview`
swaks:
**`swaks`**: Swiss Army Knife SMTP, the all-purpose SMTP transaction tester.

**Examples:**
1. Deliver a standard test email to `user@example.com` on port 25 of `test-server.example.net`:
   `swaks {{[-t|--to]}} {{user@example.com}} {{[-s|--server]}} {{test-server.example.net}}`
2. Deliver a standard test email, requiring CRAM-MD5 authentication as user `me@example.com`. An "X-Test" header will be added to the email body:
   `swaks {{[-t|--to]}} {{user@example.com}} {{[-f|--from]}} {{me@example.com}} {{[-a|--auth]}} {{CRAM-MD5}} {{[-au|--auth-user]}} {{me@example.com}} --header-X-Test "{{test_email}}"`
3. Test a virus scanner using EICAR in an attachment. Don't show the message DATA part:
   `swaks {{[-t|--to]}} {{user@example.com}} --attach - {{[-s|--server]}} {{test-server.example.com}} {{[-n|--suppress-data]}} {{path/to/eicar.txt}}`
4. Test a spam scanner using GTUBE in the body of an email, routed via the MX records for `example.com`:
   `swaks {{[-t|--to]}} {{user@example.com}} --body {{path/to/gtube_file}}`
5. Deliver a standard test email to `user@example.com` using the LMTP protocol via a UNIX domain socket file:
   `swaks {{[-t|--to]}} {{user@example.com}} --socket {{/var/lda.sock}} --protocol {{LMTP}}`
swaplabel:
**`swaplabel`**: Print or change the label or UUID of a swap area.

**Examples:**
1. Display the current label and UUID of a swap area:
   `swaplabel {{path/to/file}}`

swapoff:
**`swapoff`**: Disable devices and files for swapping.

1. Disable a given swap area:

2. Disable all swap areas in `/proc/swaps`:

swapon:

switch_root:
**`switch_root`**: Use a different filesystem as the root of the mount tree.

swupd:

swww:

sxiv:

synopkg:
**`synopkg`**: Package management utility for Synology DiskStation Manager.

synoupgrade:

sysctl:

sysdig:

systemctl-add-requires:
**`systemctl-add-requires`**: Add `Requires` dependencies to a target for one or more units.

systemctl-add-wants:

systemctl-bind:

systemctl-cancel:

systemctl-condrestart:

systemctl-condstop:

systemctl-daemon-reload:

systemctl-default:

systemctl-edit:

systemctl-halt:

systemctl-hibernate:

systemctl-import-environment:

2. Import multiple variables:

systemctl-is-active:

systemctl-is-enabled:

systemctl-is-system-running:

systemctl-kexec:

systemctl-list-automounts:

systemctl-list-jobs:
